body: ## First Part · Zarathustra’s Prologue

When Zarathustra was thirty years old, he left his home and the lake of his home and went into the mountains. There he enjoyed his spirit and his solitude, and for ten years did not tire of it. But at last his heart changed, and one morning he rose with the dawn, stepped before the sun, and spoke to it thus:
“You great star! What would your happiness be, if you did not have those for whom you shine?
“For ten years you have come up here to my cave: you would have grown weary of your light and of this road, without me, my eagle and my serpent.
“But we waited for you every morning, took your overflow from you, and blessed you for it.
“Look! I am weary of my wisdom, like a bee that has gathered too much honey. I need hands held out to take it.
“I want to give it away and share it out, until the wise among men are glad once more of their folly, and the poor once more of their riches.
“For that I must go down into the depths: as you do in the evening, when you go behind the sea and bring light even to the underworld, you overflowing star!
“Like you, I must *go under*, as men call it, the men to whom I want to go down.
“So bless me, then, you calm eye that can look without envy even on too great a happiness!
“Bless the cup that wants to overflow, so that the water may flow golden from it and carry the reflection of your delight everywhere!
“Look! This cup wants to be empty again, and Zarathustra wants to be a man again.”
Thus began Zarathustra’s going-under.

Zarathustra went down the mountain alone, and no one met him. But when he came into the forest, there suddenly stood before him an old man, who had left his holy hut to look for roots in the forest. And the old man spoke thus to Zarathustra:

“This wanderer is no stranger to me: many years ago he passed this way. Zarathustra he was called; but he has changed. Then you carried your ashes up the mountain: will you now carry your fire into the valleys? Are you not afraid of the punishment for arsonists?
“Yes, I recognise Zarathustra. His eye is clear, and no disgust hides around his mouth. Does he not walk like a dancer?
“Zarathustra has changed; Zarathustra has become a child; Zarathustra is awake: what do you want now among the sleepers?
“You lived in solitude as in the sea, and the sea carried you. Alas, do you want to climb ashore? Alas, do you want to drag your own body again?”
Zarathustra answered: “I love mankind.”
“Why,” said the saint, “did I go into the forest and the wilderness? Was it not because I loved mankind far too much?
“Now I love God: mankind I do not love. Man is too imperfect a thing for me. Love of man would kill me.”
Zarathustra answered: “What did I say about love! I am bringing mankind a gift.”
“Give them nothing,” said the saint. “Rather take something from them, and carry it with them: that will do them most good, if only it does you good!
“And if you want to give to them, give no more than alms, and make them beg for that!”
“No,” answered Zarathustra, “I do not give alms. I am not poor enough for that.”
The saint laughed at Zarathustra and spoke thus: “Then see that they accept your treasures! They are suspicious of hermits and do not believe that we come to give.
“Our footsteps sound too lonely to them through the streets. And as when, at night in their beds, they hear a man walking long before sunrise, they probably ask themselves: where is the thief going?
“Do not go to men; stay in the forest! Better still, go to the animals! Why will you not be as I am: a bear among bears, a bird among birds?”
“And what does the saint do in the forest?” asked Zarathustra.
The saint answered: “I make songs and sing them; and when I make songs, I laugh, weep and hum: that is how I praise God.
“With singing, weeping, laughing and humming I praise the God who is my God. But what do you bring us as a gift?”

When Zarathustra had heard these words, he bowed to the saint and said: “What would I have to give you! But let me go quickly, so that I take nothing from you!” And so they parted from each other, the old man and the man, laughing as two boys laugh.
But when Zarathustra was alone, he said to his heart: “Could it be possible! This old saint in his forest has not yet heard that *God is dead*!”

When Zarathustra came into the nearest town, which lies on the edge of the forest, he found a great crowd of people gathered in the market place: for it had been announced that a tightrope walker would perform. And Zarathustra spoke thus to the people:
“I teach you the Overman. Man is something that shall be overcome. What have you done to overcome him?
“All beings so far have created something beyond themselves: and do you want to be the ebb of this great flood, and would you rather go back to the beasts than overcome man?
“What is the ape to man? A laughing-stock or a painful shame. And man shall be just that for the Overman: a laughing-stock or a painful shame.
“You have made your way from worm to man, and much in you is still worm. Once you were apes, and even now man is more ape than any ape.
“But even the wisest among you is only a discord and a cross between plant and ghost. But do I bid you become ghosts or plants?
“Look, I teach you the Overman!
“The Overman is the meaning of the earth. Let your will say: the Overman *shall be* the meaning of the earth!
“I beg you, my brothers, *stay faithful to the earth*, and do not believe those who speak to you of hopes beyond this world! They are poisoners, whether they know it or not.
“They are despisers of life, dying and poisoned themselves, of whom the earth is weary: so let them go!

“Once, sin against God was the greatest sin; but God died, and these sinners died with him. To sin against the earth is now the most terrible thing, and to honour the entrails of the unknowable more highly than the meaning of the earth!
“Once the soul looked with contempt on the body, and then this contempt was the highest thing: it wanted the body thin, hideous and starved. So it thought to escape the body and the earth.
“Oh, this soul was itself thin, hideous and starved: and cruelty was the delight of this soul!
“But you too, my brothers, tell me: what does your body say about your soul? Is your soul not poverty and filth and a wretched contentment?
“Truly, man is a polluted stream. One must be a sea to take in a polluted stream without becoming unclean.
“Look, I teach you the Overman: he is this sea; in him your great contempt can go under.
“What is the greatest thing you can experience? It is the hour of the great contempt. The hour in which even your happiness disgusts you, and so do your reason and your virtue.
“The hour when you say: ‘What does my happiness matter! It is poverty and filth and a wretched contentment. But my happiness ought to justify existence itself!’
“The hour when you say: ‘What does my reason matter! Does it long for knowledge as the lion for its food? It is poverty and filth and a wretched contentment!’
“The hour when you say: ‘What does my virtue matter! It has not yet made me rage. How weary I am of my good and my evil! It is all poverty and filth and a wretched contentment!’
“The hour when you say: ‘What does my justice matter! I do not see that I am fire and coal. But the just man is fire and coal!’
“The hour when you say: ‘What does my pity matter! Is not pity the cross on which he is nailed who loves mankind? But my pity is no crucifixion.’
“Have you ever spoken like this? Have you ever cried out like this? Ah, if only I had heard you cry out like this!
“Not your sin: your moderation cries out to heaven; your very meanness in your sinning cries out to heaven!
“Where is the lightning that would lick you with its tongue? Where is the madness with which you should be inoculated?
“Look, I teach you the Overman: he is this lightning, he is this madness!”

When Zarathustra had spoken thus, one of the people cried out: “We have heard enough about the tightrope walker; now let us see him too!” And all the people laughed at Zarathustra. But the tightrope walker, who thought the words were meant for him, began his performance.
But Zarathustra looked at the people and wondered. Then he spoke thus:
“Man is a rope, tied between beast and Overman: a rope over an abyss.
“A dangerous crossing, a dangerous on-the-way, a dangerous looking-back, a dangerous shuddering and standing still.
“What is great in man is that he is a bridge and not a goal: what can be loved in man is that he is a *going-over* and a *going-under*.
“I love those who do not know how to live except as those who go under, for they are those who go over.
“I love the great despisers, because they are the great reverers, and arrows of longing for the other shore.
“I love those who do not first look behind the stars for a reason to go under and be sacrificed, but who sacrifice themselves to the earth, so that the earth may one day belong to the Overman.
“I love him who lives in order to know, and who wants to know so that the Overman may one day live. And so he wills his own going-under.
“I love him who works and invents so as to build the house for the Overman and to prepare earth, animal and plant for him: for so he wills his own going-under.
“I love him who loves his virtue: for virtue is the will to go under, and an arrow of longing.
“I love him who keeps back not one drop of spirit for himself, but wants to be wholly the spirit of his virtue: so he strides as spirit over the bridge.
“I love him who makes of his virtue his inclination and his destiny: so for his virtue’s sake he wants to live on, and to live no longer.
“I love him who does not want to have too many virtues. One virtue is more virtue than two, because it is more of a knot for destiny to hang on.
“I love him whose soul squanders itself, who wants no thanks and gives nothing back: for he always gives and does not want to keep himself.
“I love him who is ashamed when the dice fall in his favour, and who then asks: am I a cheat? For he wants to perish.
“I love him who throws golden words ahead of his deeds and always does more than he promises: for he wills his own going-under.
“I love him who justifies the people of the future and redeems the people of the past: for he wants to perish of the people of the present.
“I love him who chastises his God because he loves his God: for he must perish of his God’s wrath.
“I love him whose soul is deep even in its wounds, and who can perish of a small experience: so he gladly goes over the bridge.
“I love him whose soul is so overfull that he forgets himself, and all things are in him: so all things become his going-under.
“I love him who has a free spirit and a free heart: so his head is only the entrails of his heart, but his heart drives him to go under.
“I love all those who are like heavy drops falling one by one from the dark cloud that hangs over mankind: they announce that the lightning is coming, and they perish as heralds.
“Look, I am a herald of the lightning and a heavy drop from the cloud: but this lightning is called Overman.”

When Zarathustra had spoken these words, he looked at the people again and was silent. “There they stand,” he said to his heart; “there they laugh: they do not understand me; I am not the mouth for these ears.
“Must one first smash their ears, so that they learn to hear with their eyes? Must one rattle like kettledrums and preachers of repentance? Or do they believe only those who stammer?
“They have something they are proud of. What do they call it, this thing that makes them proud? They call it education; it sets them apart from goatherds.
“That is why they do not like to hear the word ‘contempt’ about themselves. So I will speak to their pride.
“So I will speak to them of the most contemptible thing: and that is the *last man*.”
And Zarathustra spoke thus to the people:
“It is time for man to set himself a goal. It is time for man to plant the seed of his highest hope.
“His soil is still rich enough for it. But one day this soil will be poor and tame, and no tall tree will be able to grow from it any more.
“Alas! The time is coming when man will no longer shoot the arrow of his longing beyond man, and the string of his bow will have forgotten how to whir!
“I tell you: one must still have chaos in oneself to give birth to a dancing star. I tell you: you still have chaos in you.
“Alas! The time is coming when man will give birth to no more stars. Alas! The time of the most contemptible man is coming, the man who can no longer despise himself.
“Look! I show you the *last man*.
“‘What is love? What is creation? What is longing? What is a star?’ So asks the last man, and blinks.
“The earth has become small then, and on it hops the last man, who makes everything small. His kind is as hard to wipe out as the flea-beetle; the last man lives longest.
“‘We have invented happiness,’ say the last men, and blink.
“They have left the places where it was hard to live: for one needs warmth. One still loves one’s neighbour and rubs against him: for one needs warmth.
“To fall ill and to be mistrustful seem sinful to them: one walks carefully. A fool, whoever still stumbles over stones or people!
“A little poison now and then: that makes for pleasant dreams. And much poison at the end, for a pleasant death.
“One still works, for work is entertainment. But one takes care that the entertainment does not tire one.
“One no longer becomes poor or rich: both are too much trouble. Who still wants to rule? Who still wants to obey? Both are too much trouble.
“No shepherd and one herd! Everyone wants the same thing; everyone is the same: whoever feels differently goes voluntarily into the madhouse.
“‘Formerly the whole world was mad,’ say the most refined, and blink.
“One is clever and knows everything that has happened: so there is no end to the mockery. One still quarrels, but one soon makes up: otherwise it upsets the stomach.
“One has one’s little pleasure for the day and one’s little pleasure for the night: but one honours health.
“‘We have invented happiness,’ say the last men, and blink.”

And here ended the first speech of Zarathustra, which is also called “the Prologue”: for at this point he was interrupted by the shouting and delight of the crowd. “Give us this last man, O Zarathustra,” they cried, “make us into these last men! Then we will make you a present of the Overman!” And all the people cheered and clicked their tongues. But Zarathustra grew sad and said to his heart:
“They do not understand me: I am not the mouth for these ears.
“I have lived too long in the mountains, it seems; I have listened too much to brooks and trees: now I speak to them as to goatherds.
“My soul is unmoved and bright as the mountains in the morning. But they think I am cold, and a mocker with terrible jokes.
“And now they look at me and laugh: and while they laugh, they hate me too. There is ice in their laughter.”

But then something happened that struck every mouth dumb and made every eye stare. For meanwhile the tightrope walker had begun his performance: he had stepped out of a little door and was walking along the rope, which was stretched between two towers so that it hung over the market place and the people. Just as he was in the middle of his way, the little door opened once more, and a fellow in motley, like a clown, sprang out and went with quick steps after the first. “Forward, lame-foot,” cried his terrible voice, “forward, sluggard, smuggler, pale-face! Or I’ll tickle you with my heel! What are you doing here between the towers? In the tower is where you belong; you should be locked up; you are blocking the way for one better than you!” And with every word he came nearer and nearer; but when he was only one step behind him, there happened the terrible thing that struck every mouth dumb and made every eye stare: he let out a yell like a devil and leapt over the man who stood in his way. But this man, seeing his rival triumph like this, lost his head and the rope; he threw away his pole, and, faster than the pole, like a whirl of arms and legs, he plunged into the depths. The market place and the people were like the sea when a storm drives into it: everyone fled apart and over one another, and most of all where the body was bound to come down.

But Zarathustra stood still, and the body fell right beside him, badly mangled and broken, but not yet dead. After a while consciousness returned to the shattered man, and he saw Zarathustra kneeling beside him. “What are you doing there?” he said at last. “I knew long ago that the devil would trip me up. Now he is dragging me off to hell: will you stop him?”
“On my honour, friend,” answered Zarathustra, “all that you speak of does not exist: there is no devil and no hell. Your soul will be dead even sooner than your body: so fear nothing any more!”

The man looked up mistrustfully. “If you speak the truth,” he said then, “I lose nothing when I lose my life. I am not much more than an animal that has been taught to dance by blows and scraps of food.”
“Not so,” said Zarathustra. “You made danger your calling; there is nothing contemptible in that. Now you perish by your calling: for that I will bury you with my own hands.”
When Zarathustra had said this, the dying man answered no more; but he moved his hand, as if he were seeking Zarathustra’s hand to thank him.

Meanwhile evening came, and the market place hid itself in darkness: then the people dispersed, for even curiosity and terror grow tired. But Zarathustra sat on the ground beside the dead man, sunk in thought, and so he forgot the time. At last, though, night came, and a cold wind blew over the lonely man. Then Zarathustra rose and said to his heart:
“Truly, Zarathustra has had a fine catch today! He caught no man, but a corpse.
“Human existence is uncanny and still without meaning: a clown can become its fate.
“I want to teach men the meaning of their being: which is the Overman, the lightning from the dark cloud of man.
“But I am still far from them, and my meaning does not speak to their senses. To men I am still something between a fool and a corpse.
“Dark is the night, dark are Zarathustra’s ways. Come, cold and stiff companion! I will carry you to where I can bury you with my own hands.”

When Zarathustra had said this to his heart, he loaded the corpse on his back and set off. And he had not gone a hundred paces when a man crept up to him and whispered in his ear, and look! The one who spoke was the clown from the tower. “Leave this town, O Zarathustra,” he said; “too many people here hate you. The good and the just hate you, and call you their enemy and despiser; the believers of the true faith hate you, and call you a danger to the crowd. It was your luck that they laughed at you: and truly, you talked like a clown. It was your luck that you joined yourself to the dead dog; by humbling yourself like that, you saved yourself for today. But leave this town, or tomorrow I shall leap over you, a living man over a dead one.” And when he had said this, the man vanished; but Zarathustra went on through the dark streets.

At the town gate he met the gravediggers: they shone their torch in his face, recognised Zarathustra, and mocked him a great deal. “Zarathustra is carrying off the dead dog: fine, that Zarathustra has become a gravedigger! For our hands are too clean for this roast. Does Zarathustra want to steal the devil’s morsel from him? Well then! Good luck with your meal! As long as the devil is not a better thief than Zarathustra! He’ll steal them both, he’ll eat them both!” And they laughed together and put their heads together.

Zarathustra said not a word to this and went on his way. When he had walked for two hours, past forests and swamps, he had heard too much of the hungry howling of wolves, and he grew hungry himself. So he stopped at a lonely house in which a light was burning.
“Hunger falls upon me like a robber,” said Zarathustra. “In forests and swamps my hunger falls upon me, and in the deep of night.
“My hunger has strange moods. Often it comes to me only after a meal, and today it did not come all day: where can it have been?”
And with that Zarathustra knocked at the door of the house. An old man appeared; he carried the light and asked: “Who comes to me and to my bad sleep?”
“A living man and a dead one,” said Zarathustra. “Give me something to eat and drink; I forgot to during the day. He who feeds the hungry refreshes his own soul: so says wisdom.”

The old man went away, but came back at once and offered Zarathustra bread and wine. “This is a bad region for the hungry,” he said; “that is why I live here. Beast and man come to me, the hermit. But tell your companion to eat and drink too; he is more tired than you.” Zarathustra answered: “My companion is dead; I shall hardly persuade him.” “That is no business of mine,” said the old man sulkily; “whoever knocks at my door must take what I offer him. Eat, and fare you well!”

Then Zarathustra walked for another two hours, trusting to the road and the light of the stars: for he was used to walking at night and liked to look into the face of all that sleeps. But when the morning grew grey, Zarathustra found himself in a deep forest, and no path showed itself to him any more. Then he laid the dead man in a hollow tree at his head, for he wanted to protect him from the wolves, and laid himself down on the ground and the moss. And at once he fell asleep, tired in body but with an untroubled soul.

Zarathustra slept long, and not only the dawn passed over his face, but the morning too. But at last his eyes opened: in wonder Zarathustra looked into the forest and the stillness; in wonder he looked into himself. Then he rose quickly, like a sailor who suddenly sees land, and shouted for joy: for he saw a new truth. And he spoke thus to his heart:
“A light has dawned on me: I need companions, and living ones; not dead companions and corpses that I carry with me wherever I go.
“But living companions I need, who follow me because they want to follow themselves, and to go where I want to go.
“A light has dawned on me: let Zarathustra speak not to the people, but to companions! Zarathustra shall not become the shepherd and the dog of a herd!
“To lure many away from the herd: that is why I came. The people and the herd shall be angry with me: Zarathustra wants to be called a robber by the shepherds.
“Shepherds, I say; but they call themselves the good and the just. Shepherds, I say; but they call themselves the believers of the true faith.
“Look at the good and the just! Whom do they hate most? The one who breaks their tablets of values, the breaker, the lawbreaker: but he is the creator.
“Look at the believers of every faith! Whom do they hate most? The one who breaks their tablets of values, the breaker, the lawbreaker: but he is the creator.
“The creator seeks companions, not corpses, and not herds or believers either. The creator seeks fellow creators, those who write new values on new tablets.
“The creator seeks companions, and fellow harvesters: for everything with him stands ripe for harvest. But he lacks the hundred sickles: so he tears off the ears of corn and is angry.
“The creator seeks companions, and such as know how to whet their sickles. They will be called destroyers and despisers of good and evil. But they are the harvesters and the celebrants.
“Zarathustra seeks fellow creators, fellow harvesters and fellow celebrants: what has he to do with herds and shepherds and corpses!
“And you, my first companion, farewell! I buried you well in your hollow tree; I hid you well from the wolves.
“But I am leaving you; the time is up. Between dawn and dawn a new truth came to me.
“I am not to be a shepherd, nor a gravedigger. Never again will I speak to the people; for the last time I have spoken to a dead man.
“I will join the creators, the harvesters, the celebrants: I will show them the rainbow and all the steps to the Overman.
“I will sing my song to the hermits, alone and in pairs; and whoever still has ears for the unheard-of, I will make his heart heavy with my happiness.
“I want to reach my goal; I go my way; I shall leap over the hesitant and the dawdlers. So let my going be their going-under!”

Zarathustra had said this to his heart when the sun stood at noon: then he looked up questioningly, for above him he heard the sharp cry of a bird. And look! An eagle was sweeping through the air in wide circles, and on it hung a serpent, not like prey but like a friend: for she was coiled around his neck.
“They are my animals!” said Zarathustra, and rejoiced in his heart.
“The proudest animal under the sun and the wisest animal under the sun: they have gone out to scout.
“They want to find out whether Zarathustra is still alive. Truly, am I still alive?
“I found it more dangerous among men than among animals; dangerous are the ways Zarathustra goes. May my animals lead me!”
When Zarathustra had said this, he remembered the words of the saint in the forest, sighed, and spoke thus to his heart:
“Would that I were wiser! Would that I were wise from the ground up, like my serpent!
“But I am asking for the impossible: so I ask my pride instead always to go with my wisdom!
“And if one day my wisdom leaves me (ah, it loves to fly away!), may my pride then fly with my folly!”
Thus began Zarathustra’s going-under.
## Zarathustra’s Speeches · On the Three Metamorphoses
Three metamorphoses of the spirit I name for you: how the spirit becomes a camel, and the camel a lion, and the lion at last a child.
There is much that is heavy for the spirit, the strong, load-bearing spirit in which reverence dwells: its strength longs for the heavy, the heaviest.
What is heavy? So asks the load-bearing spirit; so it kneels down like the camel and wants to be well loaded.
What is the heaviest thing, you heroes? So asks the load-bearing spirit, that I may take it upon me and rejoice in my strength.
Is it not this: to humble oneself in order to wound one’s pride? To let one’s folly shine out in order to mock one’s wisdom?
Or is it this: to part from our cause when it celebrates its victory? To climb high mountains in order to tempt the tempter?
Or is it this: to feed on the acorns and grass of knowledge, and for the sake of truth to suffer hunger of the soul?
Or is it this: to be sick and send the comforters home, and make friends with the deaf, who never hear what you want?
Or is it this: to step into dirty water when it is the water of truth, and not to push away cold frogs and hot toads?
Or is it this: to love those who despise us, and to hold out our hand to the ghost when it wants to frighten us?
All these heaviest things the load-bearing spirit takes upon itself: like the camel that hurries laden into the desert, so it hurries into its desert.
But in the loneliest desert the second metamorphosis happens: here the spirit becomes a lion; it wants to seize freedom as its prey and be master in its own desert.
Here it seeks out its last master: it wants to be the enemy of him and of its last God; it wants to wrestle for victory with the great dragon.
What is the great dragon that the spirit no longer wants to call master and God? “Thou shalt” is the name of the great dragon. But the spirit of the lion says “I will”.
“Thou shalt” lies in its path, glittering with gold, a scaly beast, and on every scale shines in gold: “Thou shalt!”
Values a thousand years old glitter on these scales, and thus speaks the mightiest of all dragons: “All the value of things: it shines on me.
“All value has already been created, and all created value: that is I. Truly, there shall be no more ‘I will’!” Thus speaks the dragon.
My brothers, why is the lion needed in the spirit? Why is the beast of burden, which renounces and is reverent, not enough?
To create new values: even the lion cannot yet do that. But to create freedom for itself for new creating: that the might of the lion can do.
To create freedom for oneself, and a sacred No even to duty: for that, my brothers, the lion is needed.
To take for oneself the right to new values: that is the most terrible taking for a load-bearing and reverent spirit. Truly, to it this is robbery, the work of a beast of prey.
Once it loved “Thou shalt” as most sacred: now it must find illusion and caprice even in the most sacred, so that it may rob itself of freedom from its love: the lion is needed for this robbery.
But tell me, my brothers, what can the child do that even the lion could not? Why must the preying lion still become a child?
The child is innocence and forgetting, a new beginning, a game, a wheel rolling of itself, a first movement, a sacred Yes.
Yes, for the game of creating, my brothers, a sacred Yes is needed: the spirit now wills *its own* will; the one who was lost to the world now wins *its own* world.
Three metamorphoses of the spirit I have named for you: how the spirit became a camel, and the camel a lion, and the lion at last a child.
Thus spoke Zarathustra. And at that time he was staying in the town called the Motley Cow.
## On the Chairs of Virtue

People praised to Zarathustra a wise man who was said to speak well about sleep and virtue: he was greatly honoured and rewarded for it, and all the young men sat before his chair. To him Zarathustra went, and he sat with all the young men before his chair. And thus spoke the wise man:
“Honour and modesty before sleep! That is the first thing! And avoid all who sleep badly and lie awake at night!
“Even the thief is modest before sleep: he always steals softly through the night. But shameless is the night watchman; shamelessly he carries his horn.
“Sleeping is no small art: it takes staying awake all day for it.
“Ten times a day you must overcome yourself: that makes a good tiredness and is poppy for the soul.
“Ten times you must be reconciled with yourself again; for overcoming is bitterness, and the unreconciled sleep badly.
“Ten truths you must find in a day: otherwise you will still be seeking truth at night, and your soul will have stayed hungry.
“Ten times you must laugh in a day and be cheerful: otherwise your stomach, that father of gloom, will disturb you in the night.
“Few know it, but one must have all the virtues to sleep well. Shall I bear false witness? Shall I commit adultery?
“Shall I covet my neighbour’s maidservant? All that would go badly with good sleep.
“And even if one has all the virtues, one must understand one thing more: to send even the virtues to sleep at the right time.
“So that they do not quarrel with one another, the pretty little women! And over you, you wretch!
“Peace with God and your neighbour: so good sleep wills it. And peace even with your neighbour’s devil! Otherwise he will haunt you at night.
“Honour to the authorities, and obedience, even to crooked authorities! So good sleep wills it. Can I help it if power likes to walk on crooked legs?
“He shall always be the best shepherd for me who leads his sheep to the greenest meadow: that goes well with good sleep.
“I do not want many honours, nor great treasures: that inflames the spleen. But one sleeps badly without a good name and a little treasure.
“A little company is more welcome to me than bad company: but it must come and go at the right time. That goes well with good sleep.
“I am also very fond of the poor in spirit: they promote sleep. Blessed are they, especially if one always agrees with them.
“So the day passes for the virtuous. And when night comes, I take good care not to call sleep! Sleep, the master of the virtues, does not want to be called!
“Instead I think of what I have done and thought during the day. Chewing it over, I ask myself, patient as a cow: what were your ten overcomings?
“And what were the ten reconciliations, and the ten truths, and the ten laughs with which my heart enjoyed itself?
“Weighing such things and rocked by forty thoughts, suddenly sleep falls upon me, the uncalled, the master of the virtues.
“Sleep taps on my eyes: they grow heavy. Sleep touches my mouth: it stays open.
“Truly, on soft soles he comes to me, the dearest of thieves, and steals my thoughts: I stand there stupid as this chair.
“But I do not stand long then: already I am lying down.”
When Zarathustra heard the wise man speak thus, he laughed in his heart: for a light had dawned on him. And he spoke thus to his heart:
“This wise man with his forty thoughts is a fool to me: but I believe he knows well how to sleep.
“Happy is anyone who lives near this wise man! Such sleep is catching; it is catching even through a thick wall.
“A magic dwells even in his chair. And not in vain did the young men sit before the preacher of virtue.
“His wisdom is: stay awake in order to sleep well. And truly, if life had no meaning and I had to choose nonsense, this would be for me too the nonsense most worth choosing.
“Now I understand clearly what people once sought above all when they sought teachers of virtue. They sought good sleep for themselves, and poppy-flowered virtues to go with it!
“For all these praised wise men of the lecture chairs, wisdom was sleep without dreams: they knew no better meaning of life.
“Even today there are some like this preacher of virtue, and not always so honest: but their time is up. And they will not stand much longer: already they are lying down.
“Blessed are these sleepy ones: for they shall soon nod off.”
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On the Believers in a World Behind
Once Zarathustra too cast his illusion beyond man, like all who believe in a world behind this one. The world then seemed to me the work of a suffering and tormented God.
The world then seemed to me a dream and the poem of a God; coloured smoke before the eyes of a divinely discontented one.
Good and evil, and joy and sorrow, and I and you: coloured smoke before creative eyes, it seemed to me. The creator wanted to look away from himself: so he created the world.
It is a drunken joy for the sufferer to look away from his suffering and lose himself. A drunken joy and a losing of oneself: so the world once seemed to me.
This world, eternally imperfect, the image of an eternal contradiction and an imperfect image, a drunken joy for its imperfect creator: so the world once seemed to me.
So I too once cast my illusion beyond man, like all who believe in a world behind. Beyond man, in truth?
Ah, my brothers, this God whom I created was human work and human madness, like all gods!
He was a man, and only a poor piece of man and of I: he came to me out of my own ashes and fire, this ghost; and truly, he did not come to me from beyond!
What happened, my brothers? I overcame myself, the sufferer; I carried my own ashes to the mountain; I invented a brighter flame for myself. And look! Then the ghost *withdrew* from me!
To believe in such ghosts would now be suffering and torment for me, the convalescent: it would now be suffering and humiliation. So I speak to the believers in a world behind.
It was suffering and incapacity that created all worlds behind this one; and that brief madness of happiness which only the greatest sufferer knows.
Weariness, which wants to reach the ultimate with a single leap, with a death leap; a poor, ignorant weariness that no longer even wants to want: that created all gods and worlds behind.
Believe me, my brothers! It was the body that despaired of the body; it groped with the fingers of the deluded spirit at the last walls.
Believe me, my brothers! It was the body that despaired of the earth; it heard the belly of being speaking to it.
And then it wanted to get through the last walls with its head, and not only with its head: over into “that world”.
But “that world” is well hidden from man, that dehumanised, inhuman world which is a heavenly nothing; and the belly of being does not speak to man at all, except as man.
Truly, all being is hard to prove and hard to make speak. Tell me, my brothers, is not the strangest of all things still the best proved?
Yes, this I, and the I’s contradiction and confusion, still speaks most honestly of its being: this creating, willing, valuing I, which is the measure and the value of things.
And this most honest being, the I, speaks of the body, and it still wants the body, even when it writes poetry and raves and flutters with broken wings.
The I learns to speak more and more honestly: and the more it learns, the more words and honours it finds for the body and the earth.
My I taught me a new pride, and I teach it to men: no longer to bury one’s head in the sand of heavenly things, but to carry it freely, an earthly head that creates meaning for the earth!
I teach men a new will: to want this way which man has walked blindly, and to call it good, and no longer to creep away from it like the sick and the dying!

It was the sick and the dying who despised the body and the earth and invented the heavenly and the redeeming drops of blood: but even these sweet and gloomy poisons they took from the body and the earth!

They wanted to run away from their misery, and the stars were too far for them. Then they sighed: “Oh, if only there were heavenly paths by which to creep into another being and another happiness!” Then they invented their sly ways and their little bloody potions!
Now they imagined themselves carried away from their body and this earth, these ungrateful ones. But to whom did they owe the spasm and bliss of their carrying away? To their body and this earth.
Zarathustra is gentle with the sick. Truly, he is not angry at their kinds of comfort and ingratitude. May they become convalescents and overcomers, and create a higher body for themselves!
Nor is Zarathustra angry with the convalescent when he looks tenderly at his illusion and creeps round the grave of his God at midnight: but sickness and a sick body remain for me even in his tears.
There have always been many sickly people among those who write poetry and long for God; furiously they hate the man of knowledge, and that youngest of virtues which is called honesty.
They always look back to dark ages: then, to be sure, illusion and faith were another thing; the frenzy of reason was likeness to God, and doubt was sin.
I know these godlike ones all too well: they want to be believed in, and doubt to be sin. I know all too well, too, what they themselves believe in most.
Truly, not in worlds behind and redeeming drops of blood: they too believe most in the body, and their own body is their thing-in-itself.
But it is a sickly thing to them, and they would gladly jump out of their skins. That is why they listen to the preachers of death and themselves preach worlds behind.
Listen rather, my brothers, to the voice of the healthy body: it is a more honest and purer voice.
The healthy body, the perfect and square-built, speaks more honestly and more purely: and it speaks of the meaning of the earth.
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On the Despisers of the Body
To the despisers of the body I will speak my word. I do not want them to learn differently or teach differently, but only to say farewell to their own bodies, and so fall silent.
“I am body and soul”: so speaks the child. And why should one not speak like children?
But the awakened one, the knowing one, says: I am body entirely, and nothing besides; and soul is only a word for something about the body.
The body is a great reason, a multiplicity with one sense, a war and a peace, a herd and a shepherd.
An instrument of your body is your little reason too, my brother, which you call “spirit”: a little instrument and toy of your great reason.
You say “I” and are proud of this word. But the greater thing, in which you do not want to believe, is your body and its great reason: it does not say I, but does I.
What the senses feel, what the spirit knows, never has its end in itself. But the senses and the spirit would like to persuade you that they are the end of all things: so vain are they.
The senses and the spirit are instruments and toys: behind them lies the Self. The Self seeks with the eyes of the senses too; it listens with the ears of the spirit too.
The Self is always listening and seeking: it compares, subdues, conquers, destroys. It rules, and is the ruler of the I as well.
Behind your thoughts and feelings, my brother, stands a mighty commander, an unknown sage: his name is Self. He lives in your body; he is your body.
There is more reason in your body than in your best wisdom. And who knows why your body needs precisely your best wisdom?

Your Self laughs at your I and its proud leaps. “What are these leaps and flights of thought to me?” it says to itself. “A detour to my purpose. I am the I’s leading-string and the prompter of its ideas.”
The Self says to the I: “Feel pain here!” And then it suffers and thinks how it may suffer no more; and that is just what it *is meant* to think.
The Self says to the I: “Feel pleasure here!” Then it rejoices and thinks how it may often rejoice again; and that is just what it *is meant* to think.
To the despisers of the body I want to say a word. That they despise is the result of their esteem. What is it that created esteem and contempt and value and will?
The creating Self created esteem and contempt for itself; it created pleasure and pain for itself. The creating body created spirit for itself as a hand of its will.
Even in your folly and contempt, you despisers of the body, you serve your Self. I tell you: your Self itself wants to die and turns away from life.
It can no longer do what it most wants to do: to create beyond itself. That is what it wants most; that is its whole fervour.
But now it has become too late for that: so your Self wants to go under, you despisers of the body.
Your Self wants to go under, and that is why you became despisers of the body! For you can no longer create beyond yourselves.
And that is why you are now angry with life and the earth. There is an unconscious envy in the sidelong glance of your contempt.
I do not go your way, you despisers of the body! You are no bridges to the Overman for me!
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On Joys and Passions
My brother, if you have a virtue, and it is your virtue, you have it in common with no one.
To be sure, you want to call it by name and caress it; you want to pull its ear and amuse yourself with it.
And look! Now you have its name in common with the people, and with your virtue you have become people and herd!
You would do better to say: “Unspeakable and nameless is what gives my soul torment and sweetness, and is even the hunger of my entrails.”
Let your virtue be too high for the familiarity of names: and if you must speak of it, do not be ashamed to stammer about it.
So speak and stammer: “This is *my* good; this I love; so it pleases me entirely; only so do I want the good.
“I do not want it as the law of a God; I do not want it as a human statute or necessity: let it be no signpost for me to worlds beyond and paradises.
“It is an earthly virtue that I love: there is little cleverness in it, and least of all the reason of everyone.
“But this bird built its nest with me: that is why I love it and hold it to my heart; now it sits with me on its golden eggs.”
So you shall stammer and praise your virtue.
Once you had passions and called them evil. But now you have only your virtues: they grew out of your passions.
You laid your highest goal on the heart of these passions: then they became your virtues and joys.
And whether you came from the race of the hot-tempered, or of the lustful, or of the fanatical, or of the vengeful:
In the end all your passions became virtues, and all your devils angels.
Once you had wild dogs in your cellar: but in the end they turned into birds and lovely singers.
Out of your poisons you brewed your balm; you milked your cow, Affliction: now you drink the sweet milk of her udder.
And nothing evil grows out of you any more, except the evil that grows out of the struggle of your virtues.
My brother, if you are lucky, you have one virtue and no more: then you go more easily over the bridge.
It is a distinction to have many virtues, but a hard lot; and many have gone into the desert and killed themselves because they were weary of being the battle and battlefield of virtues.
My brother, are war and battle evil? But this evil is necessary; necessary are envy and mistrust and slander among your virtues.
Look how each of your virtues craves the highest: it wants your whole spirit, so that it may be *its* herald; it wants your whole strength in anger, hatred and love.
Every virtue is jealous of the others, and jealousy is a terrible thing. Even virtues can perish of jealousy.
Whoever is encircled by the flame of jealousy will at last, like the scorpion, turn the poisoned sting against himself.
Ah, my brother, have you never seen a virtue slander and stab itself?
Man is something that must be overcome: and therefore you shall love your virtues, for you will perish of them.
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On the Pale Criminal
You do not want to kill, you judges and sacrificers, before the animal has nodded? Look, the pale criminal has nodded: out of his eye speaks the great contempt.
“My I is something that shall be overcome: my I is to me the great contempt of man”: so speaks that eye.
That he judged himself was his highest moment: do not let the exalted one sink back into his lowness!
There is no redemption for one who suffers so from himself, except a quick death.
Your killing, you judges, shall be pity and not revenge. And as you kill, see to it that you yourselves justify life!
It is not enough that you are reconciled with the one you kill. Let your sadness be love for the Overman: so you will justify your still-living!
“Enemy” you shall say, but not “villain”; “sick man” you shall say, but not “scoundrel”; “fool” you shall say, but not “sinner”.
And you, red judge, if you were to say aloud all that you have already done in your thoughts, everyone would cry: “Away with this filth and poisonous worm!”
But the thought is one thing, the deed another, and the image of the deed another again. The wheel of cause does not roll between them.
An image made this pale man pale. He was equal to his deed when he did it: but he could not bear its image once it was done.
From then on he always saw himself as the doer of one deed. I call this madness: the exception turned for him into his essence.
A chalk line spellbinds a hen; the blow he struck spellbound his poor reason: I call this the madness *after* the deed.
Listen, you judges! There is another madness besides: and it comes before the deed. Ah, you did not crawl deep enough into this soul!
So speaks the red judge: “Why did this criminal murder? He wanted to rob.” But I tell you: his soul wanted blood, not robbery: he thirsted for the happiness of the knife!
But his poor reason did not understand this madness, and persuaded him. “What does blood matter!” it said. “Don’t you want at least to make a robbery of it? To take revenge?”
And he listened to his poor reason: its words lay on him like lead; so he robbed when he murdered. He did not want to be ashamed of his madness.
And now the lead of his guilt lies on him again, and again his poor reason is so stiff, so paralysed, so heavy.
If only he could shake his head, his burden would roll off: but who will shake this head?
What is this man? A heap of diseases that reach out into the world through the spirit: there they want to take their prey.
What is this man? A tangle of wild snakes that are seldom at peace with one another: so they go off on their own and seek prey in the world.
Look at this poor body! What it suffered and craved, this poor soul interpreted for itself: it interpreted it as murderous lust and greed for the happiness of the knife.
Whoever falls ill now is overcome by the evil that is evil now: he wants to hurt with what hurts him. But there have been other times, and another evil and good.
Once doubt was evil, and the will to be oneself. Then the sick man became a heretic and a witch: as heretic and witch he suffered and wanted to make others suffer.
But this does not want to enter your ears: it harms your good people, you tell me. But what do your good people matter to me!
Much about your good people disgusts me, and truly not their evil. I wish they had a madness of which they would perish, like this pale criminal!
Truly, I wish their madness were called truth, or loyalty, or justice: but they have their virtue in order to live long, and in a wretched contentment.
I am a railing by the torrent: let whoever can grasp me, grasp me! But I am not your crutch.
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On Reading and Writing
Of all that is written, I love only what a man writes with his blood. Write with blood, and you will learn that blood is spirit.
It is not easy to understand someone else’s blood: I hate the idle who read.
Whoever knows the reader does nothing more for the reader. Another century of readers, and the spirit itself will stink.
That everyone may learn to read spoils, in the long run, not only writing but thinking too.
Once spirit was God; then it became man; and now it is even becoming the mob.
Whoever writes in blood and in sayings does not want to be read, but learned by heart.
In the mountains the shortest way is from peak to peak; but for that you need long legs. Sayings should be peaks, and those they are spoken to should be tall and great.
The air thin and pure, danger near, and the spirit full of a cheerful malice: these go well together.
I want goblins around me, for I am brave. Courage that scares away ghosts makes goblins for itself: courage wants to laugh.
I no longer feel with you. This cloud I see beneath me, this blackness and heaviness I laugh at: that is exactly your thundercloud.
You look upward when you long to be lifted up. And I look down, because I am lifted up.
Who among you can laugh and be lifted up at the same time?
Whoever climbs the highest mountains laughs at all tragedies, in plays and in life.
Brave, carefree, mocking, violent: so wisdom wants us. She is a woman, and only ever loves a warrior.
You tell me, “Life is hard to bear.” But why else would you have your pride in the morning and your resignation in the evening?
Life is hard to bear; but do not act so tender! We are all of us fine, sturdy, load-bearing donkeys, male and female.
What do we have in common with the rosebud, which trembles because a drop of dew lies on its body?
It is true: we love life, not because we are used to living, but because we are used to loving.
There is always some madness in love. But there is always some reason in madness too.
And to me as well, who am fond of life, it seems that butterflies and soap bubbles, and whatever is like them among people, know most about happiness.
To see these light, foolish, delicate, nimble little souls flutter about: that moves Zarathustra to tears and songs.
I would believe only in a god who knew how to dance.
And when I saw my devil, I found him serious, thorough, deep, solemn: he was the spirit of gravity; through him all things fall.
One kills not with anger but with laughter. Come, let us kill the spirit of gravity!
I have learned to walk; since then I let myself run. I have learned to fly; since then I do not want to be pushed before I move.
Now I am light, now I fly, now I see myself beneath me, now a god dances through me.
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On the Tree on the Mountainside

Zarathustra’s eye had seen that a young man was avoiding him. And one evening, as he walked alone through the hills around the town called “The Motley Cow”, he found this young man as he went, sitting leaning against a tree and gazing wearily into the valley. Zarathustra took hold of the tree beside which the young man sat, and spoke thus:
“If I wanted to shake this tree with my hands, I could not do it.
But the wind, which we do not see, torments it and bends it wherever it likes. We are bent and tormented worst by invisible hands.”
At this the young man got up in dismay and said: “I hear Zarathustra, and I was just thinking of him.” Zarathustra replied:
“Why does that frighten you? But it is the same with man as with the tree.
The more he wants to rise into the heights and the light, the more strongly his roots strive earthward, downward, into the dark, the deep: into evil.”
“Yes, into evil!” cried the young man. “How is it possible that you have discovered my soul?”
Zarathustra smiled and said: “Many a soul will never be discovered, unless it is first invented.”
“Yes, into evil!” cried the young man again. “You spoke the truth, Zarathustra. I no longer trust myself since I have wanted to climb, and no one trusts me any more. How does this happen?
I change too quickly: my today refutes my yesterday. I often skip the steps when I climb, and no step forgives me for that.
When I am up there, I always find myself alone. No one speaks to me; the frost of loneliness makes me shiver. What do I want in the heights?
My contempt and my longing grow together; the higher I climb, the more I despise the one who climbs. What does he want in the heights?
How ashamed I am of my climbing and stumbling! How I mock my violent panting! How I hate the one who flies! How tired I am in the heights!”
Here the young man fell silent. And Zarathustra looked at the tree beside which they stood, and spoke thus:
“This tree stands alone here on the mountain; it has grown high above man and beast.
And if it wanted to speak, it would have no one who understood it: so high has it grown.
Now it waits and waits. What is it waiting for? It lives too near the seat of the clouds: perhaps it is waiting for the first lightning?”

When Zarathustra had said this, the young man cried out with violent gestures: “Yes, Zarathustra, you speak the truth. I longed for my going-under when I wanted to climb, and you are the lightning I was waiting for! Look, what am I still, since you appeared to us? It is envy of you that has destroyed me!” So spoke the young man, and wept bitterly. But Zarathustra put his arm round him and led him away with him.
And when they had walked together for a while, Zarathustra began to speak thus:
“It breaks my heart. Better than your words say it, your eye tells me all your danger.
You are not yet free; you are still searching for freedom. Your searching has made you sleepless and over-awake.
You want to reach the free heights; your soul thirsts for the stars. But your bad instincts thirst for freedom too.
Your wild dogs want to be free; they bark with joy in their cellar when your spirit tries to open all the prisons.
To me you are still a prisoner who imagines freedom. Ah, the soul of such prisoners becomes clever, but also cunning and bad.
The one who has freed his spirit must still purify himself. Much prison and mould is still left in him: his eye must still become pure.
Yes, I know your danger. But by my love and hope I beg you: do not throw away your love and hope!
You still feel noble, and the others still feel you are noble, those who resent you and give you dirty looks. Know that a noble person stands in everyone’s way.
A noble person stands in the way of the good too; and even when they call him good, they mean by it to put him aside.
The noble person wants to create something new, and a new virtue. The good want the old, and that the old should be preserved.
But the danger for the noble person is not that he will become one of the good, but a scoffer, a mocker, a destroyer.
Ah, I have known noble people who lost their highest hope. And then they slandered all high hopes.
Then they lived shamelessly in brief pleasures, and hardly cast their aims beyond the day.
‘Spirit is also lust,’ they said. Then the wings of their spirit broke; now it crawls about and dirties whatever it gnaws.
Once they thought of becoming heroes; now they are pleasure-seekers. To them the hero is a grief and a horror.
But by my love and hope I beg you: do not throw away the hero in your soul! Keep holy your highest hope!”
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On the Preachers of Death
There are preachers of death; and the earth is full of those to whom turning away from life must be preached.
The earth is full of the superfluous; life is spoiled by the many-too-many. Let them be lured out of this life with “eternal life”!
“The yellow ones” or “the black ones”, that is what the preachers of death are called. But I want to show them to you in other colours too.
There are the terrible ones, who carry the beast of prey around inside themselves and have no choice except lusts or tearing themselves apart. And even their lusts are a tearing of themselves apart.
They have not even become human beings yet, these terrible ones. Let them preach turning away from life, and go away themselves!
There are the consumptives of the soul: scarcely are they born before they begin to die, and long for teachings of weariness and renunciation.
They would like to be dead, and we should approve of their wish! Let us beware of waking these dead and damaging these living coffins!
They meet a sick man, or an old man, or a corpse, and at once they say, “Life is refuted!”
But only they are refuted, and their eye, which sees only this one face of existence.
Wrapped in thick gloom, and eager for the little accidents that bring death: so they wait, and clench their teeth.
Or else they reach for sweets and mock their own childishness as they do it: they cling to their straw of life, and mock that they still cling to a straw.
Their wisdom runs: “A fool, who stays alive; but such fools we are! And that is the most foolish thing about life!”
“Life is only suffering,” say others, and they do not lie. Then see to it that you stop! See to it that the life stops which is only suffering!
And let the teaching of your virtue be: “You shall kill yourself! You shall steal yourself away!”
“Lust is sin,” say some who preach death; “let us go aside and beget no children!”
“Giving birth is hard,” say others; “why give birth any more? One gives birth only to the unhappy!” And they too are preachers of death.
“Pity is needed,” say a third kind. “Take what I have! Take what I am! The less life binds me!”
If they were pitying through and through, they would spoil life for their neighbours. To be wicked: that would be their true goodness.
But they want to get free of life. What do they care if they bind others still tighter with their chains and gifts!
And you too, for whom life is furious work and unrest: are you not very tired of life? Are you not very ripe for the preaching of death?
All of you who love furious work, and the fast, the new, the strange: you bear yourselves badly; your diligence is flight, and the will to forget yourselves.
If you believed more in life, you would throw yourselves less into the moment. But you have not enough content in you for waiting, nor even for laziness!
Everywhere sounds the voice of those who preach death; and the earth is full of those to whom death must be preached.
Or “eternal life”: it is all the same to me, as long as they go away quickly!
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On War and Warriors
We do not want to be spared by our best enemies, nor by those we love from the bottom of our hearts. So let me tell you the truth!
My brothers in war! I love you from the bottom of my heart; I am and was one of you. And I am also your best enemy. So let me tell you the truth!
I know the hatred and envy of your hearts. You are not great enough not to know hatred and envy. Then be great enough not to be ashamed of them!
And if you cannot be saints of knowledge, then at least be its warriors. They are the companions and forerunners of such holiness.
I see many soldiers: I wish I saw many warriors! What they wear is called a “uniform”: may what they hide in it not be uniform!
You should be such as are always looking for an enemy: for your enemy. And with some of you there is hatred at first sight.
You should seek your enemy, wage your war, and for your thoughts! And if your thought is defeated, your honesty should still shout triumph over it!
You should love peace as a means to new wars, and the short peace more than the long.
I do not advise you to work, but to fight. I do not advise you to make peace, but to win. Let your work be a fight, let your peace be a victory!
One can be silent and sit still only when one has a bow and arrows; otherwise one chatters and quarrels. Let your peace be a victory!
You say it is the good cause that hallows even war? I tell you: it is the good war that hallows every cause.
War and courage have done more great things than love of one’s neighbour. Not your pity but your bravery has saved the unfortunate until now.
“What is good?” you ask. To be brave is good. Let the little girls say: “Good is what is pretty and touching at the same time.”
They call you heartless; but your heart is genuine, and I love the shame of your warm-heartedness. You are ashamed of your flood, and others are ashamed of their ebb.
You are ugly? Well then, my brothers! Wrap the sublime around you, the cloak of the ugly!
And when your soul grows great, it grows arrogant, and in your sublimity there is malice. I know you.
In malice the arrogant man meets the weakling. But they misunderstand each other. I know you.
You may have only enemies to be hated, not enemies to be despised. You must be proud of your enemy: then your enemy’s successes are your successes too.
Rebellion: that is the nobility of the slave. Let your nobility be obedience! Let your very commanding be an obeying!
To a good warrior “you shall” sounds more pleasant than “I will”. And everything you love, you should first have commanded to you.
Let your love of life be love of your highest hope; and let your highest hope be the highest thought of life!
But your highest thought you should let me command you, and it runs: man is something that shall be overcome.
So live your life of obedience and of war! What does long life matter! What warrior wants to be spared!
I do not spare you, I love you from the bottom of my heart, my brothers in war!
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On the New Idol
Somewhere there are still peoples and herds, but not with us, my brothers: here there are states.
The state? What is that? Well then! Now open your ears to me, for now I shall tell you my word about the death of peoples.
State is the name of the coldest of all cold monsters. Coldly it lies, too; and this lie crawls out of its mouth: “I, the state, am the people.”
It is a lie! It was creators who created peoples and hung a faith and a love over them: so they served life.
It is destroyers who set traps for the many and call them the state: they hang a sword and a hundred appetites over them.
Where there is still a people, it does not understand the state, and hates it as the evil eye and a sin against customs and rights.
This sign I give you: every people speaks its own tongue of good and evil, which its neighbour does not understand. It invented its own language in customs and rights.
But the state lies in all the tongues of good and evil; and whatever it says, it lies; and whatever it has, it has stolen.
Everything about it is false; it bites with stolen teeth, the biter. Even its insides are false.
Confusion of the tongues of good and evil: this sign I give you as the sign of the state. Truly, this sign points to the will to death! Truly, it beckons to the preachers of death!
Far too many are born: for the superfluous the state was invented!
Just look how it lures them to itself, the many-too-many! How it swallows them and chews them and chews them again!
“On earth there is nothing greater than I: I am the ordering finger of God,” so the monster roars. And it is not only the long-eared and the short-sighted who sink to their knees!
Ah, even in you, you great souls, it whispers its dark lies! Ah, it guesses out the rich hearts that like to squander themselves!
Yes, it guesses you out too, you conquerors of the old god! You grew tired in the fight, and now your tiredness serves the new idol!
It would like to set up heroes and honourable men around itself, the new idol! It likes to bask in the sunshine of good consciences, the cold monster!
It will give you everything, if you worship it, the new idol: so it buys the shine of your virtue and the look of your proud eyes.
It wants to use you as bait for the many-too-many! Yes, a hellish trick was invented there, a horse of death, jingling in the finery of divine honours!
Yes, a dying for many was invented there, which praises itself as life: truly, a heartfelt service to all preachers of death!
I call it the state where all drink poison, good and bad alike; the state, where all lose themselves, good and bad alike; the state, where the slow suicide of all is called “life”.
Just look at these superfluous ones! They steal the works of the inventors and the treasures of the wise; they call their theft “education”, and everything turns into sickness and trouble for them!
Just look at these superfluous ones! They are always sick; they vomit their bile and call it a newspaper. They devour one another and cannot even digest themselves.
Just look at these superfluous ones! They acquire riches and become poorer by them. They want power, and first of all the crowbar of power, much money; these incapable ones!
See them climb, these nimble apes! They climb over one another and so drag one another into the mud and the depths.
They all want to get to the throne: that is their madness, as if happiness sat on the throne! Often mud sits on the throne, and often the throne on the mud.
Madmen they all are to me, and climbing apes, and overheated. Their idol smells bad to me, the cold monster; they all smell bad to me together, these idolaters.
My brothers, do you want to suffocate in the fumes of their mouths and appetites? Rather break the windows and jump out into the open!
Get away from the bad smell! Get away from the idolatry of the superfluous!
Get away from the bad smell! Get away from the steam of these human sacrifices!
The earth is still free for great souls. Many places are still empty for the solitary and for pairs, where the smell of quiet seas blows.
A free life is still open to great souls. Truly, whoever owns little is owned that much less: blessed be a little poverty!
There, where the state ends, there first begins the human being who is not superfluous: there begins the song of the necessary, the single and irreplaceable melody.
There, where the state ends: look there, my brothers! Do you not see it, the rainbow and the bridges of the Overman?
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On the Flies of the Market Place
Flee, my friend, into your solitude! I see you deafened by the noise of the great men and stung by the stings of the small.
Forest and rock know how to be silent with you, with dignity. Be like the tree you love again, the broad-branched one: silent and listening, it leans over the sea.
Where solitude ends, the market place begins; and where the market place begins, there begins also the noise of the great actors and the buzzing of the poisonous flies.
In the world even the best things are worth nothing without someone who first puts them on stage: the people call these showmen great men.
The people understand little of what is great, that is, of what creates. But they have a sense for all showmen and actors of great things.
The world turns around the inventors of new values: invisibly it turns. But around the actors turn the people and fame: such is the way of the world.
The actor has spirit, but little conscience of the spirit. He always believes in whatever makes people believe most strongly: believe in him!
Tomorrow he has a new faith, and the day after tomorrow a newer one. He has quick senses, like the people, and changeable moods.
To overthrow: that, to him, means to prove. To drive mad: that, to him, means to convince. And blood counts to him as the best of all reasons.
A truth that slips only into fine ears he calls a lie and nothing. Truly, he believes only in gods that make a great noise in the world!
The market place is full of solemn buffoons, and the people boast of their great men! These are their masters of the hour.
But the hour presses them; so they press you. And from you too they want a Yes or a No. Alas, do you want to set your chair between For and Against?
Do not be jealous of these unconditional and pressing people, you lover of truth! Never yet has truth hung on the arm of the unconditional.
Because of these sudden people, go back into your security: only in the market place is one attacked with “Yes?” or “No?”
Slow is the experience of all deep wells: they must wait long before they know what has fallen into their depths.
Everything great happens away from the market place and from fame: the inventors of new values have always lived away from the market place and from fame.
Flee, my friend, into your solitude: I see you stung by poisonous flies. Flee to where a rough, strong air blows!
Flee into your solitude! You lived too near the small and the pitiful. Flee from their invisible revenge! Towards you they are nothing but revenge.
Raise your arm against them no more! They are countless, and it is not your lot to be a fly-swatter.
Countless are these small and pitiful ones; and raindrops and weeds have already brought many a proud building to ruin.
You are not a stone, but already many drops have made you hollow. You will yet break and burst from many drops.
I see you wearied by poisonous flies, I see you scratched bloody in a hundred places; and your pride will not even be angry.
They want blood from you in all innocence; their bloodless souls crave blood, and so they sting in all innocence.
But you, deep one, you suffer too deeply even from small wounds; and before you have healed, the same poisonous worm has crawled over your hand.
You are too proud to kill these greedy little things. But beware that it does not become your fate to bear all their poisonous injustice!
They buzz around you with their praise too: their praise is pushiness. They want to be near your skin and your blood.
They flatter you as they would a god or a devil; they whine before you as before a god or a devil. What does it matter! They are flatterers and whiners, and nothing more.
They often show themselves to you as lovable, too. But that has always been the cleverness of cowards. Yes, cowards are clever!
They think a great deal about you with their narrow souls; you are always worrying to them! Whatever is thought about a great deal becomes worrying.
They punish you for all your virtues. From the bottom of their hearts they forgive you only your mistakes.
Because you are gentle and just in mind, you say: “They are innocent of their small existence.” But their narrow souls think: “All great existence is guilt.”
Even when you are gentle with them, they still feel despised by you; and they repay your kindness with hidden unkindness.
Your wordless pride always goes against their taste; they rejoice when for once you are modest enough to be vain.
What we recognise in a person, we also set alight in him. So beware of the small!
In your presence they feel small, and their lowness smoulders and glows against you in invisible revenge.
Did you not notice how often they fell silent when you came up to them, and how their strength left them like smoke from a dying fire?
Yes, my friend, you are the bad conscience of your neighbours, for they are unworthy of you. So they hate you, and would like to suck your blood.
Your neighbours will always be poisonous flies; what is great in you, that itself must make them more poisonous and ever more like flies.
Flee, my friend, into your solitude, and to where a rough, strong air blows. It is not your lot to be a fly-swatter.
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On Chastity
I love the forest. It is bad to live in cities: there are too many there who are in heat.
Is it not better to fall into the hands of a murderer than into the dreams of a woman in heat?
And just look at these men: their eye says it, they know nothing better on earth than to lie with a woman.
There is mud at the bottom of their souls; and woe if their mud has spirit too!
If only you were at least perfect as animals! But innocence belongs to the animal.
Do I advise you to kill your senses? I advise you to the innocence of the senses.
Do I advise you to chastity? Chastity is a virtue in some, but in many it is almost a vice.
These people hold back, it is true; but the bitch Sensuality looks out with envy from everything they do.
Even into the heights of their virtue, and right into their cold spirit, this beast and its unrest follow them.
And how nicely the bitch Sensuality knows how to beg for a piece of spirit when a piece of meat is denied her!
You love tragedies, and everything that breaks the heart? But I am suspicious of your bitch.
Your eyes are too cruel for me, and you look lustfully at those who suffer. Has not your lust merely disguised itself and called itself pity?
And this parable too I give you: not a few who wanted to drive out their devil went into the swine themselves.
To whom chastity is hard, it should be advised against, so that it does not become the road to hell: that is, to the mud and heat of the soul.
Do I speak of dirty things? That is not the worst to me.
Not when truth is dirty, but when it is shallow, is the one who seeks knowledge reluctant to step into its water.
Truly, there are those who are chaste through and through: they are gentler of heart, they laugh more gladly and more richly than you.
They laugh at chastity too, and ask: “What is chastity?
Is chastity not foolishness? But this foolishness came to us, and not we to it.
We offered this guest shelter and heart: now it lives with us; let it stay as long as it likes!”
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On the Friend
“There is always one too many around me,” thinks the hermit. “Always once one: in the long run that makes two!”
I and Me are always too eager in conversation: how could it be borne if there were no friend?
For the hermit the friend is always the third: the third is the cork that keeps the conversation of the two from sinking into the depths.
Ah, there are too many depths for all hermits. That is why they long so for a friend, and for his height.
Our faith in others betrays what we would like to believe in ourselves. Our longing for a friend is our betrayer.
And often with love one only wants to leap over envy. And often one attacks and makes an enemy, to hide that one can be attacked.
“At least be my enemy!” So speaks true reverence, which does not dare to ask for friendship.
If you want to have a friend, you must also be willing to wage war for him; and to wage war, you must be able to be an enemy.
You should honour the enemy even in your friend. Can you go close to your friend without going over to him?
In your friend you should have your best enemy. You should be closest to him with your heart when you resist him.
You do not want to wear any clothes in front of your friend? It is to honour your friend that you give yourself to him as you are? But for that he wishes you to the devil!
Whoever hides nothing of himself is outrageous: so much reason have you to fear nakedness! Yes, if you were gods, then you might be ashamed of your clothes!
You cannot dress up finely enough for your friend: for you should be to him an arrow and a longing for the Overman.
Have you ever seen your friend asleep, to find out what he looks like? What else is your friend’s face? It is your own face, in a rough and imperfect mirror.
Have you ever seen your friend asleep? Were you not frightened that your friend looks like that? Oh my friend, man is something that must be overcome.
The friend should be a master at guessing and keeping silent: you must not want to see everything. Your dream should tell you what your friend does while awake.
Let your pity be a guessing, so that you first know whether your friend wants pity. Perhaps what he loves in you is the unbroken eye and the look of eternity.
Let your pity for your friend hide under a hard shell; you should break a tooth on it. Then it will have its delicacy and sweetness.
Are you pure air and solitude and bread and medicine to your friend? Many a man cannot loosen his own chains, and yet he is his friend’s deliverer.
Are you a slave? Then you cannot be a friend. Are you a tyrant? Then you cannot have friends.
For far too long a slave and a tyrant were hidden in woman. That is why woman is not yet capable of friendship: she knows only love.
In woman’s love there is injustice and blindness towards everything she does not love. And even in the knowing love of woman there is still ambush and lightning and night beside the light.
Woman is not yet capable of friendship: women are still cats, and birds. Or at best cows.
Woman is not yet capable of friendship. But tell me, you men, which of you is capable of friendship?
Oh, your poverty, you men, and the meanness of your souls! As much as you give your friend, I will give even to my enemy, and will not have become poorer by it.
There is comradeship: may there be friendship!
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On the Thousand and One Goals
Zarathustra saw many lands and many peoples: so he discovered the good and evil of many peoples. Zarathustra found no greater power on earth than good and evil.
No people could live without first valuing; but if it wants to preserve itself, it must not value as its neighbour values.
Much that was called good by this people was called scorn and disgrace by another: so I found it. Much I found called evil here, and there decked out with purple honours.
Never did one neighbour understand another: his soul was always amazed at his neighbour’s madness and wickedness.
A tablet of good things hangs over every people. Look, it is the tablet of its overcomings; look, it is the voice of its will to power.
Praiseworthy is what it finds hard; what is indispensable and hard it calls good; and what frees it even from the deepest need, the rare, the hardest of all, that it praises as holy.
Whatever makes it rule and win and shine, to its neighbour’s horror and envy: that it counts as the high, the first, the measure, the meaning of all things.
Truly, my brother, once you have come to know a people’s need and land and sky and neighbour, you can surely guess the law of its overcomings, and why it climbs this ladder to its hope.
“You shall always be the first and stand out above the others: your jealous soul shall love no one except your friend.” This made the soul of a Greek tremble; with it he went his path of greatness.
“To speak the truth and to be good with bow and arrow”: this seemed both dear and hard to the people from whom my name comes, the name that is both dear and hard to me.
“To honour father and mother and to do their will down to the root of the soul”: this tablet of overcoming another people hung up over itself, and became powerful and eternal by it.

“To practise loyalty, and for loyalty’s sake to stake honour and blood even on evil and dangerous things”: teaching itself so, another people mastered itself, and mastering itself so, it became pregnant and heavy with great hopes.
Truly, human beings gave themselves all their good and evil. Truly, they did not take it, they did not find it, it did not fall on them as a voice from heaven.
It was man who first put values into things, in order to preserve himself; he first created a meaning for things, a human meaning! That is why he calls himself “man”, that is: the one who values.
Valuing is creating: hear it, you creators! Valuing itself is the treasure and jewel of all valued things.
Only through valuing is there value; and without valuing, the nut of existence would be hollow. Hear it, you creators!
Change of values: that is change of the creators. Whoever must be a creator always destroys.
