First peoples were creators, and only later individuals; truly, the individual himself is still the youngest creation.
Peoples once hung a tablet of the good over themselves. Love that wants to rule and love that wants to obey created such tablets together.
The pleasure in the herd is older than the pleasure in the I; and as long as the good conscience is called herd, only the bad conscience says: I.
Truly, the cunning I, the loveless one, that wants its own advantage in the advantage of many: that is not the origin of the herd, but its going-under.
It was always lovers and creators who created good and evil. The fire of love glows in the names of all the virtues, and the fire of anger.
Zarathustra saw many lands and many peoples: Zarathustra found no greater power on earth than the works of those who love: “good” and “evil” is their name.
Truly, the power of this praising and blaming is a monster. Tell me, who will subdue it for me, brothers? Tell me, who will throw the fetter over the thousand necks of this beast?
There have been a thousand goals so far, for there have been a thousand peoples. Only the fetter for the thousand necks is still missing; the one goal is missing. Humanity still has no goal.
But tell me, my brothers: if humanity still lacks a goal, is it not humanity itself that is still lacking?
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On Love of the Neighbour
You crowd around your neighbour and have fine words for it. But I tell you: your love of your neighbour is your bad love of yourselves.
You flee to your neighbour from yourselves and would like to make a virtue of it: but I see through your “selflessness”.
The You is older than the I; the You has been declared holy, but not yet the I: so man crowds towards his neighbour.
Do I advise you to love your neighbour? Rather I advise you to flee your neighbour and to love the farthest!
Higher than love of the neighbour is love of the farthest and of what is to come; higher still than love of people is love of things and of ghosts.
This ghost that runs ahead of you, my brother, is more beautiful than you; why do you not give it your flesh and your bones? But you are afraid, and run to your neighbour.
You cannot bear yourselves and do not love yourselves enough: now you want to seduce your neighbour into love, and gild yourselves with his mistake.
I wish you could not bear all kinds of neighbours and their neighbours; then you would have to create your friend and his overflowing heart out of yourselves.
You invite a witness when you want to speak well of yourselves; and when you have seduced him into thinking well of you, you think well of yourselves.
Not only he lies who speaks against what he knows, but even more he who speaks against what he does not know. And so you speak of yourselves in company, and lie to your neighbour with yourselves.
So says the fool: “Mixing with people spoils the character, especially if one has none.”
One goes to his neighbour because he is looking for himself, and another because he would like to lose himself. Your bad love of yourselves makes your solitude a prison.
It is those farther away who pay for your love of the neighbour; and as soon as there are five of you together, a sixth must always die.
I do not love your festivals either: I found too many actors there, and even the spectators often behaved like actors.
I do not teach you the neighbour, but the friend. Let the friend be the festival of the earth to you, and a foretaste of the Overman.
I teach you the friend and his overflowing heart. But one must know how to be a sponge if one wants to be loved by overflowing hearts.
I teach you the friend in whom the world stands complete, a bowl of the good: the creating friend, who always has a complete world to give away.
And as the world rolled apart for him, so it rolls together again for him in rings, as the becoming of good through evil, as the becoming of purposes out of chance.
Let the future and the farthest be the cause of your today: in your friend you should love the Overman as your cause.
My brothers, I do not advise you to love your neighbour: I advise you to love the farthest.
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On the Way of the Creator
Do you want, my brother, to go into solitude? Do you want to seek the way to yourself? Wait a little longer, and listen to me.
“Whoever seeks easily gets lost himself. All going off alone is guilt”: so says the herd. And you belonged to the herd for a long time.
The voice of the herd will still sound in you too. And when you say, “I no longer share one conscience with you,” it will be a lament and a pain.
Look, this pain itself was born of that one conscience; and the last glimmer of that conscience still glows on your gloom.
But you want to go the way of your gloom, which is the way to yourself? Then show me your right and your strength for it!
Are you a new strength and a new right? A first movement? A wheel rolling out of itself? Can you also force stars to turn around you?
Ah, there is so much lusting for the heights! There are so many convulsions of the ambitious! Show me that you are not one of the lustful and ambitious!
Ah, there are so many great thoughts that do no more than a bellows: they puff up and make emptier.
You call yourself free? I want to hear your ruling thought, and not that you have escaped from a yoke.
Are you one who was allowed to escape a yoke? There are many who threw away their last value when they threw away their servitude.
Free from what? What does Zarathustra care! But your eye should tell me clearly: free for what?
Can you give yourself your own evil and your own good, and hang your will over yourself like a law? Can you be your own judge, and avenger of your law?
It is terrible to be alone with the judge and avenger of one’s own law. So a star is thrown out into empty space and into the icy breath of being alone.
Today you still suffer from the many, you single one; today you still have your courage whole, and your hopes.
But one day solitude will make you tired; one day your pride will bend and your courage grind its teeth. One day you will cry out, “I am alone!”
One day you will no longer see what is high in you, and see what is low in you all too near; your very sublimity will frighten you like a ghost. One day you will cry out, “Everything is false!”
There are feelings that want to kill the solitary; if they do not succeed, well, then they must die themselves! But are you able to be a murderer?
Do you already know, my brother, the word “contempt”? And the torment of your justice, to be just to those who despise you?
You force many to change their minds about you; they hold that hard against you. You came near them and yet went past: that they will never forgive you.
You go beyond them; but the higher you climb, the smaller the eye of envy sees you. But the one who flies is hated most.
“How could you be just to me!” you must say. “I choose your injustice as the share measured out to me.”
They throw injustice and dirt at the solitary; but, my brother, if you want to be a star, you must not shine any less for them because of it!
And beware of the good and the just! They like to crucify those who invent their own virtue; they hate the solitary.
Beware too of holy simplicity! Everything that is not simple is unholy to it; it also likes to play with fire, the fire of the stake.
And beware too of the fits of your love! The solitary holds out his hand too quickly to whoever he meets.
To many people you must not give your hand, but only your paw; and I want your paw to have claws too.
But the worst enemy you can meet will always be yourself; you lie in wait for yourself in caves and forests.
Solitary one, you are going the way to yourself! And your way leads past yourself and your seven devils!
You will be heretic to yourself, and witch and fortune-teller and fool and doubter and unholy one and villain.
You must want to burn yourself in your own flame: how could you become new if you had not first become ashes!
Solitary one, you are going the way of the creator: you want to create a god for yourself out of your seven devils!
Solitary one, you are going the way of the lover: you love yourself, and that is why you despise yourself, as only lovers despise.
The lover wants to create, because he despises! What does he know of love who did not have to despise precisely what he loved!
Go into your solitude with your love and with your creating, my brother; and only late will justice limp after you.
Go into your solitude with my tears, my brother. I love him who wants to create beyond himself, and so goes under.
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On Little Old and Young Women
“Why do you creep so shyly through the twilight, Zarathustra? And what are you hiding so carefully under your cloak?
Is it a treasure someone has given you? Or a child that has been born to you? Or are you now going the ways of thieves yourself, you friend of the wicked?”
Truly, my brother, said Zarathustra, it is a treasure that was given me: it is a little truth that I am carrying.
But it is unruly, like a young child; and if I do not hold its mouth, it screams too loud.
As I went my way alone today, at the hour when the sun goes down, I met a little old woman, and she spoke thus to my soul:
“Zarathustra has said many things to us women too, but he has never spoken to us about woman.”
And I answered her: “About woman one should speak only to men.”
“Speak to me too about woman,” she said; “I am old enough to forget it again straight away.”
And I gave in to the little old woman, and spoke thus to her:
Everything about woman is a riddle, and everything about woman has one answer: it is called pregnancy.
For woman, man is a means: the end is always the child. But what is woman for man?
The true man wants two things: danger and play. That is why he wants woman, as the most dangerous plaything.
Man should be brought up for war, and woman for the recreation of the warrior: all else is folly.
Fruits that are too sweet the warrior does not like. That is why he likes woman; even the sweetest woman is still bitter.
Woman understands children better than man does, but man is more childlike than woman.
In the true man a child is hidden: it wants to play. Come, you women, discover the child in man for me!
Let woman be a plaything, pure and fine, like a precious stone, lit by the virtues of a world that is not yet here.
Let the ray of a star shine in your love! Let your hope be: “May I give birth to the Overman!”
Let there be bravery in your love! With your love you should go for the one who makes you afraid!
Let your honour be in your love! Otherwise woman understands little about honour. But let this be your honour: always to love more than you are loved, and never to be second.
Let man be afraid of woman when she loves: then she makes every sacrifice, and every other thing seems worthless to her.
Let man be afraid of woman when she hates: for man is only wicked at the bottom of his soul, but woman is bad there.
Whom does woman hate most? So spoke the iron to the magnet: “I hate you most, because you attract me but are not strong enough to pull me to you.”
The happiness of man is: I will. The happiness of woman is: he wills.
“Look, now the world has just become perfect!” So thinks every woman when she obeys out of complete love.
And woman must obey, and find a depth for her surface. Woman’s soul is surface, a restless, stormy film on shallow water.
But man’s soul is deep; its current roars in underground caves: woman senses its strength, but does not understand it.
Then the little old woman answered me: “Zarathustra has said many nice things, especially for those who are young enough for them.
It is strange: Zarathustra knows little of women, and yet he is right about them! Does this happen because with woman nothing is impossible?
And now take a little truth as thanks! I am old enough for it, after all!
Wrap it up and hold its mouth: otherwise it will scream too loud, this little truth.”
“Give me, woman, your little truth!” I said. And thus spoke the little old woman:
“You are going to women? Do not forget the whip!”
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On the Bite of the Adder

One day Zarathustra had fallen asleep under a fig tree, for it was hot, and had laid his arms over his face. Then an adder came and bit him in the neck, so that Zarathustra cried out with pain. When he had taken his arm from his face, he looked at the snake; and it recognised Zarathustra’s eyes, writhed awkwardly, and tried to get away. “Not so,” said Zarathustra; “you have not yet accepted my thanks! You woke me in time; my way is still long.” “Your way is short now,” said the adder sadly; “my poison kills.” Zarathustra smiled. “When did a dragon ever die of a snake’s poison?” he said. “But take your poison back! You are not rich enough to give it to me.” Then the adder fell on his neck again, and licked his wound.
When Zarathustra once told this to his disciples, they asked: “And what, O Zarathustra, is the moral of your story?” Zarathustra answered thus:
The good and the just call me the destroyer of morals: my story is immoral.
But if you have an enemy, do not repay him evil with good: for that would shame him. Rather prove that he has done you some good.
And rather be angry than put him to shame! And when you are cursed, I do not like it that you then want to bless. Rather curse back a little!
And if a great wrong has been done to you, then quickly do five small ones besides! It is horrible to see the man who is weighed down by wrong alone.
Did you know this already? Wrong shared is half right. And let him take the wrong upon himself who can bear it!
A little revenge is more human than no revenge at all. And if the punishment is not also a right and an honour for the one who broke the law, I do not like your punishing either.
It is nobler to put yourself in the wrong than to keep the right, especially when you are right. Only one must be rich enough for it.
I do not like your cold justice; and from the eye of your judges the executioner and his cold steel always look out at me.
Tell me, where is the justice to be found that is love with seeing eyes?
Then invent for me the love that bears not only all punishment but also all guilt!
Then invent for me the justice that acquits everyone, except the one who judges!
Do you want to hear this too? In the one who wants to be just through and through, even lying becomes kindness to people.
But how could I want to be just through and through! How can I give everyone his own! Let this be enough for me: I give everyone my own.
Finally, my brothers, beware of doing wrong to any hermit! How could a hermit forget! How could he repay!
A hermit is like a deep well. It is easy to throw a stone in; but once it has sunk to the bottom, tell me, who will bring it out again?
Beware of insulting the hermit! But if you have done it, well then, kill him too!
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On the Famous Wise Men
You have served the people and the people’s superstition, all you famous wise men! And not the truth! And that is exactly why you were paid reverence.
And that too is why your unbelief was put up with, because it was a joke and a detour on the way to the people. So the master lets his slaves have their way, and even enjoys their high spirits.
But the one who is hated by the people as a wolf is by the dogs: that is the free spirit, the enemy of fetters, the one who does not worship, the one who lives in forests.
To hunt him out of his hiding place: that has always been what the people call “a sense of what is right”; against him it still sets its sharpest-toothed dogs.
“For the truth is here: the people are here, after all! Woe, woe to those who seek!” So it has always rung out.
You wanted to justify your people in its reverence: that you called “will to truth”, you famous wise men!
And your heart always said to itself: “I came from the people; from there the voice of God came to me too.”
Stiff-necked and clever, like the donkey, you have always been the people’s advocates.
And many a powerful man who wanted to get along well with the people harnessed in front of his horses a little donkey, a famous wise man.
And now, you famous wise men, I wish you would at last throw off the lion’s skin altogether!
The skin of the beast of prey, the spotted one, and the shaggy hair of the explorer, the seeker, the conqueror!
Ah, for me to learn to believe in your “truthfulness”, you would first have to break your will to revere.
Truthful: that is what I call the one who goes into godless deserts and has broken his revering heart.
In the yellow sand, burned by the sun, he may well squint thirstily at the islands rich in springs, where living things rest under dark trees.
But his thirst does not persuade him to become like these comfortable ones: for where there are oases, there are also idols.
Hungry, violent, lonely, godless: so the lion-will wants itself.
Free from the happiness of servants, released from gods and worship, fearless and fearsome, great and lonely: so is the will of the truthful one.
The truthful, the free spirits, have always lived in the desert, as lords of the desert; but in the cities live the well-fed, famous wise men, the draught animals.
For they always pull, like donkeys, the people’s cart!
Not that I am angry with them for that: but they remain servants to me, and harnessed, even when they shine in golden harness.
And often they were good servants, and worthy of praise. For so virtue speaks: “If you must be a servant, look for the one whom your service helps most!
The spirit and virtue of your master should grow through your being his servant: so you yourself grow with his spirit and his virtue!”
And truly, you famous wise men, you servants of the people! You yourselves grew with the people’s spirit and virtue, and the people through you! I say this to your credit!
But you remain the people to me, even in your virtues, the people with dull eyes, the people who do not know what spirit is!
Spirit is the life that itself cuts into life: by its own torment it increases its own knowledge. Did you know that already?
And the happiness of the spirit is this: to be anointed and consecrated by tears as the sacrificial animal. Did you know that already?
And the blindness of the blind man, and his seeking and groping, shall still bear witness to the power of the sun he looked into. Did you know that already?
And the one who seeks knowledge shall learn to build with mountains! It is little that the spirit moves mountains. Did you know that already?
You know only the sparks of the spirit: but you do not see the anvil that it is, nor the cruelty of its hammer!
Truly, you do not know the pride of the spirit! But still less could you bear the modesty of the spirit, if it ever wanted to speak!
And never yet have you been allowed to throw your spirit into a pit of snow: you are not hot enough for that! So you do not know the raptures of its coldness either.
But in everything you are too familiar with the spirit; and you have often made of wisdom a poorhouse and a hospital for bad poets.
You are not eagles: so you have not known the happiness in the terror of the spirit either. And whoever is not a bird should not camp above abysses.
You are lukewarm to me: but all deep knowledge flows cold. Ice-cold are the innermost wells of the spirit: a refreshment to hot hands and to those who act.
You stand there honourably, stiff, with straight backs, you famous wise men! No strong wind or will drives you.
Have you never seen a sail go over the sea, rounded and swelling and trembling before the violence of the wind?
Like the sail, trembling before the violence of the spirit, my wisdom goes over the sea, my wild wisdom!
But you servants of the people, you famous wise men, how could you go with me!
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## The Night Song
It is night: now all the leaping fountains speak more loudly. And my soul too is a leaping fountain.
It is night: only now do all the songs of lovers awake. And my soul too is the song of a lover.
Something unstilled, unstillable is in me; it wants to be heard. A craving for love is in me, which itself speaks the language of love.
I am light: ah, that I were night! But this is my loneliness, that I am girded round with light.
Ah, that I were dark and like the night! How I would suck at the breasts of light!
And I would even bless you, you little twinkling stars and glow-worms up there! And be happy in your gifts of light.
But I live in my own light; I drink back into myself the flames that break out of me.
I do not know the happiness of the one who takes; and I have often dreamed that stealing must be even more blessed than taking.
This is my poverty, that my hand never rests from giving; this is my envy, that I see waiting eyes and the lit-up nights of longing.
Oh, the unhappiness of all who give! Oh, the darkening of my sun! Oh, the craving to crave! Oh, the ravenous hunger in being full!
They take from me: but do I still touch their soul? There is a gulf between giving and taking; and the smallest gulf is the last to be bridged.
A hunger grows out of my beauty: I would like to hurt those I shine for, I would like to rob those I have given to: so I hunger for malice.
Drawing back my hand when a hand is already reaching out to it; hesitating like the waterfall that hesitates even as it falls: so I hunger for malice.
Such revenge my fullness devises; such spite wells up out of my loneliness.
My happiness in giving died in giving; my virtue grew tired of itself in its overflowing!
Whoever always gives is in danger of losing his shame; whoever always hands out, his hand and heart grow calloused from so much handing out.
My eye no longer overflows at the shame of those who ask; my hand has become too hard for the trembling of filled hands.
Where have the tears gone from my eye, and the down from my heart? Oh, the loneliness of all who give! Oh, the silence of all who shine!
Many suns circle in empty space: to everything that is dark they speak with their light; to me they are silent.
Oh, this is the enmity of light towards what shines: without mercy it goes its ways.
Unfair to what shines in its deepest heart, cold to suns: so every sun goes its way.
Like a storm the suns fly along their paths: that is their going. They follow their unrelenting will: that is their coldness.
Oh, it is only you, you dark ones, you night-like ones, who make warmth out of what shines! Oh, only you drink milk and refreshment from the udders of light!
Ah, there is ice around me; my hand burns itself on what is icy! Ah, there is thirst in me, that pines for your thirst!
It is night: ah, that I must be light! And thirst for what is of the night! And loneliness!
It is night: now my longing breaks out of me like a spring; I long to speak.
It is night: now all the leaping fountains speak more loudly. And my soul too is a leaping fountain.
It is night: only now do all the songs of lovers awake. And my soul too is the song of a lover.
Thus sang Zarathustra.
## The Dance Song

One evening Zarathustra was walking through the forest with his disciples; and as he was looking for a spring, he came upon a green meadow, quietly surrounded by trees and bushes, where girls were dancing together. As soon as the girls recognised Zarathustra, they stopped dancing; but Zarathustra went up to them with a friendly gesture and spoke these words:
“Do not stop dancing, you lovely girls! No spoilsport has come to you with an evil eye, no enemy of girls.
I am God’s advocate before the devil; and the devil is the spirit of gravity. How could I, you light ones, be an enemy of divine dances? Or of girls’ feet with pretty ankles?
I am a forest, it is true, and a night of dark trees: but whoever is not afraid of my darkness will also find banks of roses under my cypresses.
And he will surely find the little god too, whom girls love best: he lies beside the spring, quiet, with his eyes closed.
Truly, he has fallen asleep in broad daylight, the idler! Has he been chasing butterflies too much?
Do not be angry with me, you beautiful dancers, if I punish the little god a little! He will scream, I expect, and cry; but he is laughable even when he cries!
And with tears in his eyes he shall ask you for a dance; and I myself will sing a song for his dance:
a dancing song and a mocking song on the spirit of gravity, my supreme and most powerful devil, who they say is ‘the lord of the world’.”
And this is the song Zarathustra sang, while Cupid and the girls danced together:
Into your eye I looked lately, O life! And I seemed to myself to sink into the unfathomable.
But you pulled me out with a golden fishing rod; you laughed mockingly when I called you unfathomable.
“That is what all fish say,” you said; “what they cannot fathom is unfathomable.
But I am only changeable, and wild, and in everything a woman, and not a virtuous one:
even if you men call me ‘the deep’, or ‘the faithful’, ‘the eternal’, ‘the mysterious’.
But you men always make us presents of your own virtues. Ah, you virtuous ones!”
So she laughed, the unbelievable one; but I never believe her and her laughter when she speaks badly of herself.
And when I spoke in private with my wild wisdom, she said to me angrily: “You will, you crave, you love; that is the only reason you praise life!”
I almost answered her wickedly then, and told the angry one the truth; and one cannot answer more wickedly than when one “tells the truth” to one’s wisdom.
For this is how things stand between the three of us. From the bottom of my heart I love only life, and truly, most of all when I hate it!
But that I am fond of wisdom, and often too fond: that is because she reminds me so very much of life!
She has her eye, her laugh, and even her little golden fishing rod: how can I help it that the two look so alike?
And when life once asked me, “Who is she, then, this wisdom?” I said eagerly: “Ah, yes! Wisdom!
One thirsts for her and is never satisfied; one looks through veils, one snatches through nets.
Is she beautiful? What do I know! But the oldest carp are still caught with her as bait.
She is changeable and stubborn; I have often seen her bite her lip and comb her hair against the grain.
Perhaps she is wicked and false, and in everything a woman; but when she speaks badly of herself, that is just when she is most seductive.”
When I said this to life, she laughed maliciously and closed her eyes. “Whom are you talking about?” she said. “About me, surely?
And even if you were right, is that the kind of thing one says to my face? But now speak about your wisdom too!”
Ah, and now you opened your eye again, O beloved life! And I seemed to myself to sink into the unfathomable again.
Thus sang Zarathustra. But when the dance was over and the girls had gone away, he became sad.
“The sun went down long ago,” he said at last; “the meadow is damp, a coolness comes from the forests.
Something unknown is around me, and looks thoughtful. What! You are still alive, Zarathustra?
Why? What for? By what? Where to? Where? How? Is it not folly to go on living?
Ah, my friends, it is the evening that asks such questions out of me. Forgive me my sadness!
Evening has come: forgive me that evening has come!”
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## The Grave Song
“Over there is the island of graves, the silent one; there too are the graves of my youth. I will take an evergreen wreath of life there.”
So resolving in my heart, I crossed the sea.
O you visions and apparitions of my youth! O all you glances of love, you divine moments! How quickly you died on me! I remember you today as I remember my dead.
From you, my dearest dead, a sweet scent comes to me, a scent that loosens heart and tears. Truly, it shakes and loosens the heart of the lonely sailor.
I am still the richest and the most to be envied, I, the loneliest! For I had you, and you have me still: tell me, for whom else did such rosy apples fall from the tree?
I am still the heir and soil of your love, blooming in your memory with bright, wild-growing virtues, O you most beloved!
Ah, we were made to stay near each other, you sweet strange wonders; and you did not come to me and my longing like shy birds, no, but as the trusting to the trusting!
Yes, made for faithfulness, like me, and for tender eternities: must I now name you by your faithlessness, you divine glances and moments? I have not yet learned any other name.
Truly, you died too quickly on me, you fugitives. Yet you did not flee me, nor I you: we are innocent towards each other in our faithlessness.
To kill me, they strangled you, you songbirds of my hopes! Yes, it was always at you, my dearest, that malice shot its arrows, to hit my heart!
And it hit! For you were always what was dearest to my heart, my possession and my being possessed: that is why you had to die young, and all too soon!
They shot the arrow at the most vulnerable thing I had: that was you, whose skin is like down, and still more like the smile that dies at a glance!
But this word I will say to my enemies: what is all murder of men compared with what you did to me!
You did something worse to me than any murder of men; you took from me what cannot be brought back: so I speak to you, my enemies!
For you murdered the visions of my youth and my dearest wonders! You took my playmates from me, the blessed spirits! To their memory I lay down this wreath and this curse.
This curse against you, my enemies! For you made my eternal short, as a note breaks off in the cold night! It came to me only as a flash of divine eyes, as a moment!
So once, in a good hour, my purity spoke: “All beings shall be divine to me.”
Then you attacked me with dirty ghosts; ah, where has that good hour fled to now!
“All days shall be holy to me”: so the wisdom of my youth once spoke; truly, the speech of a joyful wisdom!
But then you enemies stole my nights from me and sold them to sleepless torment: ah, where has that joyful wisdom fled to now?
Once I longed for happy omens from birds: then you led an owl-monster across my path, a repulsive one. Ah, where did my tender longing flee to then?
Once I vowed to give up all disgust: then you turned those near and nearest to me into boils. Ah, where did my noblest vow flee to then?
As a blind man I once walked blessed paths: then you threw filth on the blind man’s path, and now he is disgusted with the old blind man’s footpath.
And when I did my hardest and celebrated the victory of my overcomings, then you made those who loved me cry out that I was hurting them most.
Truly, that has always been your doing: you embittered my best honey and the industry of my best bees.
To my charity you always sent the most shameless beggars; around my pity you always crowded the incurably shameless. So you wounded my virtue in its faith.
And when I laid my holiest down as a sacrifice, at once your “piety” set its fatter gifts beside it, so that my holiest was choked in the steam of your fat.
And once I wanted to dance as I had never danced before: I wanted to dance away over all the heavens. Then you talked my dearest singer round.
And now he struck up a gruesome, dull tune; ah, he hooted in my ears like a gloomy horn!
Murderous singer, instrument of malice, most innocent one! I was already standing ready for the best dance: then with your notes you murdered my rapture!
Only in dance do I know how to speak the parable of the highest things; and now my highest parable has stayed unspoken in my limbs!
Unspoken and unredeemed my highest hope has stayed! And all the visions and consolations of my youth have died on me!
How did I bear it? How did I get over and overcome such wounds? How did my soul rise again out of these graves?
Yes, there is something in me that cannot be wounded, that cannot be buried, something that bursts rocks: it is called my will. Silently it strides, unchanged, through the years.
It wants to go its way on my feet, my old will; its mind is hard of heart and cannot be wounded.
I am invulnerable only in my heel. You still live there and are the same, most patient one! You have always broken out through all graves!
In you lives on too what was unredeemed in my youth; and as life and youth you sit here, hoping, on yellow ruins of graves.
Yes, you are still for me the destroyer of all graves: hail to you, my will! And only where there are graves are there resurrections.
Thus sang Zarathustra.
## On Self-Overcoming
“Will to truth”: is that what you call what drives you and sets you on fire, you wisest of men?
Will to make all that exists thinkable: that is what I call your will!
You want first to make all that exists thinkable: for you doubt, with a healthy mistrust, whether it is thinkable already.
But it must fit itself to you and bend! So your will wants it. It must become smooth and subject to the spirit, as its mirror and reflection.

That is your whole will, you wisest of men, a will to power; and even when you speak of good and evil and of valuations. You still want to create the world before which you can kneel: that is your last hope and intoxication.
The unwise, of course, the people: they are like the river on which a boat floats along; and in the boat sit the valuations, solemn and masked.
You set your will and your values on the river of becoming; what the people believe to be good and evil betrays to me an old will to power.
It was you, wisest of men, who put such passengers into this boat and gave them pomp and proud names: you and your ruling will!
Now the river carries your boat further: it must carry it. It matters little if the broken wave foams and angrily contradicts the keel!
It is not the river that is your danger and the end of your good and evil, you wisest of men, but that will itself, the will to power: the unexhausted, begetting will of life.
But so that you understand my word about good and evil, I will tell you my word about life too, and about the nature of all living things.
I followed the living; I walked the greatest and the smallest paths, to know its nature.
With a hundredfold mirror I still caught its look when its mouth was shut, so that its eye might speak to me. And its eye spoke to me.
But wherever I found living things, there I also heard talk of obedience. All living things are things that obey.
And this is the second thing: whoever cannot obey himself is commanded. That is the nature of living things.
But this is the third thing I heard: that commanding is harder than obeying. And not only that the one who commands bears the burden of all who obey, and that this burden easily crushes him:
an experiment and a risk appeared to me in all commanding; and whenever the living thing commands, it risks itself in doing so.
Yes, even when it commands itself: even then it must pay for its commanding. It must become judge and avenger and victim of its own law.
How does this happen? So I asked myself. What persuades the living thing to obey and to command, and even in commanding to practise obedience?
Hear my word now, you wisest of men! Test it seriously, whether I have crept into the heart of life itself, and down into the roots of its heart!
Wherever I found living things, I found will to power; and even in the will of the one who serves I found the will to be master.
That the weaker should serve the stronger, its will persuades it, which wants to be master over what is weaker still: this one pleasure it does not want to do without.
And as the smaller gives itself to the greater, so that it may have pleasure and power over the smallest: so even the greatest gives itself, and for the sake of power stakes its life.
That is the surrender of the greatest: that it is risk and danger, and a throw of the dice for death.

And where there is sacrifice and service and loving looks, there too is the will to be master. By secret paths the weaker creeps into the castle and into the very heart of the more powerful, and steals power there.
And this secret life itself told me. “Look,” it said, “I am that which must always overcome itself.
Of course, you call it will to beget, or drive towards a goal, towards the higher, the farther, the more manifold: but all this is one, and one secret.
I would rather go under than renounce this one thing; and truly, where there is going under and the falling of leaves, look, there life sacrifices itself, for power!
That I must be struggle and becoming and goal and the contradiction of goals: ah, whoever guesses my will surely guesses too on what crooked paths it must go!
Whatever I create, and however much I love it, soon I must be its opponent, and my love’s: so my will wills it.
And you too, seeker of knowledge, are only a path and footprint of my will: truly, my will to power walks on the feet of your will to truth as well!
He certainly did not hit the truth who shot at it with the phrase ‘will to existence’: that will does not exist!
For what does not exist cannot will; but what is in existence, how could it still will to exist!
Only where there is life is there will too: but not will to life, but, so I teach you, will to power!
Much is valued more highly by the living than life itself; but out of the very valuing speaks the will to power!”
So life once taught me; and with this I solve for you, you wisest of men, the riddle of your hearts as well.
Truly, I tell you: good and evil that would be everlasting, that does not exist! It must overcome itself again and again out of itself.
With your values and words of good and evil you use force, you who value; and this is your hidden love, and the shining, trembling and overflowing of your souls.
But a stronger force grows out of your values, and a new overcoming: on it egg and eggshell break.
And whoever must be a creator in good and evil, truly, he must first be a destroyer and break values.
So the highest evil belongs to the highest goodness: but this is the creative kind.
Let us speak of it, you wisest of men, even if it is bad. To be silent is worse; all truths kept silent become poisonous.
And let everything break that can break on our truths! There are many houses still to build!
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On the Sublime Ones
The floor of my sea is still: who would guess that it hides playful monsters!
My depth is unshakable: but it sparkles with swimming riddles and laughter.
Today I saw a sublime one, a solemn one, a penitent of the spirit: oh, how my soul laughed at his ugliness!
With his chest puffed out, like those who are drawing in breath: so he stood there, the sublime one, and silent:
hung with ugly truths, his hunting spoils, and rich in torn clothes; many thorns hung on him too, but I saw no rose yet.
He has not yet learned laughter and beauty. Gloomily this hunter came back from the forest of knowledge.
He came home from fighting with wild beasts: but out of his seriousness a wild beast still looks too, an unconquered one!
He still stands there like a tiger about to spring; but I do not like these tense souls; my taste is unfriendly to all these withdrawn ones.
And you tell me, friends, that there is no arguing about taste and tasting? But all life is an argument about taste and tasting!
Taste: that is at once the weight and the scale and the one who weighs; and woe to every living thing that wanted to live without arguing about weight and scale and weigher!
If he grew tired of his sublimity, this sublime one, only then would his beauty begin; and only then will I taste him and find him tasteful.
And only when he turns away from himself will he jump over his own shadow, and, truly, into his own sun.
Too long he sat in the shade; the cheeks of the penitent of the spirit grew pale; he almost starved on his expectations.
There is still contempt in his eye, and disgust hides at his mouth. He is resting now, it is true, but his rest has not yet lain down in the sun.
He should do as the bull does; and his happiness should smell of the earth, and not of contempt for the earth.
I would like to see him as a white bull, snorting and bellowing as he goes before the ploughshare; and his bellowing should still praise everything earthly!
His face is still dark; the shadow of the hand plays on it. The sense of his eye is still in shadow.
His deed itself is still the shadow on him: the hand darkens the one who acts. He has not yet overcome his deed.
I love the bull’s neck on him, it is true: but now I want to see the angel’s eye as well.
He must also unlearn his hero’s will: he should be one who is lifted up, and not merely a sublime one; the air itself should lift him, the will-less one!
He tamed monsters, he solved riddles: but he should also redeem his monsters and riddles; he should turn them into heavenly children.
His knowledge has not yet learned to smile and to be without jealousy; his streaming passion has not yet grown still in beauty.
Truly, his longing should fall silent and sink, not in being full, but in beauty! Grace belongs to the generosity of the great-minded.
With his arm laid over his head: so the hero should rest; so he should overcome even his resting.
But to the hero above all, the beautiful is the hardest thing of all. The beautiful cannot be won by any violent will.
A little more, a little less: that is just what counts for much here, for most of all.
To stand with relaxed muscles and with the will unharnessed: that is the hardest thing for all of you, you sublime ones!
When power becomes gracious and comes down into the visible: I call such coming down beauty.
And from no one do I want beauty so much as from you, you powerful one: let your goodness be your last self-conquest.
I believe you capable of every evil: that is why I want the good from you.
Truly, I have often laughed at the weaklings who think themselves good because they have lame paws!
You should strive after the virtue of the column: it grows ever more beautiful and more delicate, but inwardly harder and more able to bear weight, the higher it rises.
Yes, you sublime one, one day you shall still be beautiful, and hold the mirror up to your own beauty.
Then your soul will shudder with divine desires; and there will be worship even in your vanity!
For this is the secret of the soul: only when the hero has left it does there come to it, in a dream, the over-hero.
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On the Land of Culture
I flew too far into the future: a horror came over me.
And when I looked around me, look! time was my only contemporary.
Then I fled backwards, homewards, and ever faster: so I came to you, you people of today, and into the land of culture.
For the first time I brought an eye for you, and a good desire: truly, I came with longing in my heart.
But what happened to me? Afraid as I was, I had to laugh! Never had my eye seen anything so motley!
I laughed and laughed, while my foot still trembled, and my heart as well: “Why, this is the home of all the paint pots!” I said.
Painted with fifty blotches on your faces and limbs: so you sat there, to my astonishment, you people of today!
And with fifty mirrors around you, flattering your play of colours and repeating it!
Truly, you could wear no better mask, you people of today, than your own face! Who could recognise you!
Written all over with the signs of the past, and these signs too painted over with new signs: so you have hidden yourselves well from all interpreters of signs!
And even if one could test the inmost heart: who would still believe that you have one! You seem to be baked out of colours and glued scraps of paper.
All ages and peoples look out motley from your veils; all customs and beliefs speak motley out of your gestures.
Whoever took away your veils and wraps and colours and gestures would have just enough left over to frighten the birds with.
Truly, I myself am the frightened bird who once saw you naked and without colour; and I flew away when the skeleton beckoned to me with love.
I would rather be a day labourer in the underworld, among the shades of the past! Why, even the people of the underworld are plumper and fuller than you!
This, yes this is bitterness to my bowels, that I can bear you neither naked nor clothed, you people of today!
Everything uncanny in the future, and everything that ever made strayed birds shudder, is truly more homely and more familiar than your “reality”.
For so you speak: “We are wholly real, and without faith or superstition.” So you puff out your chests: ah, though you have no chests!
Yes, how could you be able to believe, you motley ones! You who are paintings of everything that was ever believed!
You are walking refutations of belief itself, and the breaking of the limbs of every thought. Unbelievable: that is what I call you, you real ones!
All ages chatter against one another in your spirits; and the dreams and chatter of all ages were more real than your being awake!
You are barren: that is why you lack faith. But whoever had to create always had his prophetic dreams and signs in the stars too, and believed in belief!
You are half-open gates, at which gravediggers wait. And this is your reality: “Everything deserves to perish.”
Ah, how you stand there before me, you barren ones, how lean in the ribs! And many of you have surely noticed this yourselves.
And he said: “Did a god perhaps secretly take something from me while I slept? Truly, enough to make a little woman out of!
The poverty of my ribs is wonderful!” So many a person of today has spoken.
Yes, you make me laugh, you people of today! And especially when you are amazed at yourselves!
And woe to me if I could not laugh at your amazement, and had to drink down everything repulsive out of your bowls!
But as it is, I will take you more lightly, since I have something heavy to carry; and what does it matter to me if beetles and winged worms settle on my bundle!
Truly, it shall not become heavier for me because of that! And it is not from you, you people of today, that my great weariness shall come.
Ah, where shall I climb now with my longing! From all mountains I look out for fatherlands and motherlands.
But I found a home nowhere: I am restless in all cities, and a departure at all gates.
Strange to me, and a mockery, are the people of today, to whom my heart lately drove me; and I am driven out of fatherlands and motherlands.
So now I love only my children’s land, the undiscovered one, in the farthest sea: for that I bid my sails search and search.
In my children I will make up for being the child of my fathers; and to all the future, for this present!
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On Immaculate Perception
When the moon rose yesterday, I imagined it wanted to give birth to a sun: so broad and pregnant it lay on the horizon.
But it was a liar to me with its pregnancy; and I would sooner believe in the man in the moon than in the woman.
Of course he is not much of a man either, this shy night-wanderer. Truly, he walks over the roofs with a bad conscience.
For he is lustful and jealous, the monk in the moon, lustful for the earth and for all the joys of lovers.
No, I do not like him, this tomcat on the roofs! All those who creep around half-closed windows disgust me!
Piously and silently he walks along on carpets of stars: but I do not like any soft-treading man’s feet on which not even a spur jingles.
Every honest man’s step speaks; but the cat steals away across the floor. Look, the moon comes along like a cat, and dishonestly.
This parable I give to you sentimental hypocrites, you “pure perceivers”! I call you: lustful ones!
You too love the earth and what is earthly: I have seen through you! But there is shame in your love, and a bad conscience: you are like the moon!
Your spirit has been persuaded to despise what is earthly, but not your bowels: and they are the strongest part of you!
And now your spirit is ashamed of doing what your bowels want, and goes by secret and lying paths to escape its own shame.
“For me the highest thing would be,” so your lying spirit says to itself, “to look at life without desire, and not like a dog with its tongue hanging out:
to be happy in looking, with a will that has died, without the grasp and greed of selfishness; cold and ash-grey all over the body, but with drunken moon-eyes!”
“For me the dearest thing would be,” so the seduced one seduces himself, “to love the earth as the moon loves it, and to touch its beauty with the eye alone.
And let this be called the immaculate perception of all things: that I want nothing from things, except to be allowed to lie before them like a mirror with a hundred eyes.”
Oh, you sentimental hypocrites, you lustful ones! You lack innocence in desire: and so now you slander desiring!
Truly, you do not love the earth as creators, as begetters, as those who delight in becoming!
Where is innocence? Where there is the will to beget. And whoever wants to create beyond himself has, for me, the purest will.
Where is beauty? Where I must will with my whole will; where I want to love and go under, so that an image does not remain merely an image.
Loving and going under: these have rhymed since eternity. Will to love: that means being willing to die as well. So I speak to you cowards!
But now your unmanned squinting wants to be called “contemplation”! And whatever lets itself be fingered by cowardly eyes is to be christened “beautiful”! Oh, you defilers of noble names!
But this shall be your curse, you immaculate ones, you pure perceivers, that you will never give birth, even if you lie broad and pregnant on the horizon!
Truly, you fill your mouths with noble words: and are we to believe that your hearts are overflowing, you liars?
But my words are small, despised, crooked words: I gladly pick up what falls under the table at your meals.
With them I can still tell hypocrites the truth! Yes, my fish bones, shells and prickly leaves shall tickle the noses of hypocrites!
There is always bad air around you and your meals: your lustful thoughts, your lies and secrets are in the air!
Dare first to believe yourselves: yourselves and your bowels! Whoever does not believe himself always lies.
You hung the mask of a god in front of yourselves, you “pure ones”: your horrible coiling worm crept into the mask of a god.
Truly, you deceive, you “contemplative ones”! Zarathustra too was once the fool of your divine skins; he did not guess the coils of snakes they were stuffed with.
I once imagined I saw a god’s soul playing in your games, you pure perceivers! I once imagined there was no better art than your arts!
Distance hid from me the snake-filth and the bad smell, and that a lizard’s cunning crept lustfully about here.
But I came near you: then the day came to me, and now it is coming to you; the moon’s love affair has come to an end!
Just look! There he stands, caught and pale, before the dawn!
For she is coming already, the glowing one: her love for the earth is coming! All sun-love is innocence and the creator’s desire!
Just look how impatiently she comes over the sea! Do you not feel the thirst and the hot breath of her love?
She wants to suck at the sea and drink its depth up to her height: and the desire of the sea rises with a thousand breasts.
It wants to be kissed and sucked by the sun’s thirst; it wants to become air and height and a footpath of light, and light itself!
Truly, like the sun I love life and all deep seas.
And this is what I call knowledge: everything deep shall rise up, to my height!
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On Scholars
As I lay asleep, a sheep ate at the ivy wreath on my head; it ate, and said as it did so: “Zarathustra is no longer a scholar.”
It said this, and went away, stiff and proud. A child told me about it.
I like to lie here, where the children play, by the broken wall, among thistles and red poppies.
To the children I am still a scholar, and to the thistles and red poppies too. They are innocent, even in their malice.
But to the sheep I am no longer one: so my lot wills it; blessed be it!
For this is the truth: I have moved out of the house of the scholars, and I slammed the door behind me too.
Too long my soul sat hungry at their table; I am not trained, as they are, for knowing as for cracking nuts.
I love freedom and the air over fresh earth; I would rather sleep on ox-hides than on their dignities and respectabilities.
I am too hot and scorched by my own thoughts: it often takes my breath away. Then I must go out into the open, away from all dusty rooms.
But they sit cool in the cool shade: in everything they want only to be spectators, and they take care not to sit where the sun burns on the steps.
Like those who stand in the street and gape at the people passing by: so they too wait and gape at thoughts that others have thought.

If you take hold of them with your hands, they give off dust like flour sacks, and without meaning to; but who would guess that their dust comes from grain, and from the yellow delight of summer fields?

When they act wise, their little sayings and truths make me shiver: there is often a smell about their wisdom, as if it came from the swamp; and truly, I have already heard the frog croaking out of it!

They are skilful, they have clever fingers: what does my simplicity want beside their complexity! Their fingers understand all threading and knotting and weaving: so they knit the stockings of the spirit!
They are good clockworks: only take care to wind them up properly! Then they show the hour without error, and make a modest noise as they do it.
They work like mills and stamping machines: just throw them your grain! They know how to grind corn small and make white dust out of it.
They watch each other’s fingers closely and do not trust one another an inch. Inventive in small cunning, they wait for those whose knowledge walks on lame feet: they wait like spiders.
I have always seen them prepare poison carefully; and they always put glass gloves on their fingers while they did it.
They know how to play with loaded dice too; and I found them playing so eagerly that they sweated.
We are strangers to one another, and their virtues go even more against my taste than their falsehoods and loaded dice.
And when I lived with them, I lived above them. They resented me for that.
They do not want to hear that anyone walks above their heads; and so they put wood and earth and rubbish between me and their heads.
So they muffled the sound of my steps: and until now I have been heard worst by the most learned.
They put all human faults and weaknesses between themselves and me: in their houses they call it a “false floor”.
But in spite of this I walk with my thoughts above their heads; and even if I wanted to walk on my own mistakes, I would still be above them and their heads.
For people are not equal: so justice speaks. And what I want, they may not want!
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On Poets
“Since I have come to know the body better,” said Zarathustra to one of his disciples, “the spirit is only, as it were, spirit to me; and all that is ‘imperishable’ is only a parable too.”
“I have heard you say that once before,” answered the disciple; “and then you added: ‘But the poets lie too much.’ Why did you say that the poets lie too much?”
“Why?” said Zarathustra. “You ask why? I am not one of those who may be asked for their why.
Is my experience from yesterday, then? It is long ago that I experienced the reasons for my opinions.
Would I not have to be a barrel of memory, if I wanted to have my reasons with me too?
It is already too much for me to keep my opinions themselves; and many a bird flies away.
And now and then I find a stray creature in my dovecote too, one that is strange to me, and that trembles when I lay my hand on it.
But what did Zarathustra once say to you? That the poets lie too much? But Zarathustra too is a poet.
Do you believe, then, that he spoke the truth here? Why do you believe it?”
The disciple answered: “I believe in Zarathustra.” But Zarathustra shook his head and smiled.
Faith does not make me blessed, he said, least of all faith in me.
But suppose someone said in all seriousness that the poets lie too much: he is right; we lie too much.
We also know too little and are bad learners: so we have to lie.
And which of us poets has not watered his wine? Many a poisonous hotchpotch has been made in our cellars; many an indescribable thing has been done there.
And because we know little, we are heartily fond of the poor in spirit, especially when they are young women!
And we are even greedy for the things that old women tell each other in the evenings. That is what we ourselves call the eternal feminine in us.
And as if there were a special secret way to knowledge, which is blocked to those who learn something: so we believe in the people and their “wisdom”.
But all poets believe this: that whoever lies in the grass or on lonely slopes and pricks up his ears will learn something of the things that are between heaven and earth.
And when tender feelings come to them, the poets always think that nature herself is in love with them:
and that she creeps to their ear to tell them secrets and loving flatteries: they boast of this and puff themselves up before all mortals!
Ah, there are so many things between heaven and earth that only the poets have dreamed of!
And especially above the heavens: for all gods are a poet’s parable, a poet’s trickery!
Truly, we are always drawn upward, that is, to the realm of the clouds: on these we set our motley bags of skin and then call them gods and Overmen.
For they are just light enough for these chairs, all these gods and Overmen!
Ah, how tired I am of all the inadequate that insists on being an event! Ah, how tired I am of the poets!

When Zarathustra spoke so, his disciple was angry with him, but he kept silent. And Zarathustra too was silent; and his eye had turned inward, as if it were looking into far distances. At last he sighed and drew breath.
I am of today and of before, he then said; but there is something in me that is of tomorrow and the day after tomorrow and of some day to come.
I grew tired of the poets, the old and the new: they are all superficial to me, and shallow seas.
They did not think deeply enough: that is why their feeling did not sink to the bottom.
A little lust and a little boredom: that has still been their best reflection.
All their harp-jingling is to me the breath and flitting of ghosts; what have they ever known of the fervour of sounds!
They are not clean enough for me either: they all muddy their waters, so that they may seem deep.
And they like to present themselves as reconcilers: but to me they remain go-betweens and mixers, half-and-halfs and unclean!
Ah, I cast my net into their seas, and wanted to catch good fish; but I always pulled up the head of some old god.
So the sea gave the hungry man a stone. And they themselves may well come from the sea.
Certainly, one finds pearls in them: all the more are they themselves like hard shellfish. And instead of a soul I have often found salty slime in them.
They have learned its vanity from the sea too: is not the sea the peacock of peacocks?
Even before the ugliest of all buffaloes it spreads out its tail; it never tires of its lace fan of silver and silk.
The buffalo looks on defiantly, close to the sand in his soul, closer still to the thicket, but closest of all to the swamp.
What are beauty and sea and peacock finery to him! This parable I tell the poets.
Truly, their spirit itself is the peacock of peacocks and a sea of vanity!
The poet’s spirit wants spectators, even if they are buffaloes!
But I grew tired of this spirit; and I see the time coming when it will grow tired of itself.
I have already seen the poets changed, and turning their gaze against themselves.
I have seen penitents of the spirit coming: they grew out of the poets.
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On Great Events

There is an island in the sea, not far from Zarathustra’s blessed isles, on which a volcano constantly smokes; of it the people say, and especially the old women among the people, that it has been set like a boulder before the gate of the underworld; and through the volcano itself the narrow path leads downward to this gate of the underworld.

Now at the time when Zarathustra was staying on the blessed isles, it happened that a ship cast anchor at the island where the smoking mountain stands; and its crew went ashore to shoot rabbits. But towards the hour of noon, when the captain and his men were together again, they suddenly saw a man coming towards them through the air, and a voice said clearly: “It is time! It is high time!” But when the figure was nearest to them (it flew past quickly like a shadow, in the direction of the volcano), they recognised with the greatest dismay that it was Zarathustra; for they had all seen him before, except the captain himself, and they loved him as the people love: that is, with love and awe in equal parts.
“Look there!” said the old helmsman. “There goes Zarathustra to hell!”

At the same time as these sailors landed on the fire island, the rumour went round that Zarathustra had disappeared; and when his friends were asked, they said he had gone on board a ship by night, without saying where he meant to travel.

So there was some unrest; and after three days the sailors’ story was added to this unrest, and now all the people said that the devil had taken Zarathustra. His disciples laughed at this talk, it is true; and one of them even said: “I would sooner believe that Zarathustra has taken the devil.” But at the bottom of their souls they were all full of worry and longing: so their joy was great when on the fifth day Zarathustra appeared among them.
And this is the story of Zarathustra’s conversation with the fire-dog.
The earth, he said, has a skin; and this skin has diseases. One of these diseases, for example, is called “man”.
And another of these diseases is called “fire-dog”: about him people have told themselves many lies, and let themselves be told many.
To get to the bottom of this secret I went over the sea; and I have seen the truth naked, truly! barefoot up to the neck.
I know now what the fire-dog is about; and likewise all the devils of eruption and overthrow, of whom it is not only old women who are afraid.
“Come out, fire-dog, out of your depth!” I cried, “and confess how deep this depth is! Where does it come from, what you are snorting up there?
You drink plentifully from the sea: your salty eloquence gives that away! Indeed, for a dog of the depths you take your food too much from the surface!
At most I take you for the ventriloquist of the earth: and whenever I have heard devils of overthrow and eruption speak, I have found them like you: salty, lying and shallow.
You know how to roar and to darken things with ashes! You are the best of braggarts, and you have learned well enough the art of making mud boil.
Wherever you are, there must always be mud nearby, and much that is spongy, hollow, squeezed in: it wants to be free.
‘Freedom’ is what you all like best to roar: but I have unlearned belief in ‘great events’ whenever there is much roaring and smoke around them.
And believe me, friend Hellish Racket! The greatest events are not our loudest but our stillest hours.
Not around the inventors of new noise, but around the inventors of new values does the world turn; it turns inaudibly.
And just admit it! Little had ever happened when your noise and smoke cleared away. What does it matter that a city became a mummy and a statue lies in the mud!
And I say this word too to those who overthrow statues. It is surely the greatest folly to throw salt into the sea and statues into the mud.
The statue lay in the mud of your contempt: but it is just its law that out of contempt its life and living beauty grow again!
With more divine features it rises now, and seductive in its suffering; and truly! it will yet thank you for overthrowing it, you overthrowers!
But this advice I give to kings and churches and everything that is weak with age and virtue: just let yourselves be overthrown! So that you may come back to life, and virtue come back to you!”
So I spoke before the fire-dog: then he interrupted me sulkily and asked: “Church? What is that?”
“Church?” I answered. “That is a kind of state, and the most deceitful kind. But be quiet, you hypocrite dog! You surely know your own kind best already!
Like yourself, the state is a hypocrite dog; like you it likes to speak with smoke and roaring, to make people believe, like you, that it speaks from the belly of things.
For the state wants at all costs to be the most important animal on earth; and people believe it, too.”

When I had said this, the fire-dog behaved as if mad with envy. “What?” he cried. “The most important animal on earth? And people believe it, too?” And so much steam and such horrible voices came out of his throat that I thought he would choke with anger and envy.
At last he grew quieter, and his panting eased; but as soon as he was quiet, I said, laughing:
“You are angry, fire-dog: so I am right about you!
And so that I may stay right, hear about another fire-dog: he really speaks from the heart of the earth.
His breath breathes gold and golden rain: so his heart wills it. What are ashes and smoke and hot slime to him now!
Laughter flutters out of him like a bright cloud; he is averse to your gurgling and spitting and the grumbling of your bowels!
But the gold and the laughter he takes from the heart of the earth: for, just so that you know it, the heart of the earth is of gold.”
When the fire-dog heard this, he could not bear to listen to me any longer. Ashamed, he drew in his tail, said in a small voice “Bow-wow!”, and crept down into his cave.
So Zarathustra told it. But his disciples hardly listened to him: so great was their eagerness to tell him about the sailors, the rabbits and the flying man.
“What am I to make of it!” said Zarathustra. “Am I a ghost, then?
But it must have been my shadow. You have surely heard something already of the wanderer and his shadow?
But this much is certain: I must keep it on a shorter leash; otherwise it will spoil my reputation yet.”
And once more Zarathustra shook his head and wondered. “What am I to make of it!” he said again.
“Why did the ghost cry: ‘It is time! It is high time!’
For what, then, is it high time?”
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## The Soothsayer
“...and I saw a great sadness come over mankind. The best grew tired of their works.
A teaching went out, and a faith ran beside it: ‘All is empty, all is the same, all has been!’
And from all the hills it echoed: ‘All is empty, all is the same, all has been!’
We have harvested, it is true: but why did all our fruits turn rotten and brown? What fell down from the evil moon last night?
All our work was in vain; our wine has turned to poison; an evil eye has scorched our fields and hearts yellow.
We have all grown dry; and if fire falls on us, we fly up like ashes: yes, we have made even fire tired.
All our wells have dried up, even the sea has drawn back. All the ground wants to split open, but the depths will not swallow!
‘Ah, where is there still a sea in which one could drown?’ So our lament sounds, out over flat swamps.
Truly, we have grown too tired even to die; now we stay awake and live on, in burial vaults!”
So Zarathustra heard a soothsayer speak; and his prophecy went to his heart and changed him. He went about sad and tired; and he became like those of whom the soothsayer had spoken.
“Truly,” he said to his disciples, “it will not be long before this long twilight comes. Ah, how shall I save my light through it!
Let it not suffocate in this sadness! It is meant to be a light for more distant worlds, and for the most distant nights!”

So, troubled in his heart, Zarathustra went about; and for three days he took no food or drink, had no rest, and lost his speech. At last it happened that he fell into a deep sleep. But his disciples sat around him in long night watches, and waited anxiously to see whether he would wake and speak again and be cured of his gloom.
And this is the speech Zarathustra made when he woke; but his voice came to his disciples as if from far away.
“Hear the dream I dreamed, my friends, and help me guess its meaning!
It is still a riddle to me, this dream; its meaning is hidden in it and imprisoned, and does not yet fly above it on free wings.
I had renounced all life, so I dreamed. I had become a night-watchman and a guardian of graves, there in the lonely mountain castle of death.
Up there I guarded his coffins: the musty vaults stood full of these signs of victory. Life that had been overcome looked out at me from glass coffins.
I breathed the smell of dusty eternities: my soul lay sultry and dusty. And who could have aired his soul there!
The brightness of midnight was always around me, loneliness crouched beside it; and, as the third, a death-rattling silence, the worst of my women friends.
I carried keys, the rustiest of all keys; and I knew how to open the creakiest of all gates with them.
Like a bitter, evil croaking the sound ran through the long corridors when the wings of the gate were raised: this bird cried out unkindly; it did not like being woken.
But it was more fearful still, and more heart-gripping, when it fell silent again and everything around was still, and I sat alone in that treacherous silence.
So time went by me and crept, if there still was time: what do I know of it! But at last that happened which woke me.
Three times blows struck the gate, like thunder; the vaults echoed and howled three times: then I went to the gate.
‘Alpa!’ I cried, ‘who is carrying his ashes up the mountain? Alpa! Alpa! Who is carrying his ashes up the mountain?’
And I pressed the key and lifted at the gate and struggled. But it was not yet open a finger’s breadth:
then a roaring wind tore its wings apart: whistling, shrieking and cutting, it threw a black coffin towards me.
And in the roaring and whistling and shrieking the coffin burst open and spat out a thousandfold laughter.
And out of a thousand grimaces of children, angels, owls, fools and child-sized butterflies it laughed and mocked and roared at me.
I was horribly frightened by it: it threw me to the ground. And I screamed with horror as I had never screamed.
But my own scream woke me: and I came to myself.”
So Zarathustra told his dream, and then fell silent: for he did not yet know the meaning of his dream. But the disciple he loved most rose quickly, took Zarathustra’s hand and said:
“Your life itself explains this dream to us, O Zarathustra!
Are you not yourself the wind with its shrill whistling that tears open the gates of the castles of death?
Are you not yourself the coffin full of life’s bright malice and angel-grimaces?
Truly, like a thousandfold children’s laughter Zarathustra comes into all the death chambers, laughing at these night-watchmen and guardians of graves, and whoever else rattles gloomy keys.
You will frighten them and knock them over with your laughter; fainting and waking will prove your power over them.
And even when the long twilight comes, and the weariness of death, you will not set in our sky, you advocate of life!
You have let us see new stars and new splendours of the night; truly, you have spread laughter itself over us like a bright tent.
Now children’s laughter will always pour out of coffins; now a strong wind will always come victorious over all weariness of death: of this you yourself are our guarantee and our soothsayer!
Truly, it was they yourself you dreamed, your enemies: that was your hardest dream!
But as you woke from them and came to yourself, so they shall wake from themselves, and come to you!”

So spoke the disciple; and all the others now crowded around Zarathustra and took him by the hands and tried to persuade him to leave his bed and his sadness and come back to them. But Zarathustra sat upright on his couch, with a strange look. Like one coming home from a long time abroad, he looked at his disciples and searched their faces; and still he did not recognise them. But when they lifted him and set him on his feet, look, all at once his eye changed; he understood everything that had happened, stroked his beard, and said in a strong voice:
“Well then! This has had its time; but see to it, my disciples, that we have a good meal, and soon! So I mean to do penance for bad dreams!
But the soothsayer shall eat and drink at my side: and truly, I will yet show him a sea in which he can drown!”
Thus spoke Zarathustra. But then he looked for a long time into the face of the disciple who had played the interpreter of dreams, and shook his head.
## On Redemption
One day, as Zarathustra was crossing the great bridge, the cripples and beggars surrounded him, and a hunchback spoke to him thus:

“Look, Zarathustra! The people too learn from you and are coming to believe in your teaching: but for them to believe you completely, one thing more is needed: you must first convince us cripples too! Here you have a fine selection, and truly, a chance with more than one forelock to seize it by! You can heal the blind and make the lame walk; and from the one who has too much behind him you could surely take a little away too: that, I think, would be the right way to make the cripples believe in Zarathustra!”

But Zarathustra answered the one who spoke thus: “If you take away the hunchback’s hump, you take away his spirit: so the people teach. And if you give the blind man his eyes, he sees too many bad things on earth, so that he curses the one who healed him. But whoever makes the lame man walk does him the greatest harm: for hardly can he walk when his vices run away with him: so the people teach about cripples. And why should Zarathustra not learn from the people too, if the people learn from Zarathustra?

But it is the least thing to me, since I have been among men, to see: ‘This one lacks an eye, and that one an ear, and a third a leg, and there are others who have lost their tongue or their nose or their head.’

I see, and have seen, worse things, and many so abominable that I would not like to speak of each of them, and of some I would not like even to keep silent: namely, people who lack everything except that they have too much of one thing; people who are nothing more than a big eye, or a big mouth, or a big belly, or something else big: I call such people inverse cripples.

And when I came out of my solitude and crossed this bridge for the first time, I did not trust my eyes, and looked, and looked again, and said at last: ‘That is an ear! An ear as big as a man!’ I looked still more closely: and indeed, under the ear something else was moving, something pitifully small and poor and thin. And truly, the enormous ear sat on a little thin stalk; but the stalk was a man! Anyone who put a glass to his eye could even make out a little envious face; and also that a bloated little soul dangled from the stalk. But the people told me that the big ear was not only a man, but a great man, a genius. But I never believed the people when they spoke of great men; and I kept my belief that it was an inverse cripple, who had too little of everything and too much of one thing.”
When Zarathustra had spoken thus to the hunchback, and to those whose mouthpiece and advocate he was, he turned to his disciples with deep displeasure and said:
“Truly, my friends, I walk among men as among the fragments and limbs of men!
This is the terrible thing for my eye, that I find man broken into pieces and scattered, as over a battlefield and a butcher’s field.
And if my eye flees from the now to the past, it always finds the same: fragments and limbs and dreadful accidents, but no men!
The now and the past on earth, ah, my friends, that is what I find most unbearable; and I would not know how to live if I were not also a seer of what must come.
A seer, one who wills, a creator, a future himself and a bridge to the future; and ah, also, as it were, a cripple on this bridge: all this is Zarathustra.
And you too have often asked yourselves: ‘Who is Zarathustra to us? What shall we call him?’ And, like me, you gave yourselves questions for answers.
Is he one who promises? Or one who fulfils? A conqueror? Or an heir? An autumn? Or a ploughshare? A doctor? Or one who has been cured?
Is he a poet? Or one who is truthful? A liberator? Or a tamer? A good man? Or an evil one?
I walk among men as among the fragments of the future: that future which I see.
And this is all my poetry and striving: to compose into one and bring together what is fragment and riddle and dreadful accident.
And how could I bear to be a man, if man were not also a poet and a guesser of riddles and the redeemer of chance!
To redeem those who are past, and to transform every ‘It was’ into ‘Thus I willed it!’: that alone I would call redemption!
Will: that is the name of the liberator and the bringer of joy; so I have taught you, my friends! But now learn this as well: the will itself is still a prisoner.
Willing frees: but what is the name of that which puts even the liberator in chains?
‘It was’: that is the name of the will’s gnashing of teeth and its loneliest misery. Powerless against what has been done, it is an angry spectator of everything past.
The will cannot will backwards; that it cannot break time and time’s craving: that is the will’s loneliest misery.
Willing frees: what does willing itself devise to get free of its misery and mock its prison?
Ah, every prisoner becomes a fool! The imprisoned will, too, redeems itself foolishly.
That time does not run backwards: that is its fury; ‘That which was’: that is the name of the stone it cannot roll.
And so it rolls stones out of fury and ill-humour, and takes revenge on whatever does not feel fury and ill-humour as it does.
So the will, the liberator, became a doer of harm: and on everything that can suffer it takes revenge for not being able to go back.
This, yes, this alone is revenge itself: the will’s ill will against time and its ‘It was’.
Truly, a great folly lives in our will; and it became a curse to everything human that this folly learned to think!
The spirit of revenge: my friends, that has so far been mankind’s best reflection; and where there was suffering, there was always to be punishment.
For ‘punishment’ is what revenge calls itself: with a lying word it pretends to have a good conscience.
And because there is suffering in the one who wills, since it cannot will backwards, willing itself and all life were to be punishment!
And now cloud after cloud rolled over the spirit, until at last madness preached: ‘Everything passes away, therefore everything deserves to pass away!’
‘And this itself is justice, that law of time that it must devour its children’: so madness preached.
‘Things are ordered morally, according to justice and punishment. Oh, where is redemption from the flux of things and from the punishment called existence?’ So madness preached.
‘Can there be redemption if there is eternal justice? Ah, the stone It was cannot be rolled: all punishments must be eternal too!’ So madness preached.
‘No deed can be annihilated: how could it be undone by punishment! This, this is what is eternal in the punishment called existence, that existence must also eternally be deed and guilt again!
Unless the will at last redeemed itself, and willing became not-willing’: but you know, my brothers, this fable-song of madness!
I led you away from these fable-songs when I taught you: ‘The will is a creator.’
Every ‘It was’ is a fragment, a riddle, a dreadful accident, until the creating will says to it: ‘But thus I willed it!’
Until the creating will says to it: ‘But thus I will it! Thus shall I will it!’
But has it ever spoken so? And when does this happen? Has the will been unharnessed from its own folly yet?
Has the will become its own redeemer and bringer of joy yet? Has it unlearned the spirit of revenge and all gnashing of teeth?
