## The Wanderer

It was midnight when Zarathustra set off over the ridge of the island, so as to reach the other shore early in the morning: for there he meant to take ship. There was a good harbour there, where foreign ships too liked to anchor; they took with them many a person who wanted to go over the sea from the blessed isles. Now as Zarathustra climbed the mountain, he thought on the way of all the lonely wandering he had done since his youth, and of how many mountains and ridges and peaks he had already climbed.
“I am a wanderer and a mountain climber,” he said to his heart. “I do not love the plains, and it seems I cannot sit still for long.
And whatever comes to me now as fate and experience, there will be wandering in it and mountain climbing: in the end one experiences only oneself.
The time is past when accidents could still happen to me; and what could still fall to me now that was not already my own!
It only returns, it comes home to me at last: my own self, and whatever of it has long been abroad and scattered among all things and accidents.
And I know one thing more: I am standing now before my last peak, and before what has been saved up for me longest. Ah, I must climb my hardest path! Ah, I have begun my loneliest wandering!
But whoever is of my kind does not escape such an hour: the hour that says to him: ‘Only now are you going your way of greatness! Peak and abyss: they are now joined in one!
You are going your way of greatness: now what was until now your last danger has become your last refuge!
You are going your way of greatness: now this must be your best courage, that there is no longer any way behind you!
You are going your way of greatness; no one shall creep after you here! Your own foot has wiped out the way behind you, and over it is written: Impossibility.
And if from now on all ladders fail you, then you must know how to climb on your own head: how else would you climb upward?
On your own head, and away over your own heart! Now the gentlest thing in you must become the hardest.
Whoever has always spared himself a great deal grows sickly in the end from so much sparing. Praised be what makes hard! I do not praise the land where butter and honey flow!
To learn to look away from oneself is necessary in order to see much: this hardness is needed by every mountain climber.
But whoever is pushy with his eyes as a seeker of knowledge, how should he see more of all things than their foregrounds!
But you, O Zarathustra, wanted to see the ground and background of all things: so you must climb over yourself, up, upward, until you have even your stars beneath you!’
Yes! To look down on myself and even on my stars: only that would I call my peak; that was still left to me as my last peak!”

So Zarathustra spoke to himself as he climbed, comforting his heart with hard little sayings: for he was sore at heart as never before. And when he came to the top of the ridge, look, there the other sea lay spread out before him: and he stood still and was silent for a long time. But the night was cold at this height, and clear and bright with stars.
“I recognise my lot,” he said at last, sadly. “Well then! I am ready. My last solitude has just begun.
Ah, this black, sad sea beneath me! Ah, this pregnant, night-like sullenness! Ah, fate and sea! Now I must go down to you!
I stand before my highest mountain and before my longest wandering: that is why I must first go down deeper than I ever climbed:
deeper down into pain than I ever climbed, down into its blackest flood! So my fate wills it: well then! I am ready.
Where do the highest mountains come from? So I once asked. Then I learned that they come out of the sea.
This testimony is written in their stone and in the walls of their peaks. From the deepest the highest must come to its height.”

So Zarathustra spoke on the top of the mountain, where it was cold; but when he came near the sea and at last stood alone among the cliffs, he had grown tired on the way and more full of longing than ever before.
“Everything is still asleep now,” he said; “the sea is asleep too. Its eye looks at me drunk with sleep, and strange.
But it breathes warmly; I feel that. And I feel too that it is dreaming. Dreaming, it tosses on hard pillows.
Listen! Listen! How it groans with bad memories! Or bad expectations?
Ah, I am sad with you, you dark monster, and angry with myself on your account.
Ah, that my hand has not strength enough! Gladly, truly, I would free you from bad dreams!”
And as Zarathustra spoke so, he laughed at himself with melancholy and bitterness. “What! Zarathustra!” he said. “Do you want to sing comfort to the sea as well?
Ah, you loving fool Zarathustra, you who are blissful with trust! But you were always like this: you always came trustingly to everything terrible.
You wanted to stroke every monster. A breath of warm breath, a little soft fur on the paw: and at once you were ready to love it and coax it.
Love is the danger of the loneliest one, love of everything, if only it lives! Truly, my folly and my modesty in love are laughable!”

So Zarathustra spoke, and laughed a second time: but then he thought of the friends he had left, and, as if he had wronged them with his thoughts, he was angry with himself for his thoughts. And soon it happened that the one who had laughed wept: Zarathustra wept bitterly with anger and longing.
## On the Vision and the Riddle

When it became known among the sailors that Zarathustra was on the ship (for a man who came from the blessed isles had gone on board with him), there was great curiosity and expectation. But Zarathustra was silent for two days, and was cold and deaf with sadness, so that he answered neither looks nor questions. But on the evening of the second day he opened his ears again, though he was still silent: for there was much that was strange and dangerous to hear on this ship, which came from far away and meant to go still farther. And Zarathustra was a friend of all who make long journeys and do not care to live without danger. And look! at last, as he listened, his own tongue was loosened, and the ice of his heart broke: then he began to speak thus:
To you, the bold seekers and searchers, and whoever has ever set out with cunning sails on terrible seas;
to you, drunk on riddles, glad of the twilight, whose souls are lured by flutes to every treacherous gulf:
for you do not want to grope along a thread with a cowardly hand; and where you can guess, you hate to work it out;
to you alone I tell the riddle that I saw: the vision of the loneliest one.
Lately I walked gloomily through a corpse-coloured twilight, gloomy and hard, with lips pressed together. Not only one sun had set for me.
A path that climbed defiantly through scree, a malicious, lonely path, which neither herb nor bush cheered any more: a mountain path crunched under the defiance of my foot.
Striding silently over the mocking clink of pebbles, crushing the stone that made it slip: so my foot forced its way upward.
Upward: in spite of the spirit that drew it downward, drew it towards the abyss, the spirit of gravity, my devil and arch-enemy.
Upward: although he sat on me, half dwarf, half mole; lame; making lame; dripping lead into my ear, leaden-drop thoughts into my brain.
“O Zarathustra,” he whispered mockingly, syllable by syllable, “you stone of wisdom! You threw yourself high, but every stone that is thrown must fall!
O Zarathustra, you stone of wisdom, you sling-stone, you star-destroyer! You threw yourself so high, but every stone that is thrown must fall!
Condemned to yourself and to your own stoning: O Zarathustra, far indeed you threw the stone, but it will fall back on you!”
Then the dwarf fell silent; and that lasted a long time. But his silence weighed on me; and to be two like this is truly lonelier than to be one!
I climbed, I climbed, I dreamed, I thought; but everything weighed on me. I was like a sick man whom his bad torment makes tired, and whom a worse dream wakes again as he is falling asleep.
But there is something in me that I call courage: until now it has struck dead every despondency in me. This courage at last told me to stand still and say: “Dwarf! You! Or I!”
For courage is the best slayer: courage that attacks; for in every attack there is the sound of the band playing.
But man is the most courageous animal: with this he has overcome every animal. With the band playing he has overcome even every pain; but human pain is the deepest pain.
Courage also slays the dizziness at abysses: and where does man not stand at abysses! Is not seeing itself seeing abysses?
Courage is the best slayer: courage slays pity too. But pity is the deepest abyss: as deeply as man sees into life, so deeply does he see into suffering.
But courage is the best slayer, courage that attacks: it slays even death, for it says: “Was that life? Well then! Once more!”
In such a saying there is much sound of the band playing. Whoever has ears, let him hear.
“Stop! Dwarf!” I said. “I! Or you! But I am the stronger of us two: you do not know my abysmal thought! That you could not bear!”

Then something happened that made me lighter: for the dwarf jumped down from my shoulder, the inquisitive one! And he squatted on a stone in front of me. But just where we had stopped there was a gateway.
“Look at this gateway, dwarf!” I went on. “It has two faces. Two paths come together here: no one has yet walked either of them to its end.
This long lane back: it lasts an eternity. And that long lane out: that is another eternity.
They contradict each other, these paths; they butt each other head-on; and here, at this gateway, is where they come together. The name of the gateway is written above it: ‘Moment’.
But whoever went on along one of them, farther and farther, and ever farther: do you believe, dwarf, that these paths contradict each other eternally?”
“Everything straight lies,” the dwarf muttered contemptuously. “All truth is crooked; time itself is a circle.”
“You spirit of gravity!” I said angrily, “do not make it too easy for yourself! Or I shall leave you squatting where you squat, lame-foot; and I carried you high!
Look,” I went on, “at this moment! From this gateway, Moment, a long, eternal lane runs backward: behind us lies an eternity.
Must not whatever can run, of all things, have already run along this lane once? Must not whatever can happen, of all things, have already happened, been done, run past, once?
And if everything has been here before: what do you think, dwarf, of this moment? Must not this gateway too have been here before?
And are not all things knotted together so firmly that this moment draws after it all things that are to come? And so, itself as well?
For whatever can run, of all things: in this long lane out, too, it must run once more!
And this slow spider that crawls in the moonlight, and this moonlight itself, and I and you in the gateway, whispering together, whispering of eternal things: must we not all have been here before?
And come back, and run in that other lane, out, ahead of us, in this long, dreadful lane: must we not come back eternally?”
So I spoke, and ever more softly: for I was afraid of my own thoughts and the thoughts behind them. Then, suddenly, I heard a dog howl nearby.
Had I ever heard a dog howl like that? My thoughts ran back. Yes! When I was a child, in my most distant childhood:
then I heard a dog howl like that. And I saw it too, its hair bristling, its head raised, trembling, in the stillest midnight, when even dogs believe in ghosts:
so that I pitied it. For just then the full moon was going over the house, silent as death; just then it stood still, a round glow, still on the flat roof, as if on someone else’s property:
that was what had terrified the dog then: for dogs believe in thieves and ghosts. And when I heard it howl like that again, I pitied it again.

Where was the dwarf now? And the gateway? And the spider? And all the whispering? Was I dreaming, then? Was I waking up? All at once I stood among wild cliffs, alone, desolate, in the most desolate moonlight.
But there lay a man! And there! The dog, leaping, bristling, whining: now it saw me coming; then it howled again, then it cried out. Had I ever heard a dog cry for help like that?
And truly, what I saw, I had never seen the like of. I saw a young shepherd, writhing, choking, twitching, his face distorted, with a heavy black snake hanging out of his mouth.
Had I ever seen so much disgust and pale horror on one face? He must have been asleep. Then the snake crawled into his throat, and there it bit fast.
My hand pulled at the snake and pulled: in vain! It could not pull the snake out of his throat. Then it cried out of me: “Bite! Bite!
Bite its head off! Bite!” So it cried out of me, my horror, my hatred, my disgust, my pity, all my good and bad cried out of me with one cry.
You bold ones around me! You seekers, searchers, and whoever among you has set out with cunning sails on unexplored seas! You who are glad of riddles!
Then guess me the riddle that I saw then, interpret for me the vision of the loneliest one!
For it was a vision and a foreseeing: what did I see then in a parable? And who is it who must still come one day?
Who is the shepherd into whose throat the snake crawled like that? Who is the man into whose throat all that is heaviest and blackest will crawl like that?
But the shepherd bit, as my cry had advised him; he bit with a good bite! Far away he spat the snake’s head, and sprang up.
No longer a shepherd, no longer a man: one transformed, surrounded with light, who laughed! Never yet on earth has any man laughed as he laughed!
O my brothers, I heard a laughter that was no human laughter; and now a thirst gnaws at me, a longing that never grows still.
My longing for this laughter gnaws at me: oh, how can I bear to go on living! And how could I bear to die now!
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On Bliss Against One’s Will

With such riddles and bitterness in his heart Zarathustra crossed the sea. But when he was four days’ journey away from the blessed isles and from his friends, he had overcome all his pain: victorious and with firm feet he stood on his fate again. And then Zarathustra spoke thus to his rejoicing conscience:
“I am alone again, and I want to be, alone with the clear sky and the open sea; and again it is afternoon around me.
It was in the afternoon that I first found my friends, and in the afternoon the second time too: at the hour when all light grows stiller.
For whatever happiness is still on its way between heaven and earth now looks for a bright soul to lodge in: all light has now grown stiller with happiness.
O afternoon of my life! Once my happiness too went down into the valley to look for a lodging: then it found these open, hospitable souls.
O afternoon of my life! What did I not give up to have one thing: this living plantation of my thoughts, and this morning light of my highest hope!
The creator once looked for companions and children of his hope: and look, it turned out that he could not find them, unless he first created them himself.
So I am in the middle of my work, going to my children and returning from them: for his children’s sake Zarathustra must complete himself.
For from the bottom of the heart one loves only one’s child and one’s work; and where there is great love of oneself, it is the sign of pregnancy: so I have found.
My children are still green in their first spring, standing close together and shaken together by the winds, the trees of my garden and of my best soil.
And truly! Where such trees stand together, there are blessed isles!
But one day I will dig them up and set each one alone, so that it learns solitude and defiance and caution.
Gnarled and bent and with supple hardness it shall then stand by the sea, a living lighthouse of unconquerable life.
There, where the storms plunge down into the sea, and the mountain’s trunk drinks water, each shall one day keep his day and night watches, for his testing and his knowledge.
He shall be known and tested, to see whether he is of my kind and descent; whether he is master of a long will, silent even when he speaks, and yielding in such a way that in giving he takes:
so that one day he may become my companion, and a fellow creator and fellow celebrant of Zarathustra: one who writes my will on my tablets, for the fuller completion of all things.
And for his sake and for the sake of those like him, I must complete myself: that is why I now avoid my happiness and offer myself to every unhappiness, for my last testing and knowledge.
And truly, it was time for me to go; and the wanderer’s shadow and the longest boredom and the stillest hour, all said to me: ‘It is high time!’
The wind blew through my keyhole and said ‘Come!’ The door sprang cunningly open and said ‘Go!’
But I lay chained to my love for my children: desire laid this snare for me, the desire for love, that I should become my children’s prey and lose myself in them.
To desire: for me that already means to have lost myself. I have you, my children! In this having, everything shall be certainty and nothing desire.
But the sun of my love lay brooding on me; Zarathustra was cooking in his own juice; then shadows and doubts flew over me.
I was already longing for frost and winter: ‘Oh, that frost and winter would make me crack and crunch again!’ I sighed; then icy mists rose out of me.
My past burst its graves; many a pain buried alive woke up: it had only been sleeping, hidden in the clothes of the dead.
So everything called to me in signs: ‘It is time!’ But I did not hear: until at last my abyss stirred and my thought bit me.
Ah, abysmal thought, you who are my thought! When shall I find the strength to hear you digging and no longer tremble?
My heart pounds up to my throat when I hear you digging! Even your silence wants to strangle me, you abysmally silent one!
I have never yet dared to call you up: it was enough that I carried you with me! I was not yet strong enough for the lion’s final high spirits and wilfulness.
Your heaviness has always been terrible enough for me: but one day I shall yet find the strength and the lion’s voice that calls you up!
When I have overcome myself in that, then I will overcome myself in something greater too; and a victory shall be the seal of my completion!
Meanwhile I am still drifting on uncertain seas; chance flatters me, the smooth-tongued one; I look forward and backward, and still I see no end.
The hour of my last struggle has not yet come for me; or is it coming to me just now? Truly, sea and life look at me all around with treacherous beauty!
O afternoon of my life! O happiness before evening! O harbour on the high seas! O peace in uncertainty! How I mistrust you all!
Truly, I am mistrustful of your treacherous beauty! I am like the lover who mistrusts a smile that is too velvety.
As the jealous one pushes his beloved away from him, tender even in his harshness, so I push this blissful hour away from me.
Away with you, you blissful hour! With you there came to me a bliss against my will! Here I stand, willing for my deepest pain: you came at the wrong time!
Away with you, you blissful hour! Rather take lodging there, with my children! Hurry! And bless them before evening with my happiness!
There, evening is already near: the sun is sinking. Away, my happiness!”

Thus spoke Zarathustra. And he waited for his unhappiness all night: but he waited in vain. The night stayed clear and still, and happiness itself came nearer and nearer to him. But towards morning Zarathustra laughed to his heart and said mockingly: “Happiness is running after me. That is because I do not run after women. But happiness is a woman.”
## Before Sunrise
O sky above me, you pure one! You deep one! You abyss of light! Looking at you I shudder with divine desires.
To throw myself into your height: that is my depth! To hide myself in your purity: that is my innocence!
The god is veiled by his beauty: so you hide your stars. You do not speak: so you proclaim your wisdom to me.
Silent over the roaring sea you have risen for me today; your love and your modesty speak revelation to my roaring soul.
That you came to me beautiful, veiled in your beauty; that you speak to me silently, revealed in your wisdom:
oh, how could I not guess all the modesty of your soul! You came to me before the sun, to me, the loneliest one.
We have been friends from the beginning: grief and dread and ground we have in common; even the sun we have in common.
We do not speak to each other, because we know too much: we are silent to each other, we smile our knowledge to each other.
Are you not the light to my fire? Have you not the sister-soul to my insight?
Together we learned everything; together we learned to climb above ourselves to ourselves, and to smile without clouds:
to smile down without clouds from bright eyes and from miles away, when beneath us compulsion and purpose and guilt steam like rain.
And when I wandered alone, for whom did my soul hunger in the nights and on wrong paths? And when I climbed mountains, whom did I ever look for on mountains, if not you?
And all my wandering and mountain climbing: it was only a necessity and a makeshift of the clumsy one. My whole will wants only to fly, to fly into you!
And whom did I hate more than passing clouds and everything that stains you? And I hated even my own hatred, because it stained you!
I resent the passing clouds, these creeping beasts of prey: they take from you and me what we have in common, the tremendous, unbounded saying of Yes and Amen.
We resent these go-betweens and mixers, the passing clouds: these half-and-halfs, who have learned neither to bless nor to curse from the heart.
I would rather sit in a barrel under a closed sky, rather sit in the abyss without a sky, than see you, sky of light, stained with passing clouds!
And often I longed to pin them down with jagged golden wires of lightning, so that, like the thunder, I might beat the drum on their kettle-bellies:
an angry drummer, because they rob me of your Yes! and Amen!, you sky above me, you pure one! you bright one! you abyss of light! because they rob you of my Yes! and Amen!

For I would rather have noise and thunder and the curses of storms than this cautious, doubting cat-like calm; and among men too I hate most all soft-steppers and half-and-halfs and doubting, hesitating passing clouds.
And “whoever cannot bless shall learn to curse!”: this clear teaching fell to me from a clear sky; this star still stands in my sky even on black nights.
But I am one who blesses and one who says Yes, if only you are around me, you pure one! you bright one! you abyss of light! Then I carry my blessing Yes into all abysses.
I have become one who blesses and one who says Yes: and for that I wrestled long and was a wrestler, so that one day I might get my hands free for blessing.
But this is my blessing: to stand over every single thing as its own sky, as its round roof, its azure bell and eternal security: and blessed is he who blesses thus!
For all things are baptised at the well of eternity and beyond good and evil; but good and evil themselves are only shadows in between, and damp afflictions, and passing clouds.
Truly, it is a blessing and not a blasphemy when I teach: “Over all things stand the sky Chance, the sky Innocence, the sky Accident, the sky High Spirits.”
“By accident”: that is the oldest nobility in the world; I gave it back to all things; I set them free from slavery under purpose.
This freedom and heavenly cheerfulness I set like an azure bell over all things, when I taught that over them and through them no “eternal will” wills.
This high spirits and this folly I set in the place of that will, when I taught: “In everything one thing is impossible: rationality!”
A little reason, it is true, a seed of wisdom scattered from star to star: this leaven is mixed into all things; for the sake of folly, wisdom is mixed into all things!
A little wisdom is possible, certainly; but this blessed certainty I found in all things: that they would rather dance on the feet of chance.
O sky above me, you pure one! you high one! This is now your purity to me, that there is no eternal spider of reason and no spider’s web of reason:
that you are a dance floor for divine chances, that you are a gods’ table for divine dice and dice-players!
But you blush? Did I say what may not be said? Did I blaspheme when I wanted to bless you?
Or is it the shame of being two that made you blush? Do you bid me go and be silent, because now the day is coming?
The world is deep: and deeper than the day has ever thought. Not everything may have words before the day. But the day is coming: so let us part now!
O sky above me, you modest one! you glowing one! O you my happiness before sunrise! The day is coming: so let us part now!
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## On Old and New Tablets
Here I sit and wait, old broken tablets around me, and new tablets too, half written. When will my hour come?
The hour of my going down, my going under: for I want to go to men once more.
That is what I am waiting for now: for first the signs must come to me that it is my hour: namely, the laughing lion with the flock of doves.
Meanwhile I talk to myself, as one who has time. No one tells me anything new: so I tell myself myself.
When I came to men, I found them sitting on an old conceit: they all thought they had long known what is good and evil for man.
All talk of virtue seemed to them an old, tired thing; and whoever wanted to sleep well still talked of “good” and “evil” before going to bed.
I disturbed this sleepiness when I taught: what is good and evil, no one yet knows, unless it is the creator!
But that is the one who creates man’s goal and gives the earth its meaning and its future: only he makes it so that something is good and evil.
And I bade them overturn their old professorial chairs, and wherever that old conceit had sat; I bade them laugh at their great masters of virtue and saints and poets and saviours of the world.
I bade them laugh at their gloomy sages, and at whoever had ever sat as a black scarecrow, warning, on the tree of life.
I sat down by their great avenue of graves, and even beside carrion and vultures; and I laughed at all their past and its crumbling, decaying glory.
Truly, like preachers of repentance and fools I raised a cry of anger and outrage over all their great and small: that their best is so very small! That their worst is so very small! So I laughed.
So my wise longing cried and laughed out of me, the longing that was born on mountains, a wild wisdom truly! my great longing with its rushing wings.
And often it carried me away, and up, and off, in the middle of laughter: then I flew, shuddering, an arrow, through sun-drunk rapture:
out into distant futures that no dream has yet seen, into hotter souths than any artist ever dreamed: there, where gods dancing are ashamed of all clothes:
so that I speak in parables, and limp and stammer like poets; and truly, I am ashamed that I must still be a poet!
where all becoming seemed to me the dance of gods and the wantonness of gods, and the world let loose and unbridled and fleeing back to itself:
as an eternal fleeing from and seeking again of many gods, as the blessed contradicting of themselves, hearing themselves again, belonging to themselves again, of many gods:
where all time seemed to me a blessed mockery of moments, where necessity was freedom itself, playing blissfully with the sting of freedom:
where I also found my old devil and arch-enemy again, the spirit of gravity, and everything he created: compulsion, statute, need and consequence and purpose and will and good and evil:
for must there not be something that is danced over, danced beyond? Must there not be moles and heavy dwarfs, for the sake of the light, the lightest?
It was there too that I picked up the word “Overman” from the road, and that man is something that must be overcome:
that man is a bridge and not an end: calling himself blessed for his noon and his evening, as the way to new dawns:
the Zarathustra-word of the great noon, and whatever else I hung up over man like purple second sunsets.
Truly, I also let them see new stars, together with new nights; and over clouds and day and night I spread laughter like a bright tent.
I taught them all my poetry and striving: to compose into one and bring together what is fragment in man and riddle and dreadful accident;
as poet, guesser of riddles and redeemer of chance, I taught them to work on the future, and by creating to redeem all that was.
To redeem what is past in man and to transform every “It was”, until the will says: “But thus I willed it! Thus shall I will it”:
this I called redemption to them; this alone I taught them to call redemption.
Now I wait for my own redemption: that I may go to them for the last time.
For I want to go to men once more: among them I want to go under; dying, I want to give them my richest gift!
I learned this from the sun when it goes down, the over-rich one: then it pours gold into the sea out of inexhaustible riches,
so that even the poorest fisherman rows with golden oars! For I once saw this, and could not have my fill of tears as I watched.
Like the sun, Zarathustra too wants to go under: now he sits here and waits, old broken tablets around him, and new tablets too, half written.
Look, here is a new tablet: but where are my brothers to carry it with me down into the valley and into hearts of flesh?
So my great love of the farthest demands: do not spare your neighbour! Man is something that must be overcome.
There are many ways and means of overcoming: see to that yourself! But only a buffoon thinks: “Man can also be jumped over.”
Overcome yourself even in your neighbour: and a right that you can seize for yourself, you should not let anyone give you!
What you do, no one can do back to you. Look, there is no repayment.
Whoever cannot command himself should obey. And many can command themselves, but much is still lacking before they also obey themselves!
This is the way of noble souls: they want nothing for nothing, least of all life.
Whoever is of the mob wants to live for nothing; but we others, to whom life gave itself, we always think about what we can best give in return!
And truly, it is a noble saying that says: “What life promises us, we will keep for life!”
One should not want to enjoy where one does not give enjoyment. And one should not want to enjoy!
For enjoyment and innocence are the most bashful things: neither wants to be sought. One should have them; but one should rather seek guilt and pain!
O my brothers, whoever is a first-born is always sacrificed. Now we are first-born.
We all bleed on secret sacrificial altars; we all burn and roast in honour of old idols.
Our best is still young: that tempts old palates. Our flesh is tender, our hide only a lamb’s hide: how could we not tempt old idol-priests!
Within ourselves he still lives, the old idol-priest, who roasts our best for his feast. Ah, my brothers, how could the first-born not be sacrifices!
But so our nature wills it; and I love those who do not want to preserve themselves. Those who go under I love with all my love: for they go over.
To be true: few can do that! And whoever can, does not yet want to! But the good can do it least of all.
Oh, these good people! Good people never tell the truth; for the spirit, being good in this way is a sickness.
They give way, these good people, they give in, their heart repeats what it hears, their ground obeys: but whoever obeys does not hear himself!
Everything the good call evil must come together for one truth to be born: O my brothers, are you evil enough for this truth?
The daring venture, the long mistrust, the cruel No, the disgust, the cutting into the living: how seldom does that come together! But from such seed truth is begotten!
Beside the bad conscience all knowledge has grown until now! Break, break for me, you seekers of knowledge, the old tablets!
When the water has planks over it, when footbridges and railings span the river: truly, no one is believed then who says, “Everything is in flux.”
Rather, even the blockheads contradict him. “What?” say the blockheads, “everything is in flux? But the planks and the railings are above the river!
Above the river everything is firm, all the values of things, the bridges, concepts, all ‘good’ and ‘evil’: all of that is firm!”
But when the hard winter comes, the tamer of rivers, then even the wittiest learn mistrust; and truly, then it is not only the blockheads who say: “Should not everything stand still?”
“At bottom everything stands still”: that is a proper winter teaching, a good thing for a barren time, a good comfort for those who hibernate and sit by the stove.
“At bottom everything stands still”: but against this the thaw wind preaches!
The thaw wind, a bull that is no ploughing bull: a raging bull, a destroyer, that breaks ice with angry horns! But ice breaks footbridges!
O my brothers, is not everything in flux now? Have not all railings and footbridges fallen into the water? Who would still hold on to “good” and “evil”?
“Woe to us! Hail to us! The thaw wind is blowing!” Preach this for me, O my brothers, through all the streets!
There is an old illusion that is called good and evil. Until now the wheel of this illusion has turned around soothsayers and astrologers.
Once people believed in soothsayers and astrologers: and so they believed, “Everything is fate: you shall, because you must!”
Then again they mistrusted all soothsayers and astrologers: and so they believed, “Everything is freedom: you can, because you will!”
O my brothers, about stars and the future there has so far only been illusion, not knowledge: and so about good and evil there has so far only been illusion, not knowledge!
“You shall not rob! You shall not kill!” Such words were once called holy; before them people bent their knees and heads and took off their shoes.
But I ask you: where were there ever better robbers and killers in the world than such holy words?
Is there not in all life itself robbing and killing? And by calling such words holy, was not truth itself killed?
Or was it a preaching of death that called holy what contradicted and advised against all life? O my brothers, break, break for me the old tablets!
This is my pity for everything past, that I see it is abandoned:
abandoned to the favour, the spirit, the madness of every generation that comes and reinterprets everything that was as its bridge!
A great despot could come, a cunning monster, who with his favour and disfavour would force and strain everything past until it became for him a bridge and an omen and a herald and a cock-crow.
But this is the other danger and my other pity: whoever is of the mob, his memory goes back to his grandfather; but with the grandfather time stops.
So everything past is abandoned: for it could one day happen that the mob became master and drowned all time in shallow waters.
That is why, O my brothers, a new nobility is needed, which is the adversary of all mob and all despotism, and writes anew on new tablets the word “noble”.
For many noble ones are needed, and many kinds of noble ones, for there to be nobility! Or, as I once said in a parable: “Just this is godliness, that there are gods but no God!”
O my brothers, I consecrate you and direct you to a new nobility: you shall become begetters and breeders and sowers of the future;
truly, not to a nobility that you could buy like shopkeepers and with shopkeepers’ gold: for everything that has its price is of little worth.
Let it be your honour from now on, not where you come from, but where you are going! Your will and your foot, which wants to go beyond yourselves: let that be your new honour!
Truly not that you have served a prince (what do princes matter now!), or became a bulwark for what stands, so that it might stand more firmly!
Not that your family became courtly at courts, and you learned, bright like a flamingo, to stand for long hours in shallow ponds.
For being able to stand is a merit among courtiers; and all courtiers believe that being allowed to sit belongs to blessedness after death!
Nor that a spirit they call holy led your ancestors into promised lands, which I do not praise: for where the worst of all trees grew, the cross, there is nothing to praise in that land!
and truly, wherever this “holy spirit” led its knights, goats and geese and crossheads and cranks always ran in front on such expeditions!
O my brothers, your nobility should not look back, but out! You shall be exiles from all fatherlands and forefathers’ lands!
You shall love your children’s land: let this love be your new nobility, the undiscovered land, in the farthest sea! For it I bid your sails search and search!
In your children you shall make up for being the children of your fathers: so you shall redeem everything past! This new tablet I set up over you!
“Why live? All is vanity! Living: that is threshing straw; living: that is burning oneself and still not getting warm.”
Such ancient chatter still counts as “wisdom”; and because it is old and smells musty, it is honoured all the more. Even mould ennobles.
Children might talk like that: they fear the fire because it burned them! There is much childishness in the old books of wisdom.
And whoever is always “threshing straw”, how should he be allowed to slander threshing! Such a fool ought to have his mouth tied up!
Such people sit down at table and bring nothing with them, not even a good appetite: and now they slander, “All is vanity!”
But to eat and drink well, O my brothers, is truly no vain art! Break, break for me the tablets of the never-joyful!
“To the pure all things are pure”: so the people say. But I tell you: to swine all things become swine!
That is why the fanatics and the head-hangers, whose hearts hang down too, preach: “The world itself is a filthy monster.”
For these all have unclean spirits; but especially those who have no rest or peace unless they see the world from behind: the believers in a world behind!
To them I say to their faces, though it does not sound nice: the world is like man in this, that it has a behind: so much is true!
There is much filth in the world: so much is true! But that does not make the world itself a filthy monster!
There is wisdom in the fact that much in the world smells bad: disgust itself creates wings and powers that sense the presence of springs!
Even in the best there is something to be disgusted at; and even the best is something that must be overcome!
O my brothers, there is much wisdom in the fact that there is much filth in the world!
I heard pious believers in a world behind say such sayings to their consciences; and truly, without malice or falsehood, though there is nothing in the world more false, nor more malicious.
“Let the world be the world! Do not raise even one finger against it!”
“Let whoever wants to strangle and stab and cut and scrape people: do not raise even one finger against it! That way they will learn to renounce the world.”
“And your own reason: you yourself should choke and strangle it; for it is a reason of this world; that way you yourself will learn to renounce the world.”
Break, break for me, O my brothers, these old tablets of the pious! Break up the sayings of the slanderers of the world!
“Whoever learns much unlearns all violent desire”: that is what people whisper to each other today in all the dark alleys.
“Wisdom makes tired; nothing is worth while; you shall not desire!” This new tablet I found hanging even in open market places.
Break for me, O my brothers, break this new tablet too! The world-weary hung it up, and the preachers of death, and the jailers too: for look, it is also a sermon for slavery!
That they learned badly, and not the best, and everything too early and everything too fast; that they ate badly: that is where they got that ruined stomach;
for their spirit is a ruined stomach: it advises death! For truly, my brothers, the spirit is a stomach!
Life is a well of joy: but for the one out of whom the ruined stomach speaks, the father of gloom, all springs are poisoned.
To know: that is joy for the lion-willed! But whoever has grown tired is himself only “willed”; all the waves play with him.
And this is always the way of weak people: they lose themselves on their ways. And at last their tiredness asks: “Why did we ever go on ways? It is all the same!”
To them it sounds pleasant when it is preached: “Nothing is worth while! You shall not will!” But this is a sermon for slavery.
O my brothers, Zarathustra comes as a fresh, roaring wind to all who are tired of the way; he will make many noses sneeze yet!
My free breath blows even through walls, and into prisons and imprisoned spirits!
Willing frees: for willing is creating: so I teach. And you should learn only for creating!
And even learning you should first learn from me, learning well! Whoever has ears, let him hear!
There stands the boat: over there it goes perhaps into the great Nothing. But who wants to step into this “Perhaps”?
None of you wants to step into the boat of death! Then why do you want to be world-weary!
World-weary! And you have not even become removed from the earth! I have always found you still lusting for the earth, still in love with your own weariness of the earth!
It is not for nothing that your lip hangs down: a little earthly wish still sits on it! And in your eye, does not a little cloud of unforgotten earthly joy swim there?
There are many good inventions on earth, some useful, others pleasant: for their sake the earth is to be loved.
And there are some things so well invented that they are like a woman’s breast: useful and pleasant at the same time.
But you world-weary ones! You earth-lazy ones! You should be beaten with rods! With strokes of the rod your legs should be made lively again.

For if you are not sick people and worn-out wretches, of whom the earth is tired, then you are cunning sloths or sweet-toothed, hidden-away cats of pleasure. And if you do not want to run merrily again, then you should pass away!
One should not want to be a doctor to the incurable: so Zarathustra teaches; so you should pass away!
But it takes more courage to make an end than to make a new verse: all doctors and poets know that.
O my brothers, there are tablets that weariness created, and tablets that laziness created, the rotten kind: though they speak alike, they want to be heard differently.
Look at this man pining here! He is only a span away from his goal, but out of weariness he has lain down defiantly here in the dust: this brave man!
Out of weariness he yawns at the way and the earth and the goal and himself: he will not take one step further, this brave man!
Now the sun glows on him, and the dogs lick at his sweat: but he lies there in his defiance and would rather pine away:
pine away a span from his goal! Truly, you will have to drag him into his heaven by the hair yet, this hero!
Better still, leave him lying where he has lain down, so that sleep may come to him, the comforter, with cooling, rustling rain:
let him lie until he wakes of his own accord, until of his own accord he takes back all weariness and what weariness taught through him!
Only, my brothers, chase the dogs away from him, the lazy sneaks, and all the swarming vermin:
all the swarming vermin of the “educated”, who feast on the sweat of every hero!
I draw circles around me and holy boundaries; ever fewer climb with me onto ever higher mountains: I am building a mountain range out of ever holier mountains.
But wherever you may climb with me, O my brothers: see to it that no parasite climbs with you!
A parasite: that is a worm, a crawling, clinging worm, which wants to grow fat on your sick, sore corners.
And this is its art, that it guesses where climbing souls are tired: in your grief and ill-humour, in your tender shame it builds its disgusting nest.
Where the strong is weak, where the noble is too gentle, there it builds its disgusting nest: the parasite lives where the great have small sore corners.
What is the highest kind of all that exists, and what the lowest? The parasite is the lowest kind; but whoever is of the highest kind feeds the most parasites.
For the soul that has the longest ladder and can go down deepest: how could the most parasites not sit on that one?
the most comprehensive soul, which can run and stray and roam furthest within itself; the most necessary one, which for joy throws itself into chance;
the soul that is, which dives into becoming; the soul that has, which wants to plunge into willing and longing;
the one that flees itself, that catches up with itself in the widest circle; the wisest soul, to which folly speaks most sweetly;
the one that loves itself most, in which all things have their streaming and back-streaming, their ebb and flood: oh, how could the highest soul not have the worst parasites?
O my brothers, am I cruel, then? But I say: what is falling should be pushed as well!
Everything of today is falling, decaying: who would want to hold it up! But I, I want to push it as well!
Do you know the delight that rolls stones into steep depths? These people of today: look how they roll into my depths!
I am a prelude of better players, O my brothers! An example! Act according to my example!
And whomever you do not teach to fly, teach him, for me, to fall faster!
I love the brave: but it is not enough to be a swashbuckler; one must also know whom to strike!
And often there is more bravery in holding back and passing by, so as to save oneself for a worthier enemy!
You should have only enemies to be hated, but not enemies to be despised: you must be proud of your enemy: so I have taught once already.
For the worthier enemy, O my friends, you should save yourselves: that is why you must pass many by,
especially much rabble, which makes a noise in your ears about the people and peoples.
Keep your eye clean of their For and Against! There is much right there, much wrong: whoever watches grows angry.
To look in and to lash out: there they are one: so go away into the forests and lay your sword to sleep!
Go your ways! And let the people and peoples go theirs! Dark ways, truly, on which not a single hope still flashes like summer lightning!
Let the shopkeeper rule there, where everything that still shines is shopkeepers’ gold! It is no longer the time of kings: what calls itself the people today does not deserve kings.
Just look how these peoples now act like shopkeepers themselves: they pick out the smallest advantages from every rubbish heap!

They lie in wait for one another, they lie in wait to get something out of one another: they call that “good neighbourliness”. Oh blessed distant time, when a people said to itself: “I want to be master over peoples!”
For, my brothers: the best shall rule, and the best wants to rule! And where the teaching sounds different, there the best is lacking.
If they had bread for nothing, alas! What would they cry out for! Their livelihood: that is their real entertainment; and they shall have it hard!
They are beasts of prey: in their “working” there is still robbing, in their “earning” there is still outwitting! That is why they shall have it hard!
So they shall become better beasts of prey, finer, cleverer, more like men: for man is the best beast of prey.
Man has already robbed all the animals of their virtues: that is because of all animals man has had it hardest.
Only the birds are still above him. And if man learned to fly as well, alas! to what heights would his lust for prey fly!
This is how I want man and woman: the one fit for war, the other fit for bearing children, but both fit for dancing with head and legs.
And let the day be lost to us on which there was not one dance! And let every truth be called false to us at which there was not one laugh!
Your marrying: see to it that it is not a bad concluding! You concluded too quickly: so what follows from it is breaking the marriage!
And better still to break the marriage than to bend the marriage, to lie in the marriage! So a woman told me: “Yes, I broke the marriage, but first the marriage broke me!”
I have always found the badly matched to be the worst for revenge: they make all the world pay for the fact that they no longer walk singly.
That is why I want honest people to say to each other: “We love each other: let us see to it that we keep loving each other! Or shall our promise be a mistake?”
“Give us a term and a little marriage, so that we may see whether we are fit for the great marriage! It is a great thing always to be two!”
So I advise all honest people; and what would my love of the Overman and of everything that is to come be, if I advised and spoke otherwise!
Not only to propagate yourselves onward, but upward: to that, O my brothers, may the garden of marriage help you!
Whoever has grown wise about old origins, look, he will at last seek the springs of the future and new origins.
O my brothers, it will not be long before new peoples spring up and new springs rush down into new depths.
For the earthquake buries many wells, it creates much pining; it also lifts inner powers and secrets into the light.
The earthquake reveals new springs. In the earthquake of old peoples new springs break out.
And whoever calls out: “Look, here is a well for many who are thirsty, one heart for many who long, one will for many instruments”: around him a people gathers, that is: many who try.
Who can command, who must obey: that is tried there! Ah, with what long seeking and guessing and failing and learning and trying again!
Human society: that is an experiment, so I teach, a long seeking: but it seeks the one who commands!
an experiment, O my brothers! And not a “contract”! Break, break for me such words of the soft-hearted and half-and-half!
O my brothers! With whom does the greatest danger to all of man’s future lie? Is it not with the good and the just?
with those who say and feel in their hearts: “We already know what is good and just, and we have it too; woe to those who still seek here!”
And whatever harm the evil may do: the harm of the good is the most harmful harm!
And whatever harm the slanderers of the world may do: the harm of the good is the most harmful harm.
O my brothers, someone once looked into the hearts of the good and the just and said: “They are the Pharisees.” But he was not understood.
The good and the just themselves could not understand him: their spirit is imprisoned in their good conscience. The stupidity of the good is unfathomably clever.
But this is the truth: the good must be Pharisees; they have no choice!
The good must crucify the one who invents his own virtue! That is the truth!
But the second one who discovered their land, the land, heart and soil of the good and the just, was the one who asked: “Whom do they hate most?”
They hate the creator most: the one who breaks tablets and old values, the breaker: him they call a lawbreaker.
For the good cannot create: they are always the beginning of the end:
they crucify the one who writes new values on new tablets; they sacrifice the future to themselves; they crucify all of man’s future!
The good: they have always been the beginning of the end.
O my brothers, have you understood this word too? And what I once said of the “last man”?
With whom does the greatest danger to all of man’s future lie? Is it not with the good and the just?
Break, break for me the good and the just! O my brothers, have you understood this word too?
You flee from me? You are frightened? You tremble at this word?
O my brothers, when I bade you break the good and the tablets of the good: only then did I set man out on his high sea.
And only now does the great terror come to him, the great looking around, the great sickness, the great disgust, the great seasickness.
The good taught you false coasts and false securities; you were born and kept safe in the lies of the good. Everything has been lied about and bent out of shape to the very bottom by the good.
But whoever discovered the land “man” also discovered the land “man’s future”. Now you shall be seafarers for me, brave and patient!
Walk upright in good time, O my brothers; learn to walk upright! The sea is stormy: many want to raise themselves up again by you.
The sea is stormy: everything is in the sea. Well then! Up! You old sailors’ hearts!
What of fatherland! Our helm wants to go there, where our children’s land is! Out there, stormier than the sea, storms our great longing!
“Why so hard?” the kitchen coal once said to the diamond. “Are we not close relatives?”
Why so soft? O my brothers, so I ask you: are you not my brothers?
Why so soft, so yielding and giving way? Why is there so much denial, self-denial in your hearts? So little fate in your look?
And if you do not want to be fates and inexorable ones, how could you one day conquer with me?
And if your hardness will not flash and cut and cut through, how could you one day create with me?
For creators are hard. And it must seem bliss to you to press your hand on millennia as on wax,
bliss to write on the will of millennia as on bronze: harder than bronze, nobler than bronze. Only the noblest is completely hard.
This new tablet, O my brothers, I set up over you: become hard!
O you my will! You turning of all need, you my necessity! Keep me from all small victories!
You destiny of my soul, which I call fate! You in me! You over me! Keep me and save me for one great fate!
And your last greatness, my will, save for your last thing, so that you are inexorable in your victory! Ah, who has not been defeated by his victory!
Ah, whose eye has not darkened in this drunken twilight! Ah, whose foot has not staggered and forgotten in victory how to stand!
That I may one day be ready and ripe in the great noon: ready and ripe like glowing bronze, a cloud pregnant with lightning, and a swelling udder of milk:
ready for myself and for my most hidden will: a bow burning for its arrow, an arrow burning for its star:
a star, ready and ripe in its noon, glowing, pierced, blissful before annihilating arrows of the sun:
a sun itself, and an inexorable will of the sun, ready to annihilate in victory!
O will, turning of all need, you my necessity! Save me for one great victory!
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## The Convalescent

One morning, not long after his return to the cave, Zarathustra sprang up from his bed like a madman, cried out in a terrible voice, and behaved as if someone else were still lying on the bed who would not get up from it; and Zarathustra’s voice rang out so that his animals came running in fright, and from all the caves and hiding places near Zarathustra’s cave every creature scurried away, flying, fluttering, creeping, leaping, according to the kind of foot or wing it had been given. But Zarathustra spoke these words:
Up, abysmal thought, out of my depth! I am your cock and your dawn, sleepy worm: up! up! My voice shall crow you awake!
Unfasten the fetters of your ears: listen! For I want to hear you! Up! Up! Here is thunder enough to make even graves learn to listen!
And wipe the sleep and all the dullness and blindness out of your eyes! Hear me with your eyes too: my voice is a remedy even for those born blind.
And once you are awake, you shall stay awake for ever. It is not my way to wake great-grandmothers from their sleep only to tell them to go on sleeping!
You stir, you stretch, you rattle in your throat? Up! Up! You shall not rattle, you shall speak to me! Zarathustra calls you, the godless one!
I, Zarathustra, the advocate of life, the advocate of suffering, the advocate of the circle: I call you, my most abysmal thought!
Hail to me! You are coming: I hear you! My abyss speaks; I have turned my last depth inside out into the light!
Hail to me! Come here! Give me your hand: ha! let go! Haha! Disgust, disgust, disgust: woe is me!

But hardly had Zarathustra spoken these words when he fell down like a dead man, and remained like a dead man for a long time. But when he came to himself again, he was pale and trembled and stayed lying down, and for a long time would neither eat nor drink. He was like this for seven days; but his animals did not leave him by day or night, except that the eagle flew out to fetch food. And whatever it fetched and seized it laid on Zarathustra’s bed: so that in the end Zarathustra lay among yellow and red berries, grapes, rosy apples, sweet-smelling herbs and pine cones. But at his feet lay two lambs, which the eagle had with difficulty stolen from their shepherds.
At last, after seven days, Zarathustra sat up on his bed, took a rosy apple in his hand, smelled it, and found its smell lovely. Then his animals thought the time had come to speak to him.
“O Zarathustra,” they said, “you have been lying like this for seven days now, with heavy eyes: will you not at last get on your feet again?
Step out of your cave: the world is waiting for you like a garden. The wind is playing with heavy fragrances that want to come to you; and all the streams would like to run after you.
All things long for you, since you have stayed alone for seven days. Step out of your cave! All things want to be your doctors!
Has some new knowledge come to you, a sour, heavy one? You lay like leavened dough; your soul rose and swelled over all its edges.”
“O my animals,” answered Zarathustra, “go on chattering like this and let me listen! It refreshes me so to hear you chatter: where there is chatter, the world already lies before me like a garden.
How lovely it is that there are words and sounds: are not words and sounds rainbows and illusory bridges between things eternally apart?
To each soul belongs another world; for each soul every other soul is a world behind.
It is just between the most alike that illusion lies most beautifully; for the smallest gap is the hardest to bridge.
For me, how could there be anything outside me? There is no outside! But we forget this with all sounds; how lovely it is that we forget!
Have not names and sounds been given to things so that man may refresh himself with things? It is a beautiful folly, speaking: with it man dances over all things.
How lovely is all speaking and all the lying of sounds! With sounds our love dances on bright rainbows.”
“O Zarathustra,” said the animals then, “to those who think as we do, all things dance by themselves: they come and give each other their hands and laugh and run away, and come back.
Everything goes, everything comes back; the wheel of being rolls eternally. Everything dies, everything blossoms again; the year of being runs eternally.
Everything breaks, everything is joined anew; the same house of being builds itself eternally. Everything parts, everything greets itself again; the ring of being stays eternally true to itself.
In every Now being begins; around every Here rolls the ball There. The middle is everywhere. Crooked is the path of eternity.”
“O you buffoons and barrel organs!” answered Zarathustra, and smiled again. “How well you know what had to be fulfilled in seven days:
and how that monster crawled into my throat and choked me! But I bit its head off and spat it away from me.
And you, you have already made a hurdy-gurdy song of it? But now I lie here, still tired from that biting and spitting away, still sick from my own redemption.
And you watched all this? O my animals, are you cruel too? Did you want to watch my great pain, as men do? For man is the cruellest animal.
At tragedies, bullfights and crucifixions he has so far felt best on earth; and when he invented hell for himself, look, that was his heaven on earth.
When the great man cries out, the little man runs up at once; and his tongue hangs out of his mouth with lust. But he calls it his ‘pity’.
The little man, especially the poet, how eagerly he accuses life in words! Listen to him, but do not fail to hear the delight that is in all accusing!
Such accusers of life: life overcomes them with a wink of the eye. ‘You love me?’ says the shameless one; ‘wait a little, I have no time for you yet.’

Man is the cruellest animal towards himself; and in everything that calls itself ‘sinner’ and ‘cross-bearer’ and ‘penitent’, do not fail to hear the voluptuousness that is in this lamenting and accusing!
And I myself, do I want to be man’s accuser by this? Ah, my animals, this alone I have learned so far, that man needs what is worst in him for what is best in him:
that everything worst is his best strength, and the hardest stone for the highest creator; and that man must become better and more evil:
it was not to this stake of torture that I was nailed, to know that man is evil; but I cried out as no one has yet cried out:
‘Ah, that his worst is so very small! Ah, that his best is so very small!’
The great disgust with man: that was what choked me and had crawled into my throat; and what the soothsayer prophesied: ‘All is the same, nothing is worth while, knowledge chokes.’
A long twilight limped ahead of me, a sadness tired to death, drunk with death, which spoke with a yawning mouth.
‘He returns eternally, the man you are tired of, the little man’: so my sadness yawned, and dragged its foot, and could not fall asleep.
The human earth turned into a cave for me, its breast sank in; everything living became to me human decay and bones and mouldering past.
My sighing sat on all human graves and could no longer get up; my sighing and questioning croaked and choked and gnawed and lamented by day and night:
‘Ah, man returns eternally! The little man returns eternally!’
Naked I had once seen both, the greatest man and the smallest man: all too like each other, all too human even the greatest!
All too small the greatest! That was my disgust with man! And eternal return even of the smallest! That was my disgust with all existence!
Ah, disgust! Disgust! Disgust!” So spoke Zarathustra, and sighed and shuddered; for he remembered his sickness. But then his animals would not let him go on speaking.
“Do not speak any further, you convalescent!” so his animals answered him, “but go out, where the world is waiting for you like a garden.
Go out to the roses and bees and flocks of doves! But above all to the songbirds: so that you may learn singing from them!
For singing is for convalescents; the healthy may talk. And even when the healthy want songs, they want other songs than the convalescent.”
“O you buffoons and barrel organs, be quiet!” answered Zarathustra, and smiled at his animals. “How well you know what comfort I invented for myself in seven days!
That I must sing again: that comfort I invented for myself, and this recovery: do you want to make a hurdy-gurdy song of that straight away too?”
“Do not speak any further,” his animals answered him again; “rather, you convalescent, first make yourself a lyre, a new lyre!
For look, O Zarathustra! For your new songs new lyres are needed.
Sing and overflow, O Zarathustra, heal your soul with new songs: so that you may bear your great fate, which has not yet been any man’s fate!
For your animals know well, O Zarathustra, who you are and must become: look, you are the teacher of the eternal return; that is now your fate!
That you must be the first to teach this teaching: how could this great fate not also be your greatest danger and sickness!
Look, we know what you teach: that all things return eternally, and we ourselves with them, and that we have already been here an eternal number of times, and all things with us.
You teach that there is a great year of becoming, a monster of a great year: it must, like an hourglass, turn itself over again and again, so that it may run down and run out anew:
so that all these years are the same as each other, in the greatest and in the smallest; so that we ourselves are the same in every great year, in the greatest and in the smallest.
And if you wanted to die now, O Zarathustra: look, we know too how you would speak to yourself then; but your animals beg you not to die yet!
You would speak without trembling, rather breathing a sigh of happiness: for a great heaviness and sultriness would be taken from you, you most patient one!
‘Now I die and vanish,’ you would say, ‘and in a moment I am nothing. Souls are as mortal as bodies.
But the knot of causes in which I am entangled returns: it will create me again! I myself belong to the causes of the eternal return.
I come again, with this sun, with this earth, with this eagle, with this snake: not to a new life or a better life or a similar life:
I come back eternally to this same, selfsame life, in the greatest and in the smallest, to teach again the eternal return of all things,
to speak again the word of the great noon of earth and man, to proclaim the Overman to men again.
I spoke my word, I break on my word: so my eternal lot wills it; as a proclaimer I perish!
The hour has now come when the one who goes under blesses himself. So Zarathustra’s going-under ends.’”

When the animals had spoken these words, they fell silent and waited for Zarathustra to say something to them: but Zarathustra did not hear that they were silent. Rather he lay still, with his eyes closed, like one asleep, though he was not asleep: for he was talking with his soul. But the snake and the eagle, finding him so silent, respected the great stillness around him and carefully went away.
## On the Great Longing
O my soul, I taught you to say “today” as you say “once” and “formerly”, and to dance your round-dance over every Here and There and Yonder.
O my soul, I freed you from all corners; I swept dust, spiders and twilight off you.
O my soul, I washed the little shame and the corner-virtue off you, and persuaded you to stand naked before the eyes of the sun.
With the storm that is called “spirit” I blew over your surging sea; I blew all clouds away; I even strangled the strangler that is called “sin”.
O my soul, I gave you the right to say No like the storm, and to say Yes as the open sky says Yes: still as light you stand, and now go through denying storms.
O my soul, I gave you back freedom over the created and the uncreated: and who knows, as you know, the delight of what is to come?
O my soul, I taught you the contempt that does not come like the gnawing of worms, the great, the loving contempt, which loves most where it despises most.
O my soul, I taught you to persuade so that you persuade even the grounds to come to you: like the sun, which persuades even the sea up to its height.
O my soul, I took from you all obeying, bending of the knee and saying “Lord”; I gave you yourself the name “turning of need” and “fate”.
O my soul, I gave you new names and bright playthings; I called you “fate” and “circumference of circumferences” and “umbilical cord of time” and “azure bell”.
O my soul, I gave your soil all wisdom to drink, all new wines, and also all the strong wines of wisdom, old beyond memory.
O my soul, I poured every sun on you, and every night and every silence and every longing: then you grew up for me like a vine.
O my soul, over-rich and heavy you stand there now, a vine with swelling udders and crowded brown golden grapes:
crowded and pressed by your happiness, waiting in your overflowing, and still bashful at your waiting.
O my soul, there is now nowhere a soul that would be more loving and more embracing and more comprehensive! Where would future and past be closer together than in you?
O my soul, I have given you everything, and all my hands have become empty for you: and now! Now you say to me, smiling and full of melancholy: “Which of us has to give thanks?
Has not the giver to give thanks that the receiver received? Is giving not a need? Is receiving not mercy?”
O my soul, I understand the smile of your melancholy: your over-richness itself now stretches out longing hands!
Your fullness looks out over roaring seas and searches and waits; the longing of over-fullness looks out of the smiling sky of your eyes!
And truly, O my soul! Who could see your smile and not melt into tears? The angels themselves melt into tears at the over-goodness of your smile.
It is your goodness and over-goodness that does not want to lament and weep: and yet, O my soul, your smile longs for tears, and your trembling mouth for sobs.
“Is not all weeping a lamenting? And all lamenting an accusing?” So you say to yourself, and that is why, O my soul, you would rather smile than pour out your sorrow:
pour out in streaming tears all your sorrow over your fullness, and over all the vine’s urgent longing for the vintner and the vintner’s knife!
But if you will not weep, nor weep out your purple melancholy, then you will have to sing, O my soul! Look, I myself smile, who foretell this to you:
sing with a roaring song, until all seas grow still to listen to your longing,
until over still, longing seas the boat floats, the golden wonder, around whose gold all good, bad, wonderful things leap:
and many great and small animals too, and everything that has light, wonderful feet, so that it can run on violet-blue paths,
towards the golden wonder, the boat that comes of its own will, and towards its master: but that is the vintner, who waits with a diamond knife,
your great deliverer, O my soul, the nameless one, for whom only future songs will find names! And truly, your breath already smells of future songs;
already you glow and dream, already you drink thirstily at all deep, resounding wells of comfort, already your melancholy rests in the bliss of future songs!
O my soul, now I have given you everything, and even my last, and all my hands have become empty for you: that I bade you sing, look, that was my last!
That I bade you sing, speak now, speak: which of us now has to give thanks? But better still: sing to me, sing, O my soul! And let me give thanks!
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## The Other Dance Song
“Into your eye I looked lately, O life: I saw gold glinting in your night-eye; my heart stood still with delight:
I saw a golden boat glinting on dark waters, a sinking, drinking, again beckoning golden rocking-boat!
At my foot, mad for dancing, you threw a glance, a laughing, questioning, melting rocking-glance:
only twice you shook your rattle with your little hands, and already my foot was rocking with dance-madness.
My heels reared up, my toes listened to understand you: for the dancer carries his ear in his toes!
I leapt towards you: then you fled back from my leap; and the tongue of your fleeing, flying hair licked towards me!
I leapt away from you and from your snakes: then you stood already half turned, your eye full of longing.
With crooked glances you teach me crooked paths; on crooked paths my foot learns tricks!
I fear you near, I love you far; your fleeing lures me, your seeking stops me: I suffer, but what would I not gladly have suffered for you!
You whose coldness kindles, whose hatred seduces, whose flight binds, whose mockery moves:
who would not hate you, you great binder, entwiner, temptress, seeker, finder! Who would not love you, you innocent, impatient, wind-swift, child-eyed sinner!
Where are you pulling me now, you paragon and tomboy? And now you flee me again, you sweet wild thing and ingrate!
I dance after you, I follow you even on a faint trail. Where are you? Give me your hand! Or just one finger!
Here are caves and thickets: we shall lose our way! Stop! Stand still! Do you not see owls and bats whirring?
You owl! You bat! You want to make a fool of me? Where are we? It was from the dogs that you learned this howling and yapping.
You bare your little white teeth at me sweetly; your wicked eyes spring at me out of your curly little mane!
This is a dance over stick and stone: I am the hunter; will you be my dog or my chamois?
Now beside me! And quickly, you wicked jumper! Now up! And over! Alas! I fell myself as I jumped!
Oh, see me lying there, you high spirits, and begging for mercy! I would gladly walk lovelier paths with you!
the paths of love through quiet bright bushes! Or there along the lake: there goldfish swim and dance!
You are tired now? Over there are sheep and sunsets: is it not lovely to sleep when shepherds play the flute?
You are so terribly tired? I will carry you there; just let your arms sink! And if you are thirsty, I might have something, but your mouth will not drink it!
Oh, this cursed, nimble, supple snake and slippery witch! Where have you gone? But on my face I feel from your hand two spots and red blotches!
I am truly tired of always being your sheepish shepherd! You witch, until now I have sung to you; now you shall scream for me!
To the beat of my whip you shall dance and scream for me! I did not forget the whip, did I? No!”
Then life answered me thus, and held her delicate ears as she did so:
“O Zarathustra! Do not crack your whip so terribly! You know very well: noise murders thoughts, and just now such tender thoughts are coming to me.
We are both two real good-for-nothings and do-no-harms. Beyond good and evil we found our island and our green meadow, we two alone! So we must be good to each other!
And even if we do not love each other from the bottom of our hearts, must one bear a grudge because one does not love from the bottom of the heart?
And that I am fond of you, and often too fond, you know: and the reason is that I am jealous of your wisdom. Ah, this mad old fool of a wisdom!
If your wisdom ever ran away from you, ah! then my love would quickly run away from you too.”
Then life looked thoughtfully behind her and around her and said softly: “O Zarathustra, you are not faithful enough to me!
You do not love me nearly as much as you say; I know you are thinking of leaving me soon.
There is an old, heavy, heavy booming bell: it booms at night up to your cave:
when you hear this bell strike the hour at midnight, then between one and twelve you think of it,
you think of it, O Zarathustra, I know, that you will soon leave me!”
“Yes,” I answered hesitantly, “but you know this too...” And I said something into her ear, right in among her tangled, yellow, foolish tresses.
“You know that, O Zarathustra? No one knows that.”
And we looked at each other, and looked at the green meadow over which the cool evening was just running, and wept together. But then life was dearer to me than all my wisdom had ever been.
Thus spoke Zarathustra.

## The Song of Melancholy
When Zarathustra made these speeches, he was standing near the entrance to his cave; but with the last words he slipped away from his guests and fled into the open for a short while.
“O pure smells around me,” he cried, “O blessed stillness around me! But where are my animals? Come here, come here, my eagle and my snake!
Tell me, my animals: these higher men, all of them, do they perhaps not smell good? O pure smells around me! Only now do I know and feel how much I love you, my animals.”

And Zarathustra said again: “I love you, my animals!” But the eagle and the snake pressed close to him as he spoke these words, and looked up at him. So the three of them were together in silence, and sniffed and sipped the good air together. For the air out here was better than among the higher men.
But hardly had Zarathustra left his cave when the old sorcerer got up, looked around cunningly, and said: “He has gone out!
And already, you higher men (let me tickle you with this name of praise and flattery, as he does himself), already my wicked spirit of deceit and magic is attacking me, my melancholy devil,
who is an adversary of this Zarathustra from the very bottom: forgive him! Now he wants to work his magic before you; just now it is his hour; in vain I wrestle with this evil spirit.

To all of you, whatever honours you may give yourselves with words, whether you call yourselves ‘the free spirits’ or ‘the truthful’ or ‘the penitents of the spirit’ or ‘the unfettered’ or ‘the great longers’:
to all of you who suffer from the great disgust as I do, for whom the old god died and no new god yet lies in cradles and nappies: to all of you my evil spirit and magic devil is well disposed.
I know you, you higher men, I know him; I know this monster too, whom I love against my will, this Zarathustra: he himself often seems to me like a beautiful mask of a saint,
like a new, strange masquerade in which my evil spirit, the melancholy devil, takes pleasure: I love Zarathustra, so it often seems to me, for the sake of my evil spirit.
But already he is attacking me and forcing me, this spirit of melancholy, this devil of the evening twilight: and truly, you higher men, he has a mind to
just open your eyes! he has a mind to come naked; whether male or female I do not yet know: but he is coming, he is forcing me, alas! Open your senses!
The day is dying away; evening is coming now to all things, even the best things; hear now and see, you higher men, what devil, whether man or woman, this spirit of evening melancholy is!”
So spoke the old sorcerer, looked around cunningly, and then reached for his harp.
