## On Science

So sang the sorcerer; and all who were there together went unnoticed, like birds, into the net of his cunning and melancholy delight. Only the conscientious one of the spirit was not caught: he quickly took the harp away from the sorcerer and cried: “Air! Let good air in! Let Zarathustra in! You make this cave sultry and poisonous, you wicked old sorcerer!
You lead us astray, you false, subtle one, to unknown desires and wildernesses. And woe when such as you make a fuss and a show about truth!
Woe to all free spirits who are not on their guard against such sorcerers! It is all over with their freedom: you teach and lure back into prisons,
you old melancholy devil; out of your lament sounds a decoy whistle; you are like those who with their praise of chastity secretly invite to sensual pleasures!”

So spoke the conscientious one; but the old sorcerer looked around, enjoyed his victory, and swallowed for its sake the annoyance the conscientious one caused him. “Be quiet!” he said in a modest voice. “Good songs want to echo well; after good songs one should be silent for a long time.
That is what all these do, the higher men. But you have understood little of my song, I suppose? There is little of a magic spirit in you.”
“You praise me,” replied the conscientious one, “by separating me from yourself; well then! But you others, what do I see? You are all still sitting there with lustful eyes:
you free souls, where has your freedom gone! You are almost like, it seems to me, those who have long watched wicked naked girls dancing: your souls are dancing themselves!
In you, you higher men, there must be more of what the sorcerer calls his evil spirit of magic and deceit: we must be different.
And truly, we talked and thought together enough before Zarathustra came home to his cave for me not to know that we are different.
We seek different things up here, too, you and I. For I seek more security; that is why I came to Zarathustra. For he is still the firmest tower and will,
today, when everything is shaking, when all the earth quakes. But you, when I see the eyes you make, it almost seems to me that you seek more insecurity,
more shudders, more danger, more earthquake. You long, it almost seems to me so (forgive my presumption, you higher men),
you long for the worst, most dangerous life, which makes me most afraid, for the life of wild animals, for forests, caves, steep mountains and treacherous chasms.
And it is not those who lead you out of danger that please you most, but those who lead you away from all paths, the seducers. But if such longing in you is real, it still seems impossible to me.
For fear is man’s inherited and basic feeling; everything is explained by fear, original sin and original virtue. Out of fear my virtue too grew, and it is called: science.
For fear of wild animals was bred into man longest, including the animal he hides within himself and fears: Zarathustra calls it ‘the inner beast’.
Such long, old fear, at last grown subtle, spiritual, intellectual: today, it seems to me, it is called science.”

So spoke the conscientious one; but Zarathustra, who was just coming back into his cave and had heard and guessed the last speech, threw a handful of roses at the conscientious one and laughed at his “truths”. “What!” he cried. “What did I just hear? Truly, it seems to me you are a fool, or I am one myself: and I will turn your ‘truth’ on its head, quick as a flash.
For fear is our exception. But courage and adventure and delight in the uncertain, in what has not been dared: courage seems to me the whole prehistory of man.
He envied the wildest, most courageous animals all their virtues and robbed them of them: only so did he become man.
This courage, at last grown subtle, spiritual, intellectual, this human courage with eagle’s wings and serpent’s cleverness: that, it seems to me, is called today...”

“Zarathustra!” cried all who sat together, as if from one mouth, and they laughed a great laugh; and something rose from them like a heavy cloud. The sorcerer laughed too, and said cleverly: “Well then! He has gone, my evil spirit!
And did I not warn you against him myself, when I said that he was a deceiver, a spirit of lies and deceit?
Especially when he shows himself naked. But what can I do about his tricks! Did I create him and the world?
Well then! Let us be good again and in good spirits! And even if Zarathustra looks angry (just look at him! he has a grudge against me):
before night comes, he will learn to love and praise me again; he cannot live long without doing such foolish things.
He loves his enemies: he understands this art best of anyone I have seen. But he takes his revenge for it, on his friends!”

So spoke the old sorcerer, and the higher men applauded him: so that Zarathustra went around and shook his friends’ hands with malice and love, as one who has something to make good and to apologise for to all of them. But when he came to the door of his cave as he did so, look, he already longed again for the good air out there and for his animals, and wanted to slip out.
## Among Daughters of the Desert
“Do not go away!” said the wanderer, who called himself Zarathustra’s shadow. “Stay with us, or the old dull gloom might attack us again.
That old sorcerer has already given us the worst he has, and look, the good pious pope there has tears in his eyes and has set sail again on the sea of melancholy.
These kings may still put on a good face before us: they learned that best of all of us today! But if they had no witnesses, I bet the wicked game would start again with them too,
the wicked game of passing clouds, of damp melancholy, of overcast skies, of stolen suns, of howling autumn winds,
the wicked game of our howling and crying for help: stay with us, O Zarathustra! There is much hidden misery here that wants to speak, much evening, much cloud, much stale air!
You fed us with strong men’s food and powerful sayings: do not let the soft, womanish spirits attack us again for dessert!
You alone make the air around you strong and clear! Did I ever find such good air on earth as with you in your cave?
I have seen many lands, after all; my nose has learned to test and judge many kinds of air: but with you my nostrils taste their greatest delight!
Unless, unless... oh, forgive an old memory! Forgive me an old dessert song that I once composed among daughters of the desert:
for with them there was the same good, bright, oriental air; there I was furthest from cloudy, damp, melancholy old Europe!
Then I loved such oriental girls, and other blue kingdoms of heaven, over which no clouds and no thoughts hang.
You would not believe how nicely they sat there when they were not dancing, deep, but without thoughts, like little secrets, like riddles tied with ribbons, like dessert nuts,
bright and strange indeed! but without clouds: riddles that let themselves be guessed: for the love of such girls I composed a dessert psalm then.”

So spoke the wanderer and shadow; and before anyone answered him, he had already seized the old sorcerer’s harp, crossed his legs, and looked around calmly and wisely; but with his nostrils he slowly and questioningly drew in the air, like one tasting new, strange air in new lands. Then he began to sing with a kind of roar.

## The Awakening

After the song of the wanderer and shadow, the cave was suddenly full of noise and laughter; and since the assembled guests were all talking at once, and even the ass, with such encouragement, no longer kept quiet, a slight distaste and mockery towards his visitors came over Zarathustra, though he was glad of their cheerfulness. For it seemed to him a sign of recovery. So he slipped out into the open and spoke to his animals.
“Where has their distress gone now?” he said, and already he himself breathed more easily after his slight disgust. “With me, it seems, they have unlearned crying out in distress!
though, unfortunately, not yet crying out.” And Zarathustra held his ears, for just then the ass’s Ee-aw mingled strangely with the jubilant noise of these higher men.
“They are merry,” he began again, “and who knows? perhaps at their host’s expense; and if they have learned to laugh from me, it is still not my laughter that they have learned.
But what does it matter! They are old people: they recover in their own way, they laugh in their own way; my ears have put up with worse already, and did not grow cross.
This day is a victory: he is already giving way, he is fleeing, the spirit of gravity, my old arch-enemy! How well this day means to end, which began so badly and heavily!
And it wants to end. Already evening is coming: he rides over the sea, the good rider! How he sways, the blissful one, coming home, in his purple saddles!
The sky looks on clearly, the world lies deep: oh, all you strange ones who came to me, it is worth while living with me!”
So spoke Zarathustra. And again the shouting and laughter of the higher men came out of the cave: then he began anew.
“They are biting, my bait is working; their enemy too is giving way, the spirit of gravity. Already they are learning to laugh at themselves: do I hear right?
My men’s food is working, my sayings full of sap and strength: and truly, I did not feed them on vegetables that cause wind! But on warriors’ food, on conquerors’ food: I woke new desires.
There are new hopes in their arms and legs; their hearts are stretching. They are finding new words; soon their spirit will breathe high spirits.
Such food may not be for children, of course, nor for longing little women old and young. Their insides are persuaded differently; I am not their doctor and teacher.
Disgust is leaving these higher men: well then! that is my victory. In my kingdom they are growing safe; all stupid shame runs away; they are pouring themselves out.
They are pouring out their hearts, good hours are coming back to them, they are celebrating and chewing the cud: they are growing grateful.
That I take as the best sign: they are growing grateful. Not long now, and they will think up festivals and put up memorials to their old joys.
They are convalescents!” So Zarathustra spoke joyfully to his heart and looked out; but his animals pressed close to him and honoured his happiness and his silence.

But suddenly Zarathustra’s ear took fright: for the cave, which until then had been full of noise and laughter, all at once became deathly still; and his nose smelled a sweet-smelling smoke and incense, as of burning pine cones.

“What is happening? What are they doing?” he asked himself, and crept up to the entrance, so that he could watch his guests unnoticed. But, wonder upon wonder! what did he have to see with his own eyes!

“They have all become pious again, they are praying, they are mad!” he said, and was astonished beyond measure. And indeed! all these higher men, the two kings, the retired pope, the wicked sorcerer, the voluntary beggar, the wanderer and shadow, the old soothsayer, the conscientious one of the spirit and the ugliest man: they were all lying on their knees like children and believing old women, and worshipping the ass. And just then the ugliest man began to gurgle and snort, as if something unspeakable wanted to come out of him; but when he had really brought it to words, look, it was a pious, strange litany in praise of the worshipped and incensed ass. And this litany ran thus:
Amen! And praise and honour and wisdom and thanks and glory and strength be to our God, from everlasting to everlasting!
But the ass cried Ee-aw.
He carries our burden, he has taken the form of a servant, he is patient of heart and never says No; and whoever loves his God chastises him.
But the ass cried Ee-aw.
He does not speak: except that he always says Yes to the world he created: so he praises his world. It is his cunning that does not speak: so he is seldom in the wrong.
But the ass cried Ee-aw.
He goes through the world unnoticed. Grey is the colour of the body in which he wraps his virtue. If he has spirit, he hides it; but everyone believes in his long ears.
But the ass cried Ee-aw.
What hidden wisdom it is that he wears long ears and only ever says Yes and never No! Has he not created the world in his own image, that is, as stupid as possible?
But the ass cried Ee-aw.
You go straight ways and crooked ones; you care little what seems straight or crooked to us men. Beyond good and evil is your kingdom. It is your innocence not to know what innocence is.
But the ass cried Ee-aw.
Look how you push no one away from you, neither the beggars nor the kings. You suffer the little children to come to you, and when the wicked boys lure you, you say simply Ee-aw.
But the ass cried Ee-aw.
You love she-asses and fresh figs; you are no despiser of food. A thistle tickles your heart when you happen to be hungry. In that lies a god’s wisdom.
But the ass cried Ee-aw.
## The Ass Festival
But at this point in the litany Zarathustra could no longer control himself; he cried Ee-aw himself, louder still than the ass, and leapt into the middle of his guests, who had gone mad.
“But what are you doing there, you children of men?” he cried, pulling those who prayed up from the floor. “Woe if anyone other than Zarathustra saw you:
everyone would judge that with your new faith you were the worst blasphemers or the most foolish of all old women!
And you yourself, you old pope, how does it fit with you that you worship an ass here as God like this?”
“O Zarathustra,” answered the pope, “forgive me, but in matters of God I am even more enlightened than you. And that is only fair.
Better to worship God in this form than in no form at all! Think about this saying, my noble friend: you will quickly guess that there is wisdom in such a saying.
The one who said ‘God is a spirit’ took the biggest step and leap towards unbelief that has yet been taken on earth: such a word is not easily made good again on earth!
My old heart leaps and skips because there is still something on earth to worship. Forgive that, O Zarathustra, to an old pious pope’s heart!”
“And you,” said Zarathustra to the wanderer and shadow, “you call yourself and imagine yourself a free spirit? And you carry on such idolatry and priestcraft here?
Truly, you are behaving worse here than with your wicked brown girls, you wicked new believer!”
“Bad enough,” answered the wanderer and shadow, “you are right: but what can I do about it! The old god lives again, O Zarathustra, say what you will.
The ugliest man is to blame for it all: he has raised him up again. And if he says that he once killed him: with gods, death is always only a prejudice.”
“And you,” said Zarathustra, “you wicked old sorcerer, what have you done! Who will believe in you from now on, in this free age, if you believe in such divine asininities?
It was a stupidity, what you did; how could you, clever one, do such a stupid thing!”
“O Zarathustra,” answered the clever sorcerer, “you are right, it was a stupidity; and it has been hard enough for me too.”

“And you above all,” said Zarathustra to the conscientious one of the spirit, “consider, and put your finger to your nose! Does nothing here go against your conscience? Is your spirit not too clean for this praying and the fumes of these praying brothers?”
“There is something in it,” answered the conscientious one, and put his finger to his nose, “there is something in this spectacle that even does my conscience good.
Perhaps I may not believe in God: but it is certain that God seems most believable to me in this form.
God is said to be eternal, according to the testimony of the most pious: whoever has so much time takes his time. As slowly and as stupidly as possible: with that, such a one can get very far indeed.
And whoever has too much spirit might well fall in love with stupidity and folly itself. Think about yourself, O Zarathustra!
You yourself, truly! even you might well become an ass out of overflowing wisdom.
Does not a perfect sage like to go by the most crooked ways? The evidence shows it, O Zarathustra: your evidence!”

“And you yourself, finally,” said Zarathustra, and turned towards the ugliest man, who was still lying on the floor, raising his arm to the ass (for he was giving it wine to drink). “Speak, you unspeakable one, what have you done!
You seem transformed to me, your eye glows, the cloak of the sublime lies around your ugliness: what have you done?
Is it true, then, what they say, that you raised him up again? And what for? Was he not killed and done away with for good reason?
You yourself seem awakened to me: what have you done? What have you turned round? Why have you converted? Speak, you unspeakable one!”
“O Zarathustra,” answered the ugliest man, “you are a rogue!
Whether he still lives, or lives again, or is thoroughly dead: which of us two knows that best? I ask you.
But one thing I know; I learned it from you yourself once, O Zarathustra: whoever wants to kill most thoroughly, laughs.
‘One kills not with anger but with laughter’: so you once said. O Zarathustra, you hidden one, you destroyer without anger, you dangerous saint: you are a rogue!”
But then it happened that Zarathustra, astonished at nothing but such roguish answers, sprang back to the door of his cave and, turned towards all his guests, cried in a strong voice:
“O you buffoons, all of you, you clowns! Why do you disguise and hide yourselves from me!
How each of your hearts wriggled with delight and malice, because at last you had once again become like little children, that is, pious,
because at last you did again what children do, that is, prayed, folded your hands and said ‘dear God’!
But now leave this nursery, my own cave, where all childishness is at home today. Cool off out here your hot children’s high spirits and the noise of your hearts!
Of course: unless you become as little children, you shall not enter into that kingdom of heaven. (And Zarathustra pointed upward with his hands.)
But we do not want to enter into the kingdom of heaven at all: we have become men, so we want the kingdom of earth.”
And once more Zarathustra began to speak. “O my new friends,” he said, “you strange ones, you higher men, how well you please me now,
since you have become cheerful again! Truly, you have all blossomed: it seems to me that such flowers as you need new festivals,
a little brave nonsense, some divine service and ass festival, some old cheerful Zarathustra-fool, a roaring wind that blows your souls bright.
Do not forget this night and this ass festival, you higher men! You invented that with me; I take that as a good sign: only convalescents invent such things!
And if you celebrate it again, this ass festival, do it for love of yourselves, do it for love of me too! And in remembrance of me!”
Thus spoke Zarathustra.
## The Drunken Song

Meanwhile, however, one after another had stepped out into the open and into the cool, thoughtful night; but Zarathustra himself led the ugliest man by the hand, to show him his night-world and the great round moon and the silver waterfalls near his cave. There at last they stood still together, old people all of them, but with comforted, brave hearts, and wondering within themselves that they felt so well on earth; and the secrecy of the night came closer and closer to their hearts. And again Zarathustra thought to himself: “Oh, how well they please me now, these higher men!” But he did not say it aloud, for he respected their happiness and their silence.

But then that happened which was the most astonishing thing of that long astonishing day: the ugliest man began once more and for the last time to gurgle and snort, and when he had brought it to words, look, a question sprang round and clean out of his mouth, a good, deep, clear question, which moved the heart in the body of everyone who heard him.
“My friends, all of you,” said the ugliest man, “what do you think? For the sake of this day, I am content for the first time to have lived my whole life.
And it is not yet enough for me to bear witness to so much. It is worth while to live on earth: one day, one festival with Zarathustra has taught me to love the earth.
‘Was that life?’ I will say to death. ‘Well then! Once more!’
My friends, what do you think? Will you not, like me, say to death: Was that life? For Zarathustra’s sake, well then! Once more!”

So spoke the ugliest man; and it was not long before midnight. And what do you suppose happened then? As soon as the higher men heard his question, they all at once became aware of their transformation and recovery, and of who had given it to them: then they sprang towards Zarathustra, thanking, honouring, caressing him, kissing his hands, each in his own way: so that some laughed and some wept. But the old soothsayer danced with pleasure; and if, as some storytellers think, he was full of sweet wine then, he was certainly still fuller of sweet life, and had renounced all weariness. There are even those who tell that the ass danced then: for it was not for nothing that the ugliest man had given it wine to drink before. This may be so or otherwise; and if in truth the ass did not dance that evening, greater and stranger wonders happened then than the dancing of an ass would be. In short, as Zarathustra’s saying goes: “What does it matter!”

But Zarathustra, when this happened with the ugliest man, stood there like a drunken man: his look went dim, his tongue stammered, his feet swayed. And who could guess what thoughts ran over Zarathustra’s soul then? But clearly his spirit drew back and fled ahead and was in far distances, and as it were “on a high ridge, as it is written, between two seas,

wandering between past and future as a heavy cloud.” Gradually, however, while the higher men held him in their arms, he came back a little to himself and fended off with his hands the crowd of those who honoured him and were anxious about him; but he did not speak. All at once, though, he turned his head quickly, for he seemed to hear something: then he put his finger to his lips and said: “Come!”

And at once it became still and secret all around; but from the depths the sound of a bell came slowly up. Zarathustra listened to it, as did the higher men; but then he put his finger to his lips a second time and said again: “Come! Come! It is getting near midnight!” and his voice had changed. But still he did not move from the spot: then it became still more quiet and secret, and everything listened, even the ass, and Zarathustra’s animals of honour, the eagle and the snake, and likewise Zarathustra’s cave and the great cool moon and the night itself. But Zarathustra put his hand to his lips for the third time and said:
Come! Come! Come! Let us walk now! It is the hour: let us walk into the night!
You higher men, it is getting near midnight: so I will say something into your ears, as that old bell says it into my ear,
as secretly, as terribly, as heartily as that midnight bell says it to me, which has experienced more than one man:
which counted the heartbeats of pain of your fathers already: ah! ah! how it sighs! how it laughs in its dream! the old, deep, deep midnight!
Quiet! Quiet! Things are heard now that may not be spoken aloud by day; but now, in the cool air, when all the noise of your hearts too has grown still,
now it speaks, now it is heard, now it creeps into night-time souls that are over-awake: ah! ah! how it sighs! how it laughs in its dream!
do you not hear how secretly, terribly, heartily it speaks to you, the old, deep, deep midnight? O man, take care!
Woe is me! Where has time gone? Did I not sink into deep wells? The world is asleep.
Ah! Ah! The dog howls, the moon shines. I would rather die, die, than tell you what my midnight heart is thinking now.
Now I have died already. It is gone. Spider, why do you spin around me? Do you want blood? Ah! Ah! The dew is falling, the hour is coming:
the hour when I shiver and freeze, which asks and asks and asks: “Who has heart enough for it?
who shall be master of the earth? Who will say: thus shall you run, you great and small rivers!”
the hour is drawing near: O man, you higher man, take care! This speech is for fine ears, for your ears: what does the deep midnight declare?
It carries me away, my soul is dancing. Day’s work! Day’s work! Who shall be master of the earth?
The moon is cool, the wind is silent. Ah! Ah! Did you fly high enough yet? You danced: but a leg is still not a wing.
You good dancers, now all joy is over, wine has become dregs, every cup has grown brittle, the graves stammer.
You did not fly high enough: now the graves stammer, “Redeem the dead! Why is the night so long? Does the moon not make us drunk?”
You higher men, redeem the graves, wake the corpses! Ah, what is the worm still digging? The hour is drawing near, drawing near,
the bell is booming, the heart still rattles, the woodworm is still digging, the heart’s worm. Ah! Ah! The world is deep!
Sweet lyre! Sweet lyre! I love your sound, your drunken croaking sound! From how long ago, from how far away your sound comes to me, from far away, from the ponds of love!
You old bell, you sweet lyre! Every pain has torn at your heart, father-pain, fathers’ pain, forefathers’ pain; your speech has grown ripe,
ripe like golden autumn and afternoon, like my hermit’s heart: now you speak: the world itself has grown ripe, the grape is turning brown,
now it wants to die, to die of happiness. You higher men, do you not smell it? A smell is welling up secretly,
a fragrance and smell of eternity, a rosy-blissful, brown, golden-wine smell of old happiness,
of drunken midnight-dying-happiness, which sings: the world is deep, and deeper than the day was aware!
Leave me! Leave me! I am too pure for you. Do not touch me! Has not my world just become perfect?
My skin is too pure for your hands. Leave me, you stupid, clumsy, dull day! Is not midnight brighter?
The purest shall be masters of the earth, the most unknown, the strongest, the midnight souls, who are brighter and deeper than any day.
O day, you grope for me? You feel for my happiness? Am I rich to you, lonely, a treasure pit, a chamber of gold?
O world, you want me? Am I worldly to you? Am I spiritual to you? Am I divine to you? But day and world, you are too clumsy:
have cleverer hands, reach for deeper happiness, for deeper unhappiness, reach for some god, do not reach for me:
my unhappiness, my happiness is deep, you strange day, but still I am no god, no god’s hell: deep is its woe.
God’s woe is deeper, you strange world! Reach for God’s woe, not for me! What am I! A drunken, sweet lyre,
a midnight lyre, a bell-toad that no one understands, but which must speak, before the deaf, you higher men! For you do not understand me!
Gone! Gone! O youth! O noon! O afternoon! Now evening has come, and night and midnight; the dog howls, the wind:
is the wind not a dog? It whines, it yaps, it howls. Ah! Ah! how it sighs! how it laughs, how it rattles and gasps, the midnight!
How soberly it speaks just now, this drunken poetess! Has it gone beyond its drunkenness? Has it become over-awake? Is it chewing the cud?
it is chewing over its woe, in its dream, the old deep midnight, and still more its joy. For joy, even if woe is deep: joy is deeper still than heart’s despair.
You vine! Why do you praise me? Did I not cut you? I am cruel, you bleed: what does your praise of my drunken cruelty want?
“What has become perfect, everything ripe, wants to die!” so you speak. Blessed, blessed be the vintner’s knife! But everything unripe wants to live: woe!
Woe says: “Go! Away, woe!” But everything that suffers wants to live, so that it may become ripe and joyful and longing,
longing for what is further, higher, brighter. “I want heirs,” so says everything that suffers, “I want children, I do not want myself.”
But joy does not want heirs, nor children; joy wants itself, wants eternity, wants recurrence, wants everything eternally the same.
Woe says: “Break, bleed, heart! Walk, leg! Wing, fly! Onward! Upward! Pain!” Well then! Up! O my old heart: woe says: “Go!”
You higher men, what do you think? Am I a soothsayer? A dreamer? A drunkard? An interpreter of dreams? A midnight bell?
A drop of dew? A vapour and fragrance of eternity? Do you not hear it? Do you not smell it? My world has just become perfect; midnight is also noon,
pain is also a joy, a curse is also a blessing, night is also a sun: go away, or you will learn: a wise man is also a fool.
Did you ever say Yes to a single joy? Oh, my friends, then you said Yes to all woe as well. All things are chained together, threaded together, in love,
if you ever wanted one time twice, if you ever said, “You please me, happiness! Quick! Moment!” then you wanted everything back!
everything anew, everything eternally, everything chained, threaded, in love: oh, then you loved the world,
you eternal ones, love it eternally and always: and to woe too you say: go, but come back! For all joy wants eternity!
All joy wants the eternity of all things, wants honey, wants dregs, wants drunken midnight, wants graves, wants the comfort of tears at graves, wants gilded sunset;
what does joy not want! It is thirstier, heartier, hungrier, more terrible, more secret than all woe; it wants itself, it bites into itself, the ring’s will wrestles in it;
it wants love, it wants hatred, it is over-rich, it gives, throws away, begs for someone to take it, thanks the one who takes, it would like to be hated;
so rich is joy that it thirsts for woe, for hell, for hatred, for disgrace, for the cripple, for the world: for this world, oh, you know it well!
You higher men, it is for you that it longs, joy, the unbridled, blissful one, for your woe, you failures! All eternal joy longs for failures.
For all joy wants itself, and so it wants heart’s grief too! O happiness, O pain! Oh, break, heart! You higher men, learn it: joy wants eternity,
joy wants the eternity of all things, wants deep, deep eternity!
Have you learned my song now? Have you guessed what it wants? Well then! Up! You higher men, now sing me my round!
Sing me now yourselves the song whose name is “Once More”, whose meaning is “for all eternity!” Sing, you higher men, Zarathustra’s round!

## The Sign
But in the morning after this night Zarathustra sprang up from his bed, girded his loins, and came out of his cave, glowing and strong, like a morning sun that comes out of dark mountains.
“You great star,” he said, as he had once said before, “you deep eye of happiness, what would all your happiness be, if you did not have those for whom you shine!
And if they stayed in their rooms while you were already awake and coming and giving and handing out: how your proud shame would be angry at that!
Well then! They are still asleep, these higher men, while I am awake: these are not my right companions! It is not for them that I am waiting here in my mountains.
I want to go to my work, to my day: but they do not understand what the signs of my morning are; my step is no call to wake for them.
They are still asleep in my cave; their dream is still chewing on my midnights. The ear that listens for me, the obeying ear, is lacking in their limbs.”

Zarathustra had said this to his heart when the sun rose: then he looked up questioningly, for he heard above him the sharp cry of his eagle. “Well then!” he called up. “So it pleases me and so it is fitting for me. My animals are awake, for I am awake.
My eagle is awake and honours the sun as I do. With eagle’s claws he reaches for the new light. You are my right animals; I love you.
But I still lack my right men!”

So spoke Zarathustra; but then it happened that he suddenly heard himself swarmed and fluttered around as if by countless birds; and the whirring of so many wings and the crowding round his head was so great that he closed his eyes. And truly, it fell on him like a cloud, like a cloud of arrows pouring itself out over a new enemy. But look, here it was a cloud of love, and over a new friend.

“What is happening to me?” thought Zarathustra in his astonished heart, and slowly sat down on the big stone that lay beside the entrance to his cave. But as he reached around him and above him and below him with his hands, and fended off the tender birds, look, something stranger still happened to him: for as he did so he reached, without noticing, into a thick, warm, shaggy mane; and at the same time a roar sounded in front of him, a soft, long lion’s roar.

“The sign is coming,” said Zarathustra, and his heart was changed. And in truth, when it grew light before him, a mighty yellow animal lay at his feet and pressed its head against his knees and would not leave him for love, and behaved like a dog that finds its old master again. But the doves were no less eager with their love than the lion; and each time a dove flitted across the lion’s nose, the lion shook its head and wondered and laughed at it.

To all this Zarathustra said only one thing: “My children are near, my children”; then he became quite silent. But his heart was loosened, and tears dropped from his eyes and fell on his hands. And he paid no more attention to anything, and sat there motionless, and no longer fended off the animals. Then the doves flew to and fro and settled on his shoulder and caressed his white hair and did not tire of tenderness and rejoicing. But the strong lion kept licking the tears that fell on Zarathustra’s hands, and roared and growled shyly as it did so. So these animals behaved.

All this lasted a long time, or a short time: for, properly speaking, there is no time on earth for such things. But meanwhile the higher men in Zarathustra’s cave had woken up, and were arranging themselves into a procession to go out to meet Zarathustra and offer him their morning greeting: for when they woke they had found that he was no longer among them. But when they reached the door of the cave, and the sound of their steps ran ahead of them, the lion started violently, turned away from Zarathustra all at once, and sprang, roaring wildly, at the cave; but the higher men, when they heard it roar, all cried out as if with one mouth, and fled back, and were gone in an instant.

But Zarathustra himself, dazed and strange, rose from his seat, looked around him, stood there in amazement, questioned his heart, collected himself, and was alone. “What was it I heard?” he said at last, slowly. “What has just happened to me?”

And already memory came to him, and he understood at a glance everything that had happened between yesterday and today. “Here is the stone,” he said, and stroked his beard, “on which I sat yesterday morning; and here the soothsayer came to me, and here I first heard the cry I heard just now, the great cry of distress.
O you higher men, it was your distress that that old soothsayer prophesied to me yesterday morning,
to your distress he wanted to seduce and tempt me: ‘O Zarathustra,’ he said to me, ‘I come to seduce you to your last sin.’
To my last sin?” cried Zarathustra, and laughed angrily at his own words: “What was it that was saved up for me as my last sin?”
And once more Zarathustra sank into himself, and sat down again on the big stone and thought. Suddenly he sprang up:
“Pity! Pity for the higher man!” he cried, and his face turned to bronze. “Well then! That has had its time!
My suffering and my pity: what does it matter! Am I striving for happiness? I am striving for my work!
Well then! The lion has come, my children are near, Zarathustra has grown ripe, my hour has come:
this is my morning, my day is beginning: rise now, rise, you great noon!”
Thus spoke Zarathustra, and left his cave, glowing and strong, like a morning sun that comes out of dark mountains.
